full_judgment:
Md Imman Ali j : This Civil Appeal, by leave, is directed against the judgment and order dated 14-5-2009 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 3099 of 2007 making the Rule absolute.

2. The facts of the case, in brief, are that the appellant as plaintiff filed Small Causes Suit No. 4 of 2003 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge and Small Causes Court, Sylhet Sadar, for eviction of the defendant-respondent on the averments, inter alia, that the suit premises belonged to Mina Raza Chowdhury and others under whom the defendant was a tenant at a monthly rent of Taka 500. Mina Raza Chowdhury sold the suit premises to the plaintiff by a registered kabala No. 14815/2001 dated 31-12-2001. The said fact of the sale by Mina Raza Chowdhury was duly notified to the defendant. When the plaintiff demanded rent from the defendant in the first part of January, 2002 she stated that she had paid rent in advance up to December, 2002 to the ex-landlord, Mina Raza Chowdhury. On query by the plaintiff, Mina Raza Chowdhury admitted the said fact of payment of advance rent to her and handed over to her the part of the receipt of the landlord showing receipt of rent. The plaintiff and her husband jointly decided to construct multi-storied building in the suit premises and the other 3 (three) adjacent shops which her husband purchased earlier, by demolishing the existing dilapidated shops and, accordingly, got a plan approved by Sylhet Pourashava on 10-3-2002. After approval of the plan, the plaintiff approached the defendant in the first part of the month of April, 2002 to vacate the suit premises by receiving back the advance rent paid by her. In presence of the witnesses the defendant agreed to deliver vacant possession of the suit premises in December, 2002. Thereafter, in the first part of January, 2003 when the plaintiff asked the defendant to hand over possession of the suit premises she took time on this or that plea. Subsequently, though the plaintiff requested the defendant again and again to hand over vacant possession of the suit premises, she did not hand over vacant possession of the suit premises. Since January, 2003 the defendant did not pay any rent to the plaintiff and thus she became a defaulter. The plaintiff requires the suit premises bona fide for reconstruction. As the defendant did not vacate the suit premises, the plaintiff issued a notice to her on 9-3-2003 through her Advocate under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act determining the tenancy with the expiry of 31-3-2003 asking her to deliver vacant possession of the suit premises, otherwise legal steps would be taken to evict her and also to realise the arrear rents from her. The defendant duly received the said notice yet did not vacate the suit premises, hence the plaintiff filed the suit.

3. The suit was contested by the defendant by filing written statement contending, inter alma, that she has been running a business in the suit premises in the name "Adorsha Library" under the landlord, Mina Raza Chowdhury and others. The defendant was not aware of the fact of transfer of ownership. Mina Raza Chowdhury having refused to accept rent from her, she sent the rent by money order. As the rent sent by the defendant through money order was refused by the landlord Mina Raza Chowdhury, she has been depositing the rent with the House Rent Controller in House Rent Control Case No. 11 of 2003. The suit premises is not an old one and the same is not required to be re-built. The defendant not being a tenant under the plaintiff, the suit for evicting her was not maintainable in law and as such, the same was liable to be dismissed.

4. Upon hearing the parties and considering the evidence and materials on record, the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Sylhet, by his judgment and decree dated 28-6-2007 decreed the suit. Being aggrieved by the said judgment and decree, the defendant filed Civil Revision No. 3099 of 2007 before the High Court Division and obtained Rule, which upon hearing was made absolute. Hence, the plaintiff filed civil petition for leave to appeal No. 2153 of 2009.

5. Leave was granted to consider the following submissions of the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner: "I. That in view of the admitted fact that the defendant is a monthly tenant and she has been depositing rent with the House Rent Controller in the name of the previous landlord the High Court Division erred in law in holding that the tenant acquired "a right of permanent tenancy in the suit premises under the landlord whichever he/she may be" so was not ejectable. II. That the High Court Division committed error of law in holding that the defendant had no knowledge about the transfer of the suit premises to the plaintiff* by Mina Raza Chowdhury and others, inasmuch as notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act determining the tenancy was duly served upon her besides the other evidence that immediately after purchase of the suit premises the plaintiff informed her about the fact of such purchase and asked her to pay rent. III. That the defendant did not pay any rent to the plaintiff since March of 2003 thereby she became a defaulter, therefore, she was liable to be evicted, the deposit of rent by her with the House Rent Controller in the name of previous landlord could not save her from being a defaulter, the Court of Small Causes rightly decreed the suit in finding her a defaulter, but the High Court Division failed to consider this apparent factual and legal aspect of the case and thus erred in law in dismissing the suit by the impugned judgment and order. IV. That the High Court Division totally misconceived the provision of section 18(Uma) of the Baribliara Niantran Ain, 1991 and also failed to consider clause (e) of subsection (1) of the said section of the Ain in deciding the question of bona fide requirement of the plaintiff and thus, erred in law in making the Rule absolute setting aside those of the Court of Small Causes."

6. Mr Abdul Quayum, learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant made submissions in line with the grounds upon which leave was granted. The learned Advocate further submitted that the High Court Division misconceived the law and fact and came to a wrong finding that the respondent tenant is not a defaulter. He submitted that the High Court Division did not consider that the tenant was a defaulter and as the structures are dilapidated the appellant got a plan approved from the Pourashava for reconstruction, hence the landlord has a bona fide legal necessity. The High Court Division erroneously found that reconstruction and renovation is not a bona fide necessity under the law for eviction of a monthly tenant thus committed error of law occasioning failure of justice. He lastly submitted that the High Court Division did not advert to the material findings arrived at by the trial Court yet reversed the judgment of the trial Court thus committed error of law occasioning failure of justice.

7. Mr Md Taufique Hossain, learned Advocate-on-Record appearing on behalf of the respondent made submissions in support of the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division. He submitted that the High Court Division rightly found that the plaintiff could not establish that the transfer of ownership of the case property was made with the knowledge of the defendant tenant and moreover, even after such transfer the. former landlord Mina Raza Chowdhury took advance rent for the whole year of 2002 AD and that payment was also admitted and acknowledged by the plaintiff and when Mina Raza Chowdhury refused to accept rent from the defendant she was compelled to deposit rent regularly to the rent controller and so the defendant could not be treated as defaulter and therefore, the judgment of the High Court Division is sustainable in law. He further submitted that the High Court Division rightly found that the defendant purchased the transferable tenancy right in the suit premises from the previous tenant who transferred the same to her with due acknowledgement of the landlord and so she is not an ordinary monthly ejectable tenant and she has been paying rent regularly and so cannot be evicted and, therefore, the judgment of the High Court Division is sustainable in law. The learned Advocate also submitted that the High Court Division having rightly found that the landlord on receipt of salami granted transferable tenancy right to the defendant tenant, the question of bona fide requirement is not relevant in the instant case and further renovation of a market or commercial centre cannot be treated as a bona fide requirement and for such renovation or reconstruction a permanent tenant cannot be evicted and, therefore, the judgment of the High Court Division is liable to be upheld. He also submitted that the High Court Division rightly found that the defendant acquired a right of permanent tenancy in the suit premises and she has been paying rent regularly to the Rent Controller and the owner of the suit premises can withdraw the rent deposited with the Rent Controller and the defendant is not an ordinary ejectable monthly tenant and therefore, the judgment of the High Court Division is sustainable in law. He submitted that the Small Causes Court failed to consider that the defendant is not an ordinary monthly tenant under Mina Raza Chowdhury in that the suit premises belonged to former Zaminder Dewan Talebur Raza Chowdhury which was originally leased out to one Abdur Razzak by taking salami from him who transferred his leasehold right to one Rafique Ahmed Chowdhury who transferred it to his father Chan Miah Chowdhury who again transferred it to the father of the defendant and, subsequently, the father of the defendant transferred it to him and on the occasion of each transfer the landlord, including Chan Miah Chowdhury took salami from the transferee and all such transactions were made with the acknowledgment of the landlord Mina Raza Chowdhury and hence the defendant and her predecessor are not ordinary monthly ejectable tenant but has got perpetual tenancy right and hence the present suit for ejectment is not maintainable and, as such, the High Court Division rightly reversed the judgment of the Small Causes Court. The learned Advocate submitted that from the materials on record it is seen that the transfer of ownership of the suit premises was not informed by the plaintiff to the defendant formally and even after the alleged transfer Mina Raza Chowdhury took rent for one year in advance (for the year 2002 AD) from the defendant and so the alleged transfer was made without any knowledge of the defendant and the defendant purchased the transferable monthly tenancy in the suit premises. He submitted that the High Court Division was right in holding that the defendant acquired a right of permanent tenancy in the suit premises and so there was "no scope to evict" her therefrom and the payment of rent with the House Rent Controller did not make her a monthly ejectable tenant and she cannot be termed as defaulter. The learned Judge of Small Causes Court failed to appreciate that the notice tinder section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act is invalid for not containing the actual description of the suit premises and the suit premises being vague and unspecified the judgment of the Small Causes Court is not sustainable in law which has been rightly reversed by the High Court Division. He submitted that the learned Judge of the Small Causes Court committed an error of law in not considering that the plaintiff failed to prove her case of attornment and the defendant admittedly paid rent up to December 2002 and for payment of rent for the month of January 2003 went to the house of Mina Raza Chowdhury who was found absent and accordingly sent the rent by money order on 4-2-2003 and the same was returned on 22-2-2003 and filed Rent Control Case No. 11 of 2003 on 26-2-2003 and since then is depositing the rent till today and hence, the defendant cannot be termed as defaulter and therefore, the judgment of the High Court Division reversing the decision of the Small Causes Court is sustainable in law. He lastly submitted that the learned Judge of the Small Causes Court failed to give due consideration to the fact that the defendant used to run the business of "Adarsha Library" in the suit premises for long 50 years with goodwill and as permanent tenant and in the circumstances the defendant is not an ordinary monthly ejectable tenant under the Premises Rent Control Act and therefore, the judgment of the High Court Division is sustainable in law.

8. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates appearing for the parties concerned and perused the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and other connected papers on record.

9. The Small Causes Court Suit No. 4 of 2003 was filed by the respondent herein on 11-5-2003 for eviction of the monthly tenant, appellant herein for default in payment of rent, claiming also that the property being in a dilapidated condition, she wished to construct a new multi-storied building which she needed for her own use.

10. On the other hand, the appellant denied the plaintiffs claim that the building was dilapidated or that she needed the property for her own use. The appellant denied the plaintiffs claim that she had purchased the property from the original owner and stated that she was not notified about the alleged purchase. She also denied the alleged claim of the plaintiff that she had demanded rent from her.

11. The learned Senior Assistant Judge and Judge of the Small Causes Court decreed the suit upon finding that the defendant, appellant herein, had admitted that she did not pay rent to the plaintiff. He pointed out by reference to the deposition of DW 1 that the defendant was aware of the transfer of the property to the plaintiff by the previous landlord and that she intentionally did not want to know about the transfer only to avoid recognising the plaintiff as the new landlord. The learned Judge noted that even after getting notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act she did not make payment of rent to the plaintiff. He came to a finding that the defendant is a defaulter in paying rent to the plaintiff.

12. With regard to the condition of the property the learned Judge noted that it was a tin-shed house more than 50 years old as deposed by the PWs. He noted that even DW 1 admitted that other than i suit shop all other shopping malls, complex, markets in the suit area are multi-storied buildings. The plaintiff had filed a plan for a five story building which was approved by Sylhet City Corporation in' 2002. The learned judge found the claims of plaintiff to be bona fide and accordingly decreed the suit.

13. We find from the impugned judgment that the High Court Division observed that the plaintiff could not establish that the transfer of ownership was made known to the defendant or that any formal notice had been sent. It was noted also that Mina Raza Choudhury had taken advance rent for the year 2002 but refused to accept the rent thereafter which compelled the defendant to deposit the rent to the Rent Controller. Hence, it was found that the defendant was not a defaulter. The High Court Division also found that as Salami was paid, the tenancy became a permanent one and that the defendant was not an ordinary monthly evictable tenant. It was farther noted that renovation of a market or commercial centre cannot be treated as bona fide requirement and in case of such reconstruction or renovation the permanent tenant cannot be evicted. It was held that the defendant had acquired a right of permanent tenancy in the suit premise.

14. At the outset we must note our utter surprise at the finding of the High Court Division that due to payment of salami, the tenant became non-evictable. No authority has been cited for such finding. On the other hand, we note that section 10 of the Premises Rent Control Act provides that no landlord can demand any premium, salami, security or any like payment, or advance rent in excess of one month's rental. Even if there was a specific term in the tenancy agreement to pay salami, such a term would render the agreement void under section 23 of the Contract Act, as was held in the case of Mustaque Hussain vs Md Shajahan Minh, 57 DLR (AD) 60. It was further held that, "Section 10 of the Premises Rent Control Act, 1991 makes the legal practice of payment of salami prohibited and that the tenant is entitled to refund of the salami paid by him within six months of such payment under section 14 and the landlord was liable to pay fine for receiving salami under section 3 of the said Act. The widespread and long-standing practice of voluntary payment of salami in the commercial world did not make the tenant a non-ejectable one and no interest other than the tenancy right recognised by law could be created on payment of salami so as to prevent the tenant not liable to be ejected on specific legal ground for the purpose. Under section 18 of the Premises Rent Ccutrol Act the landlord is entitled to eject a tenant as soon as a monthly tenant is a defaulter or a landlord bona fide requires the premises or for building and rebuilding purpose."

15. In the above decision, the finding of the High Court Division is palpably erroneous.

16. With regard to the notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, the High Court Division simply stated that the plaintiff could not establish that the transfer of ownership was made known to the defendant or that formal notice was sent to the defendant. Such finding is clearly in oversight of the evidence and materials on record. We find that DW1 admitted having received the notice under section 106 in. March 2003. He also admitted that the said notice mentioned the fact that the plaintiff had purchased the shop premises on 31-12-2001. This is borne out by the legal notice dated 9-3-2003, which was marked as Exhibit-6. He was also aware that, apart from the suit shop, the plaintiffs husband had purchased the other three adjacent shops.

17. It is evident that in spite of finding out that the property had been purchased by the plaintiff and admittedly having received the notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, the defendant continued to deposit rent before the Rent Controller for the benefit of the original landlord rather than for the benefit of the plaintiff who claimed in her notice to have purchased the property. We find from the records that the defendant filed the Rent Control Case No. 11 of 2003 before the Rent Controller on 26-2-2003 after the original landlord, namely Mina Raza Choudhury had refused to receive rent. Thereafter, she admittedly received the legal notice under section 106 dated 9-3-2003 wherein it was stated that the plaintiff had purchased the property, but still the defendant did not in any way approach or pay rent to the plaintiff. In this regard we may profitably refer to the decision in the case of Basiruddin Ahmed vs Dhirendra Mohan Das, 1984 BCR (AD) 297. In that case it was argued that the tenants did not make any offer of rent to the plaintiffs as they had certain bona fide doubt as to whether the latter were really entitled to receive the rent. It was observed that the tenants never came to the landlords to enquire whether they were ready to accept rent from them, and the Rent Deposit Case was filed against the previous landlord who had allegedly refused to accept rent. In the instant case we also note that admittedly the defendant did not make any enquiries as to the transfer of the property to the plaintiff nor approached the plaintiff in order to pay the rent. In the aforementioned case their Lordships held that, "deposit of rent in favour of the previous landlord became totally irrelevant as soon as that landlord ceased to have any interest in the suit premises after the transfer; deposit in her favour cannot be taken as a ground to resist ejectment when sought by the new landlord to whom no rent was paid in spite of notice of the transfer. If the tenants ad any doubt about the service of the notice through lawyer they could have enquired from the landlords themselves seeking clarification." Their Lordships went on to hold that the new landlords may not be entitled to the rent prior to the transfer, but they are certainly entitled to receive rent since the transfer and this rent not having been paid the tenants were defaulters.

18. The High Court Division held that the question of bona fide requirement was not relevant since the transferable tenancy right was granted by the landlord on receipt of salami. However, in view of our observation regarding legality/illegality of salami, such finding of the High Court Division is not tenable. Moreover, from the deposition of witnesses, it is evident that the suit property is old and requires modernisation, especially since all the adjacent properties are multi-storied. Clearly the observation of the High Court Division is not in accordance with the law.

19. In view of the above discussion, we are of the opinion that the impugned judgment is not in accordance with law and calls for interference by this Division. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed, without however any order as to costs.

The judgment and order of the High Court Division is hereby set-aside.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 15-10-2017 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition Nos.9797 and 14241 of 2016)
full_judgment:
Md Nuruzzaman, J: Delay in 173 (one hundred seventy three) days in filing of the Civil Petition For Leave To Appeal No.1494 of 2018 is hereby condoned.
2. These 2(two) Civil Appeals, by leave, have arisen out of the judgment and order dated 15-10-2017 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.9797 of 2016 heard analogously with Writ Petition No.14241 of 2016 wherein the Rule issued in Writ Petition No.9797 of 2016 was made absolute and the Rule of the Writ Petition No.14241 of 2016 was discharged.
3. Both the civil appeals are heard together as both the Writs were disposed of by a single judgment and arisen out of the same property. These appeals, therefore, are dealt with by this single judgment.
4. Facts leading, to filing of this civil appeal, in short, are that,
Rule in Writ Petition No.9797 of 2016 was issued, at the instance of one Rahela Jakir and others, who have been claiming as previous tenants of the market owned by Tangail Central Co-operative Bank Limited (writ respondent No.10) situated in Tangail. In the said Rule, inaction of the writ respondents to implement the decision passed by writ respondent No.1 under the signature of one Md Mijbah Uddin Molla, Assistant Secretary, Pratistan Shakha-2, Rural Development and Co-operative Department, Bangladesh Secretariat, Dhaka as contained in Memo No.47.023. 061.027.74. 2012(Anghsa-1)34(4) dated 4-2-2016 and recommendation and decision dated 19-7-2016 issued by the writ respondent No.5, Convener, Shop Allotment Committee, Tangail Central Co-operative Bank Ltd., was called in question.
5. In Writ Petition No.14241 of 2016, the said co-operative bank obtained Rule calling in question of the judgment dated 29-5-2016 passed by the Joint Registrar of the Divisional Office of Co-operative Societies, Dhaka as Appellate Authority (writ respondent No.3) in Appeal Case No.1 of 2016 directing to allot the shops to the previous monthly tenants of the said Co-operative Bank after fixing lowest construction cost for the same, upon referring to a decision of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.4009 of 2014.
6. The writ petitioners of Writ Petition No.9797 of 2016 and others were lessees/ tenants of the Somobay Super Market situated at Puraton Adalat Road, Tangail as owned by the said Tangail Central Co-operative Bank Ltd, writ respondent No.10 (hereinafter called "Co-operative Bank"), which is a registered cooperative society. In the course of such tenancy and business, the petitioners received a letter dated 1-12-2013, issued by the said Co-operative Bank, informing them that the management committee of the Co-operative Bank took a decision to construct "a ten-storied modem market building on the land of the said super market and, accordingly, the petitioners were requested to handover vacant possession of their shops therein within 21-12-2013. Thereafter, the Co-operative Bank management put the said super market building on auction and sold the same pursuant to an auction notice dated 19-3-2014.
7. Being aggrieved by such steps, the petitioners and some other shop-tenants challenged the said auction sale by filing Writ Petition No.4009 of 2014 in the High Court Division, whereupon, Rule was issued and ad-interim order of status-quo in respect of position and possession of the shops was passed. Later on, when the said writ petition was taken up for hearing, the Co-operative bank, by filing affidavit, stated in the High Court Division that they had already taken steps for entering into agreements with previous tenants of the said market for allocation of shop-spaces in their favour in the newly built and developed market. The High Court Division then discharged the Rule by its judgment and order dated 9-9-2014 with a direction upon the writ respondents including the said Co-operative Bank management to consider the application of the petitioners in the same terms and conditions under which the Co-operative Bank had decided to allocate shop-spaces to other previous tenants. It is contended by the petitioners that, by such order, the High Court Division directed the Co-operative Bank to allot shop-spaces of the newly built market in favour of the previous tenants at the lowest price on the basis of the construction costs of the said market considering their previous tenancy. It is stated that upon obtaining approval from the Joint Registrar of the co operative authority (writ respondent No.4) with a condition that the previous tenants of the said Super Market would be given allotment of shop-spaces on preferential basis, the Co-operative Bank management started construction of the said market with new name and style of 'Samabay Shopping Complex'. However, the dispute arose between the Co-operative Bank management and the previous tenants when the Bank management started to claim exorbitant price from the writ petitioners and other previous tenants as allotment fees for allotment of spaces of the said newly constructed building and, accordingly, vide letter dated 8-2-2015 requested the previous tenants to make payment within one month. The previous tenants as well as the management of the Co-operative Bank then approached the Deputy Commissioner of Tangail for resolving the dispute. Thereupon, joint meetings were held on 11-4-2015 and 25-4-2015, attended by the representatives of the previous tenants as well the management of the Co-operative Bank and local Member of Parliament (in short, MP). It was also decided that the previous tenants would pay Taka 14,000 per square feet for the shop-space on the ground floor and Taka 13,000 per square feet on the 1st and 2nd floor of the said newly constructed market building. However, according to the petitioners, they did not pay the said amount as because the management did not share with them the design, layout plans, estimate etc. of the said shopping complex as per the decision of the said meetings. It is further stated that, in the meantime, the management of the Co-operative Bank took forceful possession of the market by removing the petitioners and their structures and started giving allotment of shop spaces in favour of outsiders receiving high prices. In such circumstances, four previous tenants of the said market filed a dispute case before the Registrar and Director General, Department of Co-operative (respondent No.2) under section 50(1)(ga) of the Samabay Samity Ain, 2001 ("the said Ain") requesting arbitration of the dispute. Accordingly, concerned Deputy Registrar (Adjudication) of the Divisional Co-operative Office conducted arbitration and, vide order dated 8-12-2015, refused to give any decision on the ground that the writ petition No.4009 of 2014, filed by some previous tenants, was still pending in the High Court Division.
8. Being aggrieved by such Award of the arbitrator, the said tenants filed Appeal Case No.1 of 2016 under section 50(4) of the said Ain and the said Appeal was finally allowed in their favour vide judgment dated 29-5-2016 passed by the Joint Registrar, Divisional Office of the Co-operative Society (respondent No.4). By this judgment, the said Joint Registrar, by referring to the direction of the High Court Division passed in Writ Petition No. 4009 of 2014, directed the parties to allot shops to the previous monthly tenants of the Co-operative Bank after fixing lowest construction price.
9. Being aggrieved by the said judgment, the Co-operative Bank filed Writ Petition No. 14241 of 2016 in the High Court Division and obtained Rule calling in question the validity of the said judgment.
10. The further case of the petitioners in Writ Petition No.9797 of 2016 is that, since the High Court Division, in the said Writ Petition No. 4009 of 2014, by its judgment dated 9-9-2014 gave specific directions, relying on the supplementary-affidavit dated 2-9-2014 submitted by the ,management of the Co-operative Bank, upon the respondents to consider the application of the petitioners to allot shop spaces in their favour in the newly constructed building "at the lowest price on the basis of construction costs considering their previous tenancy". It was observed that a right has been accrued in favour of the petitioners to have allotment of the shops in the said building at the lowest construction price after determination of the same in due process. However, according to the petitioners, since the respondents, In particular the management of the Co-operative Bank, has not yet taken any steps to determine the minimum sale price of the said shop spaces on the basis of construction price or since the said management has not yet determined the minimum construction price of the said newly constructed building, they have illegally deviated from their own assertion made in the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.4009 of 2014 and that they have violated the terms of the order passed by the High Court Division in the said writ petition. It has become incumbent on the management of the Co-operative Bank and other respondents to allot shop spaces in the newly constructed market in favour of the petitioners and other previous tenants after determining the construction cost of the said building and then to determine the price of the shop spaces to be allotted in favour of the writ petitioners. However, according to them, since the writ respondents have failed to do so in spite of such direction of the High Court Division, direction given by the Joint Registrar, Divisional Office of Co-operative Society in Appeal Case No.1 of 2016, decision of the respondent No.1 as contained in memo dated 4-2-2016 and recommendation of the Shop Allotment Committee as contained in memo dated 19-7-2016, they should be compelled to allot the shop spaces in favour of the writ petitioners and other previous tenants in the 1st and 2nd floor of the said newly constructed market on the basis of the lowest construction price after determining the same. With these averments, the writ petitioners have obtained the aforesaid Rule in Writ Petition No.9797 of 2016. It is further stated by the writ petitioners in the Writ Petition No.9797 of 2016, that the tenure of the managing committee of the said Co-operative Bank expired long ago and, as such, the committee headed by added-respondent No.12 is now functioning illegally as the management of the said Co-operative Bank and that such position has been declared by the concerned Co-operative office in their inquiry report.
11. The Rule was, in fact, opposed by the added writ respondent No.12, who is claiming to be the president of the managing committee of the said Co-operative Bank, by filing affidavit-in-opposition and supplementary-affidavit in opposition.
12. The case of the writ respondent No.12 was that, before obtaining the copy of the judgment in Writ Petition No.4009 of 2014, the parties took initiatives to resolve the disputes between them under the supervision of the Deputy Commissioner of Tangail and local MP and, accordingly, they held several meetings. The representatives of the previous tenants of the market complex participated in those meetings. In the meetings dated 11-4-2015 and 25-4-2015, it was resolved between the parties that the ground, 1st and 2nd floor of the said building would be allotted in favour of the previous tenants/possession-holders of the shops of the said market and that the price for the shop spaces would be Taka 14,000 per square feet for the ground floor, and for 1st and 2nd floors, it would be Taka 13,000 per squire feet. It is further stated by this writ respondent that pursuant to such decisions, the management of the Co-operative Bank gave letters in favour of the previous shop owners including the writ petitioners to pay the said consideration, but they did not turn up. It is further stated that the management also published notices in the local news papers requesting the previous tenants to pay consideration money in accordance with the said decision. But it did not get any response. Accordingly, the management allotted the said shops of the ground, 1st and 2nd floors in favour of some new allottees by publication of notices in the newspapers in due process and, as such, according to this writ respondent, the writ petitioners do not have any right to get allotment of shops of the said ground, 1st and 2nd floor of the newly constructed building at this stage. Though the writ petitioners agreed in the said meetings to pay the price for the said shop spaces at the rate determined therein, they started raising disputes relying on the judgment delivered by the High Court Division in the said Writ Petition No.4009 of 2014. It is pertinent to mention here that the High Court Division heard the Writ Petition No.4009 of 2014 on 17-2-2014 and 9-9-2014 and discharged the Rule by judgment dated 9-9-2014, at the time of discharging the Rule in open Court, there was no direction in any form while discharged the Rule. The certified copy of the judgment was a—ailable on 28-12-2015. The writ petitioners, in the meantime, filed Civil suits in respect of the same disputes, and upon losing in the Civil suits, they are now taking recourse to this writ petition, in particular, when the Rule in their earlier Writ Petition No.4009 of 2014, which was filed on the same subject matter, was discharged by this Court. It is further stated by the writ respondent No.12 that since shops of the ground, 1st and 2nd floor have already been allotted in favour of the 3rd party new tenants and that the possession of the said shop spaces have also been handed over, no allotments in favour of the previous tenants can be given, practically, at this stage, in respect of the shop spaces of the ground, 1st and 2nd floor. The management of the Co-operative Bank have kept the shop spaces of the 3rd floor and 5th floor for allotment in favour of previous tenants on the basis of the rate to be determined as per the direction of this Court in this writ petition.
13. The High Court Division made the Rule absolute on 27-5-2018, issued in Writ Petition No.9797 of 2016 and discharged the Rule issued in Writ Petition No.14241 of 2016 with following directions:
"I) The Registrar and Director-General, Department of Co-operative (writ respondent No.2 in Writ Petition No.9797 of 2016) is directed to take full control of the disputes between the parties in order to resolve the same as soon as possible in light with the judgment dated 29-5-2016 (Annexure-K-2 in Writ Petition 4241 of 2016) and observation and directions as contained in judgment dated 9-9-2014 in Writ Petition No. 4009 of 2014 (Annexure-A in Writ Petition.No.9797 of 2016).
2) The said Registrar and Director General of Co-operative Directorate and the Co-operative Bank itself are directed to cancel all allotments, of shop spaces in favour of new allottees in the newly constructed market building on the ground floor, 1st floor and 2nd floor and take immediate steps to allot the said shop spaces in favour of the previous tenants on the basis of the price to be determined by the said authorities upon taking opinion as regards construction price of the said building from experts, e.g. engineers from BUET. In determining construction price of the floors of the said building, the Committee should instruct the concerned experts to take into consideration the structural design of the said building.
3) After determination of the construction price as aforesaid, the Authorities and the Co-operative Bank shall proceed to allot the 'shop spaces on the ground floor, 1st floor and 2nd floor in favour of the previous tenants on preferential basis and, at this stage, if the previous tenants failed to pay the price of the said spaces as directed by the concerned authority and the Bank, they will lose their right to have allotment of shop spaces any more on preferential basis. After such allotments in favour of the previous tenants, the authority and the Co-operative bank shall be at liberty to allot the remaining shop spaces in favour of the 3rd party interested persons upon determining the price of the said shop spaces as per market value of the same.
4) Since it is reported by the inquiry officer of the office of the Co-operative society, Dhaka Division vide inquiry report dated 27-3-2016 (Annexure-E to the Writ Petition No.9797 of 2016) that there is no valid committee at present to run the functions and affairs of the co-operative Bank, the Registrar and Director General of Co-operative is directed to constitute a committee comprising of the members of their officials and some members of the Co-operative Bank, who are not the members of the present and previous executive committee, to run the affairs of the C-operative Bank in line with the decisions to be taken from time to time by the concerned officials of the office of the Registrar and Director-General of Co-operative in order to allot shop spaces in favour of the previous tenants as aforesaid. The Registrar and Directorate shall also take effective steps to constitute a new committee through election in strict compliance with the provisions of the Co-operative Society Act, 2001 and Rules made there under within shortest possible time.
5) The Registrar and Co-operative Directorate is directed to complete the process of allotment within a period of 6 (six) months from receipt of the copy of this judgment and then to handover the management of the Bank in favour of the newly elected committee as aforesaid."
14. Against the aforesaid judgment and order, Md Kudrat-e-Elahi, President of Tangail Central Co-Operative Bank Limited, Tangail have filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 321 of 2018 and Tangail Central Co-operative Bank Ltd. represented by its President filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.322 a 2018 before this Division and obtained leave, which, gave rise to the instant civil appeals.
15. Mr Probir Neogi, the learned Senior Counsel appearing on behalf of the appellant in both the appeals has submitted that the dispute between the parties, who happened to be previous landlord and tenants, being commercial in nature, the writ petition itself was not maintainable. He has pointed out that the petitioner No.1 namely Rahela Jakir was not the previous tenant, however, she has claimed that she has purchased the Shop No.24 of the 1st floor from one Advocate Ali Imam Tapan, however, her so purchase was not regularize by the authority as per her application dated 8-4-2012, thus, she has no lucas standi to file the writ petition, so, the High Court Division was wrong in making the Rule absolute in Writ Petition No.9797 of 2016. He has further submitted that having regard to the terms of the Rules in two writ petitions, the High Court Division was wrong in passing the impugned judgment with the directions contained therein travelling beyond the scope of the Rules. He has also submitted that taking decision in the meetings held on 11-4-2015 and 25-4-2015, the writ petitioners fully complied with the directions given in the judgment dated 9-9-2014 passed in Writ Petition No.4009 of 2014. He further submits that the High Court Division was wrong in issuing direction to cancel all allotments of shop spaces in favour of new allottees in the newly constructed building when the said new allottees were not parties to the writ petitions inasmuch as it is a settled principle of law and natural justice demand that an order passed affecting rights of persons not parties to the proceeding is a nullity. He also pointed out that the High Court Division while discharged the Rule, there cannot be any direction, if any, direction is given in that case, the Rule may be disposed of, therefore, it is inherent error of the High Court Division giving direction to consider the allotment of shops.
16. Mr Mostafizur Rahman Khan, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent Nos.1 and 7 in both the Appeals and the respondent Nos.1-3 in Civil Petition No.1494 of 2018 in his submission supported the judgment and order of the High Court Division. He submits that the subject matter of the dispute between the parties in Writ Petition No.9797 of 2016 was not commercial in nature, rather, involved the implementation of executive orders taken in compliance with directions contained in the judgment and order dated 9-9-2014 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.4009 of 2014. He further submits that the directions contained in the judgment of the High Court Division are not beyond terms of the Rule, rather, consequential to and in furtherance of the judgment dated 29-5-2016 passed by the Joint Registrar; Divisional Office, Dhaka in Appeal Case No.1 of 2016 and judgment dated 9-9-2014 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.4009 of 2014. He next submits that the directions contained in the judgment of the High Court Division passed while discharging the Rule in Writ Petition No.14241 of 2016 actually are less harsher upon the appellants than the directions contained in the judgment dated 29-5-2016 passed by the Joint Registrar, Divisional Office, Dhaka in Appeal Case No.1 of 2016. He finally submits that the decisions taken in the meeting held on 11-4-2015 and 25-4-2015 cannot be regarded as representing compliance with the judgment dated 9-9-2014 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.4009 of 2014 inasmuch that as on the dates of those meetings, the signed judgment had not come down, but that the certified copy of the judgment became available only on 28-12-2015 and, as such, the instant appeals may kindly be dismissed.
17. Mr AJ Mohammad Ali, the learned Senior Counsel appearing on behalf of the petitioner in Civil Petition No.1494 of 2018 has submitted that the leave petitioner was not party to the instant Writ Petition No.9797 of 2016 and she got allotment of shop in accordance with law through process of lottery as per advertisement. There was no illegality or irregularity in that process. The petitioner had paid the possession money at demand. He submitted that having regard to the terms of the Rules issued in two writ petitions in question, the High Court Division was wrong in passing the impugned judgment with directions contained therein traveling beyond the scope of the Rules. He further submitted that Writ Petition No.9797 of 2016 has been filed to seek relief relying on a decision and recommendation of the respondents Co-operative authority by letter dated 19-7-2016 (Annexure-G) suppressing the vital fact that the said letter had been withdrawn on the same date by the same authority, and after withdrawing the said letter dated 19-7-2016, the same has no force and enforceability in the eye of law and, therefore, the High Court Division illegally making the Rule absolute referring to and relying on the same invalid and unenforceable withdrawn letter dated 19-7-2017. He next submitted that the respondents practiced fraud upon the High Court Division by obtaining Rule in Writ Petition No.9797 of 2016 suppressing the material facts of withdrawing the letter dated 19-7-2015 on the same date by the same authority and they have not come with clean hands and, therefore, even on this score, the judgment dated 15-10-2017 is liable to be set-aside. He also submitted that the High Court Division by its judgment and order dated 15-10-2017 directed to cancel the allotment of 155 shop owners who on 22-8-2015 got allotment and possession after making the payment for the shops without giving them an opportunity of being heard, which is ex-facie illegal for being violative of the principles of natural justice. He further submitted that the respondents as petitioners filed the writ petition after failing to get any redress by filing Civil Suit No.18 of 2015 and 39 of 2015 before the Senor Assistant Judge, Tangail and Joint District Judge, Tangail respectively and also after being failed to get relief in Appeal No.41 of 2015 before the District Judge, Tangail instead of filing any civil revision before the High Court Division filed writ petition is not maintainable at all. He finally submitted that Writ Petition No.9797 of 2016 involves disputed question of facts which could not be entered under writ jurisdiction and moreover, huge number of civil suits and criminal cases are pending on the same issue and, therefore, the judgment and order dated 15-10-2017 determining the question of facts directing the parties beyond the terms of the Rule is not sustainable in law, and, as such, the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division is liable to be set-aside.
18. Mr Haridas Paul, the learned Advocate-on-Record appearing on behalf of the respondent No.4 in Civil Appeal No.155 of 2018 and respondent No.1 in Civil Appeal No.156 of 2018 made submissions in support of the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division.
19. We have considered the submissions of the learned Senior Counsels and Advocate-on-Record for the respective parties. Perused the impugned judgment of the High Court Division and connected other materials on record.
20. Leave was granted to examine merit worthiness of the submissions made by the learned Senior Counsel for the appellants, as under;
"The dispute between the parties, who happened to be previous landlord and tenants, being commercial in nature, the writ petition itself was not maintainable, in terms of the Rules in two writ petitions, the High Court Division was wrong in passing the impugned judgment with the directions contained therein travelling beyond the scope of the Rules, the decisions, taking in the meetings held on 11-4-2015 and 25-4-2015, the petitioners fully complied with the directions given in the judgment dated 9-9-2014 passed in Writ Petition No.4009 of 2014, the High Court Division was wrong in issuing direction to cancel all allotments of shop spaces in favour of new allottees in the newly constructed building when the said new allottees were not parties to the writ petitions inasmuch as it is a settled principle of law and natural justice that an order passed affecting rights of persons not parties to the proceeding is a nullity."
21. Now let us evaluate the papers on record, circumstances of the cases, and decisions, whether judgments and orders of High Court Division are justified or erred in law which calls for interference by this Division.
22. Factually, the High Court Division issued direction to annul all allotments of the shop spaces in favour of new allottees in the newly constructed building. However, it is too a reality that the said new allottees were not parties to the writ petitions. As such it is a spectacular violation of the rule of natural justice embodied in the maxim audi alteram partem i.e. no one can be condemned unheard. In such a situation it is a settled cardinal principle of law and demand of natural justice that an order passed affecting rights or properties of persons not parties to the proceeding is a nullity.
23. It was held by the Supreme Court of Pakistan, the then Apex Court of this land in the case of The University of Dacca through its Vice-Chancellor and The Registrar, University of Dacca vs Zakir Ahmed reported in 16 DLR (SC) 722 that:
"This Court has already had occasion to point out in at least three cases, namely, in the cases of the Chief Commissioner, Karachi vs Mrs. Dina Sohrab Katrak, 11 DLR (SC) 113, Faridsons Limited vs Government of Pakistan 13 DLR (SC) 233, and Abdur Rahman vs Collector and Deputy Commissioner, Bahawal nagar and others 16 DLR (SC) 470, that in all proceedings by whomsoever held, whether judicial or administrative, the principles of natural justice have to be observed if the proceedings might result in consequences affecting "the person or property or other right of the parties concerned." This rule applies even though there may be no positive words in the statute or legal document whereby the power is vested to take such proceedings, for, in such cases this requirement is to be implied into it as the minimum requirement of fairness."
24. The same stand was reaffirmed by this Division in the case of Abu Hanifa (Md) vs Md Shafiul Bashar and others reported in 65 DLR (AD) 243 as such:
"It has been well established that no action should be taken against a person without giving him any opportunity of being heard. In the case of University of Dhaka vs Zakir Hossain reported in 16 DLR (SC) 722 it was held that no action should be taken against a person without giving him any opportunity of being heard."
25. As the Maxim law was violated, the order portion of the High Court Division as far as it relates the direction of cancellation of the allotments of the shop spaces allotted to the new allottees, is unwarranted and of without lawful authority.
26. The remedies given in writ jurisdiction are equitable relieves. It is a settled principle of law of equity that "He who comes into equity must come with clean hands" Equitable relief, also referred to as an equitable remedy, is a type of court-ordered relief for an aggrieved party that is used when ordinary legal remedies are considered inadequate justice for the suffering party. Clean hands doctrine is an equitable defense in which the adversarial party argues that the applicant is not entitled to obtain an equitable remedy because it is acting unethically or has acted in bad faith with respect to the subject of the complaint-that is, with "unclean hands". As such, the applicant must come with clean hands and its application may be rejected for his improper conduct.
27. In the case of Oriental Bank Ltd. vs AB Siddiq (Ludu) reported in 13 BLC (AD) 144 this Division held that:
"The remedy in the writ jurisdiction is an equitable one and to seek the same one must come with clean hands."
28. The High Court Division in its impugned judgment found that—
"Therefore, it appears that, both the parties in these writ petitions have not maintained their commitment and representations as made time-to-time before the concerned authorities including this Court...Therefore, apparently, both the parties are playing wrong games against each other and they are using the process of Courts and statutory authorities for their own interest."
29. So, from the above findings, it is vividly apparent that writ petitioners-respondents were not entitled to have any remedy in the instant writ petition as it was not maintainable, because, the writ petitioners did not to come with clean hand.
30. We observed that, nevertheless, the High Court Division directed the present appellants "to consider the application of other petitioners in view of the same terms and conditions", and, even though, the appellants not only considered in compliance of that direction, they also offered, but, writ petitioners-respondents did not turn up to comply with the direction of the Court without any basis starting further litigation, however, the respondents filed the writ petitions turning away from their own stand.
31. The old tenant respondents have been claiming the shops, as per their statements of claims, they are entitled to get the shops in ground and 1st floor with cost of construction, they are not willing to pay more cost and for having their shops in other floors which should not be decided in writ jurisdiction because such decisions are purely a commercial purpose and not only that those are matter of disputed question of facts which should be proved through evidence.
<u>32. Moreover, it is too an admitted fact that there are a number of civil suits and criminal cases are pending on the self-same issues and it is a settled principle of law that civil suit and writ proceedings cannot go together on the same issues and as per mandate of the Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh the High Court Division cannot invoke writ jurisdiction if there exists equally efficacious remedy is provided by law.</u>
<u>33. Admittedly, there exists a landlord-tenant relationship between Co-operative Bank (appellants) and their previous tenants (respondents) and the nature of the dispute is commercial. Court cannot, should not as well, play a role of a negotiator between landlord-tenant relationships in a writ jurisdiction. Hence, we observe that the writ petition itself was not maintainable, and, as such, the High Court Division was wrong in making the Rule absolute in Writ Petition No.9797 of 2016.</u>
34. The focus of the writ petitions is allotment of shops to the preceding tenants of the Co-operative Bank, but the High Court Division while making the Rule absolute made observations and issued directions relating to the validity of the managing committee of the Co-operative Bank. Considering the stipulations of the Rules issued in two writ petitions, the High Court Division was erroneous in passing the impugned judgment with the directions contained therein travelling outside the scope of the Rules.
35. It is observed that the High Court Division, in one hand, held that—
"We are also of the view that, in implementing the said decision, the Co-operative Directorate and Registrar of Co-operative Society should decide whether the Management Committee headed by respondent No.12 in Writ Petition No.9797 of 2016 is a valid Managing Committee under the law..."
36. On the other hand, the High Court Division issued direction to the effect—
"4) Since it is reported by the Enquiry Officer of the Office of the Co-operative Society of Dhaka Division vide Enquiry Report dated 27-3-2016 (Annexure-E to the Writ Petition No. 9797 of 2016), that there is no valid committee at present to run the functions and affairs of the Co-operative Bank, the Registrar and Director General of Co-operative is directed to constitute a Committee comprising of the members of their officials and some members of the Co-operative Bank, who are not the members of the present and previous executive committee to run the affairs of the Co-operative Bank in line with the decisions to be taken time to time by the concerned officials of the office of Registrar and Director General of Co-operative in order to allot shop spaces in favour of the previous tenants as aforesaid. The Registrar and Directorate shall also take effective steps to constitute new committee through election in strict compliance with the provisions of the Co-operative Society Act, 2001 and Rules made thereunder within shortest possible time."
37. These views/directions are opposite to each other. As such the very basis and scheme of the impugned judgment is very much ill-founded which cannot be sustained in law.
38. From the above discussions, we find merit on the submissions of the learned Senior Counsel for the Appellants as to that in the High Court Division's own findings regarding conduct of the respondents (writ petitioners in Writ Petition No. 9797 of 2016), they are not being with clean hand are not entitled to equitable relief of writ jurisdiction. Hence, the directions given by the High Court Division in favour of one party, the previous monthly tenants (respondents), and against the other party-Co-operative Bank (appellants) could not reasonably follow. The findings/observation and direction issued by the High Court Division regarding Managing Committee of the Co-operative Bank is totally contradictory, and based on gross misconception of law. As such the impugned judgment is liable to be struck-down.
Accordingly, both the Civil Appeals are allowed. The impugned judgment of the High Court Division is set-aside. The Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.1494 of 2018 is disposed of in the light of the judgment in Civil Appeal Nos.155 and 156 of 2018.
End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated the 21st day of May, 2003 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.2833 of 1997)
full_judgment:
Md. Abdul Wahhab Miah J. This appeal, by leave, is from the judgment and order dated the 21st day of May, 2003 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.2833 of 1997 discharging the Rule.

2. Facts giving rise to this appeal are that on 21.05.1980, respondent No.1 as the plaintiff filed Title Suit No.817 of 1980 in the Court of the then Munsif (now the Assistant Judge), 2nd Court, Jhenidah, against appellant Nos.1 and 2 and the predecessor-in-interest of respondent Nos.3-10 as the defendants for declaration of title and for recovery of khan possession Subsequently, the suit being transferred to the Court of Assistant Judge, Horinakundu, Jhenidah was re-numbered as Title Suit No.267 of 1983.

3. The case of the plaintiff was that plot No.6428 comprising an area of 26 acre land under C.S Khatian No.216 belonged to Jabeda Nessa and others. Plot No.6438 was exclusively possessed by Haran amicably, Plot No.6432 was exclusively possessed by Jabeda Nessa and Ayaton Nessa. Ayaton Nessa was the wife of Haran Biswas. Ayaton Nessa and Haran died leaving behind only son, Sabder Ali. Sabder and Jabeda transferred their shares in favour of Harej Biswas by dint of settlement 44/45 years before and dakhila was granted in favour of Harej Biswas by Jabeda and Sabder, After settlement, Harej Biswas decided that he would gift .24 acre land from Plot No.2632 to his wife in lieu of her dower, but in order to save the registration expenses. Harej Biswas transferred .24 acre land from Plot No.6432 by dint of settlement. The S.A. record was wrongly prepared in the name of Rais and Sarafat Biswas in respect of Plot No.6432, but nobody's name was recorded in Plot No.6428. Harej Biswas was childless for which he transferred the rest portion of land of Plot Nos. 6432 and 6428 to his wife -Gulejan. Harej Biswas died leaving behind wife-Gulejan Nessa. Gulejan transferred her share in favour of the plaintiff on 11.05.1979. Due to the old age of Gulejan, the plaintiff kept her in his residence. Taking the advantage of the short absence of the plaintiff, defendant No.1 took away Gulejan from his residence on 29.06.1979 over which a village Salish was held and a criminal case was instituted later on. Gulejan died on 15.03.1980. Defendant Nos.1 and 2 denied the plain-tiffs title and claimed their own title in the suit land; hence the suit.

4. Defendant Nos.1(Ka)-1(Gha) and defendant Nos.2 and 4 contested the suit by filing joint written statement contending, inter alia, that the suit was not maintainable in its present form; the suit was bad for defect of parties; it was barred by the principles of estoppel, waiver and acquiescence. Haran Biswas was in exclusive possession of suit Plot No.6428 and Ayaton Nessa was in exclusive possession of suit Plot No.6432. Gulejan got .26 acres land in Plot No.6428 by dint of settlement and erected homestead thereon. Ayaton Nessa died leaving behind her heirs, Sarafat and Sabder. The S.A. record was correctly prepared in the name of Sarafat and Sabder in respect of Plot No.6432. Sabder owned and possessed his share. Thereafter, Sabder died leaving behind his son, Raisuddin, Raisuddin sold .221/2 acre land to defendant No.2, Narayan Chandra from Plot No.4632. Sarafat transferred .22 acre land to Harejuddin in 1376 B.S. from Plot No.6432. Harejuddin transferred .221/2 acre land to defendant No.1 by a registered sale deed. Gulejan Nessa sold .26 acre land to defendant No.4 from Plot No.6428 by executing a sale deed on 30.04.1979 which was registered on 16.07.1979. After purchase, the defendant was living in the house in Plot No.6428. The plaintiff never possessed the suit land. The plaintiffs kabala was forged. The suit was liable to be dismissed with cost.

5. On conclusion of trial, the learned Assistant Judge by his judgment and decree dated. 13.01.1989 decreed the suit. Against the judgment and decree of the trial Court, defendant Nos.1(Ka-)-1(Uma) and defendant Nos.2 and 4 preferred Title Appeal No.43 of 1989 in the Court of District Judge, Jhinaidah. The learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Jhinaidah hearing the appeal by his judgment and decree dated 13.05.1997 allowed the same in part, i.e. decreed the suit in respect of Plot No. in full and in respect of Plot No.6432 in part. Against the judgment and decree of the Appellate Court, defendant nos.2 and 4 filed Civil Revision No.2833 of 1997 before the High Court Division and a learned Judge of the Singe Bench by the impugned judgment and order discharged the Rule. Against the Judgment and order of the High Court Division, the said defendants preferred Civil Petition for lave to Appeal No.1097 of 2005 and leave was granted by this Court to consider the submissions made by their learned Advocate as under:

"Mr. Nurul Amin, learned advocate, appearing on behalf of petitioners submits that Golejan executed a deed in favour of defendant No.4 on 30.04.1979 and registered on 16.07.1999 and the plaintiffs case is that Golejan executed and registered the sale deed in favour of the plaintiff on 11.05.1979, that is that execution of the defendants deeds is earlier than that of the plaintiffs deed. A document that has been registered back to the date of it's execution and the question of title in between the two contestants claiming on the basis of successive documents executed by the self same vender must be determined with reference to the title of the later on the date of execution not of registration under Section 47 and as such, the Single Judge of the High Court Division misdirected himself in holding that the defendant No. 4 did not accrue any title on the basis on deed dated 16.07.1979.

Mr. Amin further submits that admittedly the defendant No. 4 is in possession and the trial Court, the Appellate Court as well as the Revisional Court nowhere in the Judgment held that the plaintiff was in possession in plot No.6428 before dispossession. So it is clear that the plaintiff never got any possession of the suit plot No.6425 and admittedly the defendant No.4 has been possessing the suit Plot No.6428 as homestead and as such the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division committed error of law is not holding that in a case of khas possession the plaintiff must prove his possession prior to file the suit."

<u>6. Mr. Nurul Amin learned Counsel, appearing for the appellants canvassed the submissions on which leave was granted. Though on behalf of respondent No.1 Syed Mahbubar Rahman, learned Advocate-on-Record, entered appearance, did not file any concise statement. Therefore, in view of the provision of rule 3 of Order XIX of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh (Appellate Division) Rules, 1988, we did not allow him to make any submission on behalf of the plaintiff respondent.</u>

7. From the schedule to the plaint as well as the case of the plaintiff as made out in the plaint, it appears that the plaintiff claimed 45 decimals land from Plot Nos.6432 and 26 decimals land from Plot No.6428, i.e. in total 71 decimals land. The trial Court decreed the suit in full. The Appellate Court did not give full decree in respect of Plot No.6432, it gave decree to the extent of 21 decimals land on the clear finding that the plaintiff could not adduce any evidence in support of its case that Harej Mondal actually transferred 24 decimals land in favour of Gulejan Nessa in lieu of her dower. Against this finding the plaintiff did not file any revision which showed that the plaintiff accepted the finding of the Appellate Court; the High Court Division on consideration of the evidence did not find any error in the said finding of the Appellate Court and affirmed the said finding. From the leave granting order as quoted hereinbefore , it is also apparent that leave was granted in respect of the finding of the High Court Division in respect of Plot.6428 only. So we would confine ourselves as to the claim of the plaintiffs title in respect of Plot No.6428 only.

8. Mr. Nurul Amin by referring to the statements made in the plaint and also the evidence of PW 1 tried to argue that the plaintiff never made any allegation that the sale deed executed and registered by Gulejan in favour of defendant No.4 was forged and fraudulent, but the Courts below decreed the suit on the finding that the document of the defendant was forged and fraudulent. He wanted to submit that this finding of the Courts below was contrary to the evidence on record and the pleading of the plaintiff. Therefore, the impugned judgment and order could not be sustained.

<u>9. From the plaint, it appears that the plaintiff prayed for declaration of title to the suit land and for recovery of khas possession. The plaintiff claimed title to the suit land on the basis of registered sale deed executed by Gulejan in his favour on 21.05.1979. The plaintiffs further case was that after purchase of the suit land, he got possession thereof and of the two suit plots, he was using the homestead on Plot No.6428 for his own men and another plot by cultivation. In this connection, it may further be stated that initially the suit was filed for declaration of title and confirmation of possession. Subsequently, prayer was added for recovery of khas possession. Both the Courts below believed the plaintiffs case that during pendency of the suit, the defendants dispossessed him. Although both the Courts below concurrently found that the kabala of the defendant was executed much later than the kabala of the plaintiff, yet on the insistence of Mr. Nurul Amin we have gone through the evidence on record, both oral and documentary, particularly, the evidence of the DWs. The reason for such approach of us was that admittedly the deed of the plaintiff by Gulejan was registered much earlier than the deed of the defendant. There is a presumption of correctness of the judicial and official Act in view of the provision of clause (e) of section 114 of the Evidence Act. The plaintiff in his plaint as well as in his deposition categorically asserted as to his acquisition of title to the suit land by virtue of his kabala from Gulejan dated 21.05.1979 and the contesting defendant did not at all challenge the deed of the plaintiff as fraudulent. The defendant did not also deny the fact that the deed of the plaintiff was not executed and registered by Gulejan. We like to observe that though section 114(e) of the Evidence Act has given a presumption as to the official Act and in the instant case, the deed of the plaintiff was registered on 21.05.1979, the contesting defendant in order to take the benefit of section 47 of the Registration Act took the plea that his deed was executed on 30.04.1979, though was registered on 16.07.1979. Section 47 of the Registration Act reads as follows:</u>

<u>"47. Time from which registered document operates-A registered document shall operate from the time from which it would have commenced to operate if no registration thereof had been required or made, and not from the time of its registration."</u>

<u>10. In order to take the advantage of section 47 of the Registration Act, the onus was squarely upon defendant No.4 to prove that his kabala was executed on the date mentioned therein, i.e. 30.04.1979, but he (defendant No.4) failed to prove the said fact which had been concurrently found by the courts below. We have gone through the evidence of the DWs. DW1 is defendant No.4, DW2 is the elder brother of the plaintiff. He did not say anything about the execution of the kabala of the defendant. Moreover, this witness was very much enemical to the plaintiff, because he himself admitted that he went to jail when his brother filed a case against him. He further stated that litigation was going on between him and his brother. DW3 is plaintiff No.2, DW4 is one Omar Ali. None of the witnesses said anything about the execution of the kabala of the defendant as claimed by him. Therefore, the presumption of correctness of the kabala of the plaintiff was not rebutted. Moreso, both the Courts below came to the specific finding that the defendant used an old stamp to show antedate and created a fraudulent deed by showing the execution of his kabala dated 30.04.1979. The High Court Division considered the evidence and found that the findings of the Courts below were correct. Mr. Nurul Amin failed to show that the Courts below either misread or failed to consider any material evidence in coming to the finding as to the dispossession of the plaintiff from the suit land by the defendants and the kabala of defendant No.4 dated 16.07.1979.</u>

11. In view of the above, we find no merit in the appeal and accordingly, the same is dismissed.

End.
