case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated February 1, 1999 passed by the High Court Division in Transfer Suit No. 1 of 1995).
full_judgment:
Md  Ruhul Amin J: This appeal by the defendant No. 6, Capital Tower (Pvt) Ltd, by leave, is against the judgment and decree of 1st February, 1999 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Transfer Suit No.1 of 1995 decreeing the same in part. (The suit initially was registered as Title Suit No. 92 of 1993 in the 1st Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka and the same was transferred to the High Court Division on a petition of the plaintiff filed under Article 110 of the Constitution).

2. Plaintiff, a registered Co-operative Society of Shopkeepers, filed the suit seeking primarily the following reliefs:

"(ক) নালিশী জমিটুকু ১-৫ নং বিবাদীগন ৬ নং বিবাদীর আনুকুলে বরাদ্দ দেওয়াসহ লীজ দলিল সম্পাদন ও রেজিষ্ট্রি করিয়া দিয়া ৬ নং বিবাদীর বরাবর দখল প্রদান করিতে না পারে তদমর্মে এক চিরস্থায়ী নিষেধাজ্ঞার হুকুমপ্রচার করিতে ডিক্রি দিতে । আর কোন কারনে ৬ নং বিবাদীর অনুকুলে কোন লিজ নামা সম্পাদিত বা নিবন্ধিত হইয়া থাকিলে তাহা পণ্ড ঘোষণা করিয়া উত্ত লিয নামা বিনষ্ট করার নির্দেশ দেওয়ার।

(খ)বিবাদীগণ প্রতি আরজির পূর্ব নালিশা ভুমি, ৬ নং বিবাদিকে বরাদ্দ পূর্বে যে, অবস্থা পরিনত করার বিবাদীগণ পরিনত করার বিবাদীগণ প্রতিকরণীয় নিষেধাজ্ঞা প্রদত্ত হওয়ার ডিক্রি দিতে।”

3.	The said suit was decreed as follows:

"It is declared that the deed of lease in respect of the suit land and in favour of the defendant No.6, Capital Tower (Pvt) Ltd registered on 6-4-1993 is null and void".

4.	The suit was filed averring primarily that the plaintiff, Mirpur Mazar Co-operative Market Society Limited, is the owner  of three-storied super market building at 1, Darus Salam, Mirpur, Dhaka on a land about three bighas leased out by the Government to the Society by the registered deed of lease dated April 24, 1981; that the land measuring 1002 square yards stood to the east of the plaintiffs market and has been described as car park in the Master Plan of the area; that the shop owners of the market have been using the said land as car park for the last 20/25 years; that in 1978 plaintiff approached the authority seeking lease of the said land and then again in 1981; that Chief Engineer (defendant No.3) in July 1981 rejected the prayer of the plaintiff stating that the said land cannot be allotted for extension of the market since the same has been shown as car park in the master plan of the Mirpur area; that later on out of 1002 square yards 714.49 square yards have been allotted to the Capital Tower (Pvt) Ltd, defendant No.6, describing the allotted plot as institutional plot.

5.	The plaintiff in the Court of Assistant Judge obtained an order of status quo but later on same was vacated. Against that plaintiff went on appeal and the appellate Court passed an order of status quo relating to possession and as to the matter of leasing out of the lanci in favour of the defendant No.6.

6. The suit was contested by the defendant Nos. 1-5 by filing a joint written statement and also by the defendant No. 6 by filing separate written statement. It was stated by the defendant Nos. 1-5 that layout plan of the area was modified and the land leased out to the defendant No.6 has been classified as institutional plot, that the defendant No. 6 filed an application to the authority for the allotment of the land for the purpose of constructing a hospital and thereupon inquiry was held, that the Allotment, Committee considered the prayer of the defendant No. 6 and took decision to lease out the land to it. It is the definite case of defendants that the allotment made to defendant No. 6 was neither improper nor illegal and the allotment has been made upon due compliance of the law. There is only layout plan of the area.

7. It is the case of the defendant No.6, that it got itself incorporated in 1992, that one of the objects of the company is to carry on business of clinic and hospital, that it filed an application to the authority for the lease of the land in question or in the alternative another specified plot for the construction of a hospital, that the authority held inquiry and allotted the land in question measuring 741.49 square yards on March 21, 1993 and thereupon possession was delivered to the Company on April 3, 1993 and the deed of lease was registered on April 6, 1993, that some land has been left out for car park on the north of the land leased out to the plaintiff.

8. The suit, in the background of the facts as mentioned above, was tried by a Division Bench of the High Court Division and decreed in the manner as stated herein before upon observing "The allegations of the PW 1 as stated above and proved by the documentary evidence as aforesaid, we hold, are sufficient to seek the relief challenging the allotment of the suit land to the defendant No.6. Right to participate in the general sense in the allotment of the government land is not a right under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, but in the instant case plaintiff accrued a right to question the propriety of the allotment of the suit land to a third person consequent to its letter, Exhibit 5 and the defendant's reply thereto, Exhibit 5(a). But we do not mean that the plaintiff had the right to participate in the allotment of the suit land and having been denied this right plaintiff can challenge the allotment on this score. But we mean that the plaintiff can challenge the process relating to the allotment as fraudulent and illegal in view of a particular fact that plaintiff's application for getting lease of the suit land was previously not accepted, In other words, plaintiff in this suit is entitled to get a negative declaration, if the plaintiff succeeds on the basis of the evidence adduced Herein rejection of plaintiff's application for allotment has created a legal recognition enforceable against a person whose application was accepted". [Exhibit  5, is the application dated April 13, 1981 of the plaintiff seeking allotment of the land measuring 1002 square yards for expansion of the market and Exhibit 5(a) is the communication from the authority rejecting the prayer for allotment of the plaintiff since the area has been shown in the "master plan" as car park]. The High Court Division, in holding the lease deed registered in favour of the defendant No. 6 collusive and fraudulent and consequently, null and void, noticed the following matters as questionable facts and circumstances, (a) that plaintiff's prayer for lease was rejected on the ground said land was marked as car park but in allotting the said land said ground was ignored, (b) that the defendant No.6 filed the application for the lease of the land at a time when it was not registered as a company, (c) that in the certified copy of the Memorandum of the Company obtained by the plaintiff, business in clinic and hospital is absent whereas in the certified copy of the Memorandum filed by the defendant No.6 in the object clause clinic and hospital has been inserted by hand writing in clause 13 of the object and the two words were inserted in an unusual place, (d) that address of the Member of Parliament, husband of one of the Directors of the Company, and two other Directors is common although DW 2 denied initially but admitted when his attention was drawn to the telephone directory of the Member of Parliament, (e) that Minister passed order on April 29, 1992 on the application of the defendant No.6 filed on April 26, 1992 seeking allotment of the land but the Directors of the Company signed the Memorandum and the Articles of the Company on June 7, 1992(f) that from the proceedings of the Allotment Committee it is seen that resolution Nos. 1-13 relates to allotment of land in favour of the affected persons while the resolution No. 14 relates to allotment of the suit land to the defendant No.6 who is not an affected person, (g) that a land must either be a residential plot or a commercial plot but the suit plot was allotted to the defendant No.6 describing same as an institutional plot, (h) that the allotment letter was of March 21, 1993, first instalment was deposited on that very date and possession was delivered on April 3, 1993, although the suit was filed on March 23, 1993 and defendant No.6 entered appearance on March 29, 1993, and the trial Court passed order to maintain status quo on April 3, 1993 and such hot haste activities speak volumes, (i) that suit land was allotted to the defendant  No.6 at the price of Taka 48,00,000 per bigha whereas commercial plots were allotted at Taka 2,20,00,000 to Taka 2,31,00,000 per bigha. The High Court Division refused the relief sought for in the form of mandatory injunction. The High Court Division also has observed that in view of the provision of Article 144 of the Constitution public property owned by the Republic or by any instrumentality of the Republic may be generally disposed of by public auction or inviting applications or tenders which will ensure fairness in the activities of the Republic and public authorities.

9. Leave was granted to consider the submissions that the High Court Division ought to have found that the suit was not maintainable in view of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and the finding of the High Court Division regarding fraudulence is without any support of evidence or other circumstances.

10. The learned Counsel for the appellant has submitted that High Court Division was in serious error in deciding the question of maintainability of the suit upon contradictory findings and in holding that the plaintiff is entitled to negative relief although relief sought was not negative one and the decree passed is also not of the negative nature. The learned Counsel continued that there is total lack of particulars of facts to substantiate allegations of fraud and there is no specification of fraudulent act either in the plaint or in the evidence and the allegation of processing of the application for allotment of the land in undue haste and finalisation of the allotment and registration of the lease deed within short time and the matter of one of the Director's relations being a Member of Parliament may be seen as one of the factors in early processing of the application for the allotment of the land but the same itself cannot be considered as fraudulence since the same in view of the evidence of DW 1 in no way shows there has been illegality in finalising the allotment of the land and the lease thereof. The learned Counsel further submitted that there was no master plan for the area and, in fact, there was a layout plan as deposed by DW 1 and the modification thereof in no way can be said to be illegal since the authority is very much competent to modify the layout plan in the changed context of the facts and circumstances with the lapse of time and in the background of the exigencies. It has also been contended from the appellant's side that although in the pleading plaintiff did not specify the element or particulars of fraud but while deposing in the suit tried to put the elements or particulars of fraud beyond the pleading and as such, the evidence so put as to perceive claim of fraud ought not to have been taken into consideration being the evidence beyond the pleading. It has lastly been submitted by the learned Counsel that merely because application for allotment of land and finalisation of the deed lease was hurriedly done and a Member of the Parliament was the relation of one of the Directors and there has been change in the layout plan and plaintiffs application for allotting him the land in question was rejected on the ground the land was shown as car park and the allegation of low price in the background of the materials on record cannot be considered as elements of fraud and the transaction in question was collusive.

11. The learned Counsel for the respondent No. 1 has submitted that as back as in 1978 and thereafter in 1981 when the plaintiff requested the authority to lease out the land but the authority rejected the same assigning reason that the land has been marked as car park in the master plan but later on the authority in an innovative manner described the leased out land as institutional plot although same is a commercial plot price whereof very much higher and then leased out the same at a very low price to the defendant No.6 and in the background of this the High Court Division was quite correct in holding that the transaction in question was collusive one.

12. The plaintiff filed the suit questioning the manner and the mode in which public property was disposed of or, in other words, public functionaries illegally leased out the land to the defendant No.6 and because of the constitutional provision manner in which the land in question was disposed of could not be considered legal and the procedure followed was not transparent.

13. It is the contention of the respondent No. 1 that there is total absence of the business of clinic and hospital in the object clauses of the Memorandum of Company or in the alternative those things have been inserted later on by handwriting in a place totally out of the context and those show insertions have been made for ulterior purpose. The learned Counsel has also submitted that although in the lease deed the plot allotted to the defendant No. 6 has been mentioned as commercial plot but the value thereof has been fixed at a price much lower than the price of commercial plot and as such, the claim of the defendant Nos. 1-5 that the land has been allotted to the defendant No. 6 upon proper pricing as institutional plot is not correct. It has also been submitted by the learned Counsel that the purpose for which the land has been allotted to the defendant No. 6 being commercial the action of the authority in charging low price thereof assigning innovative name institutional plot was illegal. The learned Counsel lastly, upon referring  to the evidence of PW 1, has submitted that the plaintiff prayed for declaring the lease deed as void and, as such, the relief so granted cannot be said incompetent.

14. The learned Additional Attorney-General appearing for the respondent Nos. 2-7 has submitted that choice of utilisation of the land so allotted is not to be weighed in terms of money but is to be weighed in the context of social welfare or in the context of purpose for which allotment of the land has been sought for and allotment made upon considering the said purpose. The learned Additional Attorney-General also submitted that the suit in view of the provision of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act is not maintainable since the relief primarily sought in respect of the subject matter of the suit as regards which plaintiff has no legal right or character and further in view of the Explanation to section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure the suit so filed is not maintainable. The learned Additional Attorney-General continued, since the plaintiff himself prayed for lease of the land for extension of market and merely because the same has not been allotted to him, but to others, he was not competent to question the lease as of right as he could not claim lease and plaintiffs suit is not bonafide one since the same has been filed only to frustrate the purpose for which the land in question has been allotted. It has lastly been submitted that price of the land has been fixed in the context of public utility as well as the benefit that would be available to the people in general.

15. Primary contention of the appellant is suit so filed is not maintainable since plaintiff has no legal title to the land allotted to the defendant No.6 or his any kind of legal character has any way been denied by the action of the defendant Nos. 1-6, or because of allotment made to the defendant No.6.

16. It is seen from the pleading of the plaintiff as well as from his evidence that in refusing his prayer for lease it was communicated to him the land in suit, as shown in master plan, is car park but later on the defendant Nos. 1-5 without compliance of the law by changing the master plan has carved out a plot from the car park and upon describing the same as institutional plot allotted the same to the defendant No. 6 although there can only be two kinds of plots, either commercial plot or residential plot. It may be mentioned in fact as seen from the evidence of DW 1 there was no master plan for the area where the land is but there was a layout plan and upon modifying the same a plot was carved out and the same has been allotted to the defendant No. 6 as institutional plot. The learned Counsel for the respondent No. 1 has submitted that changing of the layout plan is not permitted by law and in support thereof he has referred, to a decision reported in 53 DLR (AD) 79. The decision so relied upon by the respondent No. 1 is distinguishable in the background of the facts of the instant case. In the reported case, open space which was shown as public park was converted into residential plots and in that context in view of the provision of section 2(h) of the Town Improvement Act it was held that the said action of the authority being not an improvement as such change of the layout plan was found to be beyond the law. But in the instant case the land in question has been allotted upon keeping space to be used as car park and, as such, in our view it cannot be said by changing the layout plan there has been totally elimination of the car park. It is seen from the papers on record that plaintiff himself approached the authority for allotment of the land, which is claimed by it was shown in the 'master plan' as car park, for expansion of the market. The plaintiff in its letter dated April 30, 1981 approached the authority for allotting the land in question and some other land mentioning same as fallow land for extension of the market and in reply thereto it was mentioned by the authority that the said portion of the land has been shown in the 'master plan' as car park. It may be mentioned that in the letter dated 29-7-1981 (Exhibit 5(a)) mentioning of 'master plan' was totally incorrect, since there was only a layout plan of the said area of the land in question. While steps were being taken for allotment of the land to the defendant No.6 then the plaintiff addressed a letter on August 4, 1992 to the Chief Engineer, Housing and Settlement Directorate stating in case the land is allotted to defendant No. 6 that will be prejudicial to the market and that would also deprive the people from holding meeting frequently and thereupon prayed for not to allot the land to anybody. So, it is seen that plaintiff has no interest of his own in the land in suit except that in case the land is allotted to anybody that would be prejudicial to him in carrying on business or to others in holding meeting. The relief as was sought in the suit, as quoted hereinabove, in no way be considered relief in the negative form and the relief granted by the High Court Division in decreeing the suit in part, as stated above, is also not a one in the negative form. In that view of the matter the decree passed by the High Court Division upon observing that plaintiff in the facts and circumstances of the case is entitled to a decree in the negative form is erroneous.

<u>17. As to the maintainability of the suit in spite of not being one covered by the provision of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act the learned Counsel for the respondent No. 1 has referred to the decisions reported in ILR 22 Madras 270, AIR 1925 PC 36, AIR 1979 SC 114, (1911) 1 KB 410, (1953) 2 QB 18, AIR 1975 SC 1810, 9 PLR (Dhaka Series) 477 and 8 BLC (AD) 111. The principle enunciated in the aforesaid cases that outside the scope of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act declaration can be sought for, in our opinion, can hardly be disputed, but the fact remains that the relief so sought for by the plaintiff is at all available to him while he has no legal interest in the subject matter of the suit.</u>

18. The question of maintainability of the suit has been decided by the High Court Division primarily taking the view as the plaintiff filed the suit questioning propriety of the process of allotment as fraudulent and illegal since his application was earlier rejected and, as such, in the facts and circumstances of the case he is entitled to get negative declaration.

19. The High Court Division was of the view that plaintiff was competent to seek the relief challenging the allotment of the suit land to the defendant No.6, since his prayer for allotment was refused on the ground said land was kept reserved for car park. But at the same time High Court Division has observed plaintiff has no right to "participate in the allotment of the suit land" and as because his prayer for allotment has been denied for that he has no right to challenge the allotment 'on this score' and in the next has observed plaintiff can challenge the process of allotment on the ground of fraud and illegality since his application for granting lease was not previously accepted.

20. Factors that have been made basis by the High Court Division in holding the lease deed collusive and fraudulent are based on hypotheses, assumptions and presumptions as well as nonnoticing of the facts making the assumptions and presumptions unsustainable in that High Court Division failed to notice that after allotment of the suit land there is still space for car park, that the words 'hospital and clinic are very much in the official copy of the Memorandum preserved in the Office of the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies and the place wherein these words have been written cannot be said to be out of the context, that sameness of address of some of the Directors is no ground to assume fraud in any respect, that there is no logic in taking exception to the matter of sameness of the address of some of the Directors and a Member of the Parliament and to the period in which lease matter was finalised and the lease deed was registered, which High Court Division has considered 'hot haste' and to the proceeding of Allotment Committee as well as to the price of the land allotted since materials have been placed from the appellant's side showing at the relevant period price of the institutional plots was same at which appellant's land was valued and finally to the classification of the land allotted since there are materials to show some other plots in the area in question have been classified as institutional plots and the same have been allotted to the different persons.

21. There is also no basis for the High Court Division in taking exception to the mode of allotment to the appellant since from the materials on record it is seen institutional plot is allotted on the application of the Institution or Organisation and no other mode for allotment of institutional plot has been established by the respondent No.1.

22. The plaintiff is in no way affected because of readjusting of the layout plan. By the modification of the layout plan car park has totally not been vanished but only size of the car park has been reduced.

23. It has also been submitted by the learned Counsel for the respondent No. 1 that the way the land has been allotted to the appellant is not transparent or, in other words, the defendant No.6 has unjustly been favoured by allotting the land in question and said action of the authority being tainted with unfairness and as has been exercised in violation of the provision as in Article 144 of the Constitution is not sustainable in law. In support of the aforesaid submission the learned Counsel has referred to the decisions reported in 39 DLR (AD) 85. 54 DLR (AD) 88, AIR 1979 SC 1628, AIR 1980 SC 1992, AIR 1985 SC 1147, AIR 1988 SC 157 and AIR (1996) 6 SCC 530. The principle of law enunciated in the aforesaid cases as to how the state power is to be exercised in dealing with state property, awarding contract, selecting the recipients for its largesse, granting largesse, selling or leasing out its property, giving jobs, entering into contract, to obtain best available price for the public properties, ensuring fairness in the activities of the State and to ensure transparency in the exercise of the State power, are now established principles and there is hardly any occasion for taking a different view as to the principle laid down in the cases referred to above.

24. Now the question is in case of the act to which the respondent No. 1 has taken exception and has filed the suit seeking the relief as mentioned hereinabove, there has been lack of transparency in the action of the authority or the defendant No.6 has unjustly been favoured in allotting the land and in fixing the price of the land.

25. The submissions of the learned Counsel for the respondent No. 1 as to the price of the plot in question has been made considering the same as commercial plot and that description of the plot so allotted to the defendant No. 6 was an innovative one for the purpose of fixing the value at a lower price. The land so allotted has been described as an institutional plot. It is seen from the materials on record, particularly from the lease deed of the defendant No.6, the plot in question is not the one of the kind as contended by the respondent No.1 but the plot so allotted to the defendant No. 6 is institutional plot No. 5 at 1 Darns Salam Mazar Road, Mirpur. So, it is evident therefrom that the authority prior to allotting the institutional plot to the defendant No.6 allotted similar kind of plots to some others and even in the year 2001 the authority has allotted institutional plot in the same area to some other organisation. So, the contention of the respondent No. 1 that the plot in question in spite of being commercial plot has been allotted to the defendant No. 6 by giving innovative name institutional plot is not correct, rather contrary to the materials on record.

26. The learned Counsel for the respondent No. 1 has submitted that in the lease deed the plot in question has been described as commercial plot. This contention of the learned Counsel is also not correct. Since from the schedule of the lease deed it is seen that the plot so allotted to the defendant No. 6 has been described as institutional plot. The other contention of the respondent No. 1 is that the land has been allotted to the defendant No.6 at the low price or at a discount price or at a price much below the available price is also not correct, since from the appellant's side it has been submitted that period between December 1992 and April 1993 price of per bigha of the institutional land has been priced at Taka 16,00,000. The land that has been allotted to the defendant No. 6 has also been priced at Taka 16,00,000 per bigha. This assertion of the appellant has not been dislodged from the side of the respondent No.1. This being the factual position it cannot be said that the land in question has been allotted to the defendant No.6 without obtaining the best price available at the relevant time.

27. In repelling the contention of the learned Additional Attorney-General as to the maintainability of the suit in view of the provision of section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure the learned Counsel for the respondent No. 1 has referred to the decisions reported in PLD 1965 SC 671 and AIR 1958 MP 393 and thereupon has submitted that since the matter that has been brought before the Court by the respondent No. 1 for adjudication is undoubtedly a matter of civil nature the same can very much be decided by the civil Court. In our view that the matter that has been raised by the respondent No. 1 for adjudication being matter of civil nature is very much adjudicable by the civil Court, but the fact remains at all the suit framed is maintainable and we have already found the suit so framed is not maintainable as such the question of adjudication or non-adjudication of the matter in the civil Court is not material for the disposal of the appeal.

<u>28. The facts and circumstances upon noting which the High Court Division held the lease in question as collusive and fraudulent in our view in the background of the facts and circumstances noticed by us, is not legally sustainable. The mere fact that decision on the application for allotment of the land and the registration of the lease deed were taken at a short span of time can in no way be considered as an element of collusion and fraud since it is seen from the materials on record that the plot allotted to the defendant No.6 has been made upon observing the procedure relating to the allotment of the land followed by the respondent Nos. 1-5 and the land has been allotted upon pricing the same correctly. The other exception that has been taken by the High Court Division that the land allotted to the defendant No.6 ought to have been disposed of by public auction or inviting application or tender appears in view of the materials on record is not well founded since the land of institutional plot is being allotted on the application of the person seeking allotment. In the instant case it is seen that the application of the defendant No.6 was inquired into and thereupon decision for the allotment of the plot in question was taken in a meeting of the Allotment Committee and the same has been leased out to the defendant No. 6 upon pricing properly. In that view of the matter we find there is no lack of transparency in allotting the land to the defendant No.6. It has been contended from the side of the respondent No. 1 that the lease deed was made in violation of the order of status quo which was passed in presence of defendant No.6. It is seen from the materials on record that order of status quo was passed on April 4, 1993 and that deed of lease was registered on April 6, 1993, but for this the document so registered would not become invalid although defendants thereby exposed themselves to legal action. The aforesaid action of defendant Nos. 1-6 is no doubt deprecable but for that the document cannot be declared void or illegal or that fraudulent or collusive as otherwise we have found that the land in question has been allotted to the defendant No. 6 upon due compliance of the procedure for allotment of the land of the kind and at the price, as has been charged, prevalent at the relevant time in respect of the similar kind of land of the institutional plot. It has also been contended by the respondent No. 1 that the application for allotment of the land was submitted by the defendant No. 6 at a time when it was not incorporated. It is seen from the materials on record that application for allotment was submitted on April 26, 1992 and the lease deed was registered on April 6, 1993 and the Company, the defendant No. 6, was incorporated on July 4, 1992. There is no bar in law for a Company which is going to be registered to act in its name or on its behalf prior to registration and that upon registration act or acts so done prior to the registration if ratified by the Company then the act or acts so done prior to the incorporation became the act of the Company or, in other words, act or acts done prior to the incorporation upon ratification by the Company subsequent to its incorporation is always deemed to be the act of the Company or that the acts done prior to incorporation upon ratification of the Company considered to have been done by the Company. In that view of the matter even if the application for allotment of the land in question was made prior to the incorporation of the Company, there is no occasion to take exception to the application so made and, as such, the allotment made on the basis of the application so filed on April 26, 1992 cannot be said or considered as not legal.</u>

29. In view of the discussions made hereinabove we are of the view that the decree passed by the High Court Division is not sustainable in law.

30. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed. The judgment and order of the High Court Division dated February 1, 1999 in Transfer Suit No. 1 of 1995 (previously numbered as Title Suit No. 92 of 1993 of the 1st Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka) is set aside and the suit is dismissed.

There is no order as to costs.

End.

 Dr Naim Ahmed, Advocate ----- For Respondent No.9

full_judgment:
Syed Mahmud Hossain J: In this application under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, a Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why (i) letter of allotment dated 18-7-1993 issued by respondent No.2 allotting petitioner's land by number as industrial plot No, 30 appertaining to CS Plot No.177 of Begunbari Mouza, Tejgaon, Dhaka (ii) the Lease Deed No. 4511 dated 9-10- 2002 (Annexure-L), (iii) letter dated 26-5-2003 (Annexure-N) issued by the office of respondent No.2 directing to hand over possession of the case land and (iv) the threatened dispossession of the petitioner by the respondent Nos. 1-8 from petitioner's land should not be directed to have been issued and made without lawful authority, and as unconstitutional and violative of the petitioner's fundamental rights guaranteed by Articles 27, 31, 40 and 42 of the Constitution and why the respondents should not be directed not to interfere with the peaceful possession of the petitioner in the case land, and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The facts leading to the issuance of the Rule, in brief, are: The petitioner is a limited company incorporated under the Companies Act. Mrs. Madlena D Rozario (since deceased), wife of Ketu Rozario purchased the land appertaining to CS Plot No. 177 of mouza Begunbari, PS Tejgaon, Dhaka measuring an area of 1.25 acres of land from the CS recorded owners by a registered deed of sale dated 12-6-1950. The name of Mrs. Rozario was duly recorded both in SA and RS khatiansin respect of that land. The Government by an order dated 3-3-1952 requisitioned the land under section 30f the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 (hereinafter referred to as the Act) and included the same in LA Case No. 16 of 1959-60 for the purpose of cutting earth for the Railway Department. The land was subsequently de-requisitioned, released and restored to Mrs Madlena D Rozario by issuing a notice under Rule 10(2) of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Rules, 1948 issued under the joint signatures of the Additional Land Acquisition Collector, Dhaka and the Additional District Magistrate, Dhaka Despite the release and restoration of possession of the land to the original owner, the same was included in the list of enemy property in the Tejgaon Police Station VP Case No. 566 of 1968 at the behest of certain interested quarters. For proper utilisation and management including power to sell off the land, Mrs. Rozario executed and registered a general power of attorney in favour of her son, Jacob Rozario and one Edward Purification on 14-1-1986. The attorneys of the original owner entered into a contract with Md Saifur Rahman Khan on 14-1-1986 to sell 0.18 acre of land and delivered possession thereof to him. Since the attorneys refused to execute and register the deed of sale, Md Saifur Rahman Khan instituted a suit for specific performance of contract being Title Suit No. 84 of 1988 in the 2nd Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka. The suit was decreed by judgment and decree dated 15-8-1988 (Annexure-E). During pendency of the suit, the then Martial Law Government issued Martial Law Order (MLO) No. 128 dated 13-5-1986 which was published in the official Gazette on 20-5-1986 cancelling all previous letters, orders as if they had never been issued in respect of the lands acquired by erstwhile Government of East Pakistan under LA Case No. 66 of 1957-1958. LA Case No. 16/1959-1960 was also included in the schedule to that MLO for the construction of Dhaka Tongi Diversion Road. By the MLO all the previous letters, orders and instruments were cancelled and re-vested the properties described in the schedule of the MLO to the Government. The legal heirs of Mrs Rozario in compliance with the decree executed a deed of sale dated 30-9-1989 in favour of the petitioner's vendor, Md Saifur Rahman Khan. Thereafter, the attorneys of the original owner also executed a deed of exchange and transferred more land in favour of the petitioner's vendor. In this way the petitioner's vendor became owner of 0.19 acre of land appertaining to CS Plot No. 177 of Begunbari Mouza, Tejgaon, Dhaka. Since the land was released in favour of Mrs. Rozario, she made a series of applications to the different authorities including the vested property authority for release and restoration of the disputed land. Accordingly, the land was released from the list of vested property and ultimately, it was restored to the original owner. Respondent No.6, the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka filed a suit being Title Suit No. 28 of 1992 in the 3rd Court of Additional Assistant Judge, Dhaka seeking declaration that the decree dated 15-8-1988 (Annexure-E) passed in Title Suit No. 84 of 1988 and the deed of exchange dated 3-6-1989 were illegal and inoperative, and also sought for recovery of khas possession. The plaint of the suit was rejected on a contested hearing by judgment and order dated 16-5-1996 against which the Government did not prefer any appeal. Respondent No.2 issued letter dated 18-7-1993 and allotted 5 kathas of land which is the petitioner's land treating the same as industrial plot No. 30 in favour of respondent No.8, Habib Hotel International Limited but did not hand over possession thereof. The petitioner purchased 5 kathas of land from Md Saifur Rahman Khan on payment of valuable consideration and got registration of the deed of sale bearing No. 1752 dated 2-5-1996. The name of the petitioner was mutated in respect of that 5 kathas of land in Miscellaneous Case No. 144 of 1998 dated 6-10-1998. The Government recently carried out a survey in which the name of the petitioner was duly recorded. After a long lapse of 10 years of allotment, respondent No.2 executed and registered a deed of lease dated 9-10-2002 in favour of respondent No.8 but could not deliver possession thereof. When the respondents threatened to dispossess the petitioner from his purchased land, he filed a suit being Title Suit No. 189 of 2003 in the 2nd Court of the Assistant Judge, Dhaka for permanent injunction. On an application filed by the petitioner, the trial Court passed an ad-interim order directing the parties to maintain status quo which was made absolute on 21-6-2003. On an appeal by the respondents, the order of status quo was stayed on 28-6-2003. in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 175 of 2003 respondent No. 2 issued a letter dated 26-5-2003 directing the Executive Engineer, Public Works Division 3, Segunbagicha, Dhaka to arrange for handing over possession of the disputed land to respondent No.8. The respondents unilaterally obtained an order on 3-6-2003 setting aside the mutation and deleting the petitioner's name from the record of right. When it came to the knowledge of the petitioner, it filed an appeal being Miscellaneous Appeal No. 65 of 2003 before the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Dhaka and obtained an order of stay on 22-6-2003.

3. Being aggrieved by the impugned Annexure, the petitioner served a notice demanding justice upon the respondents. Though the notice was served upon them, no action was taken. The petitioner, thereafter, obtained the present Rule Nisi from this Court. The petitioner also filed a supplementary affidavit annexing certain documents on 3-1-2005.

4. Respondent No. 2 filed an affidavit- in-opposition controverting the material allegations made in the Writ Petition. The case of respondent No.2, in short, is that the entire land of CS Plot No. 177 of CS Khatian No. 49 along with other lands of different plots of that mouza was requisitioned by the Government by the order dated 28-9-1959 and 25-2-1960 under section 3 of the Act and those lands continued to be subject matter of requisition. Subsequently, the requisitioned lands were acquired by the Government and accordingly, a Gazette notification was published on 28-3-1968. Therefore, the land vested in the Government free from all encumbrances and the right, title and interest of the original owner in those lands were extinguished. By MLO 128 of 1986 acquisition of the land in question was reconfirmed. The Senior Sub-Assistant Engineer, Bangladesh Railway had no authority to write any letter dated 20-9-1986 to the Executive Engineer to de-requisition the property. The letter dated 20-9- 1986 (Annexure-H) is collusive, concocted and manufactured to grab the land of the Government. The land of CS Plot No. 177 having not been treated as vested property, the question of release of the same in pursuance of Annexure-H series does not arise.

5. Respondent No. 8 also filed an affidavit- in-opposition. The case of respondent No.8 is the same as that of respondent No.2. Respondent No. 9 also filed an affidavit-in-opposition. The case of respondent No. 9 is that the land of the disputed plot along with other lands was acquired for Railway. Therefore, it is not relevant for which purposes the land is used by the Railway Department. The Railway Department was not made a party in Title Suit No, 84 of 1988 and it was not aware of the decree passed in that suit. In MLO No. 128 of 1986, only a schedule had been given to show the acquired land to be used for Tongi Diversion Road. It does not affect, curtail or extinguish the title and ownership of Bangladesh Railway over the land acquired in LA Case No. 16 of 1959-1960. The contents, prayers and outcome of Title Suit No. 28 of 1992 and Title Suit No. 84 of 1988 do not curtail, affect or extinguish the right, title or ownership of the Railway Department over the disputed land.

6. Mr TH Khan, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that by MLO No. 128 of 1986 the Government acquired 1.04 acres of land from the disputed CS Plot No. 177 and that the rest of the land of that plot remained with the original owner Mrs Madlena D Rozario and, as such, the petitioner acquired valid right, title and interest in respect of 0.19 acre of land of CS Plot No. 177 on the basis of the decree passed in Title Suit No. 84 of 1988 for specific performance of contract. He further submits that for setting aside the decree passed in the suit for specific performance of contract, the Government filed Title Suit No.5 of 1983 and that the plaint of that suit was rejected. He continues that since rejection of plaint amounts to decree and since the Court found that the petitioner acquired valid title in respect of 0.19 acre of land, the Government subsequently cannot lease out any portion of that land to respondent No.8. Mr TH Khan lastly submits that so long the decree passed in Title Suit No. 5 of 1983 is in existence, the Government cannot claim any right, title and possession in respect of any land of CS Plot No. 177.

7. Mr Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed along with Mr KZ Alam, learned Advocates, appeared on behalf of respondent No.8. Mr Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed submits that after publication of the notification in the official Gazette the right, title and interest of the original owner, Mrs Madlena D. Rozario was extinguished in respect of CS Plot No. 177 and that the decree passed in the subsequent suit will not confer any title on the original owner and that the subsequent purchaser (the petitioner) will not acquire any right, title, interest or possession in the land of CS Plot No. 177. He further submits that MLO No.148 of 1986 deals with LA Case No. 66/1957-1958 and that part of the land of CS Plot No. 177 was shown in the schedule to that MLO for the purpose of showing the actual land required for Dhaka- Tongi Diversion Road and, as such, the MLO does not have any bearing on LA Case No. 16/1959-1960.

8. Mr AHM Mushfiqur Rahman, learned Assistant Attorney-General, appearing on behalf of respondent No.2, submits that since the disputed land of CS Plot No.177 was acquired on the basis of Gazette notification dated 28-3-1968, it absolutely vested in the Government free from all encumbrances and, as such, the petitioner cannot derive any title on the basis of the decree passed in the two suits.

9. Dr Naim Ahmed, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of respondent No.9, the Bangladesh Railway, submits that the property was acquired for the Railway Department and that the Railway Department being the requiring body ought to have been made a party in both the suits and that the Railway Department was not made a party in either of the suits and, as such; the requiring body is not bound by the decrees passed in those suits.

10. Admittedly, the disputed CS Plot No. 177 measuring an area of 1.25 acres of land appertaining to CS Khatian No. 49 (Annexure-R to the supplementary affidavit) belonged to Mrs. Madlena D. Rozario as evident from Annexure-Q, the deed of sale No. 2727 dated 2-6-1950. The petitioner admits that the land of the disputed plot was requisitioned in LA Case No. 16/1959-1960. The petitioner, however, "contends that the Government issued a notice (Annexure-C) under Rule 2) of the (Emergency), Requisition of Property Rules, 1948 for release and restoration of the requisitioned property. According to the petitioner, possession of that property was delivered to the original owner on 18-1-1960. A perusal of Annexure-C reveals that on 3-3-1952 the land of the disputed plot No. 177 was requisitioned on 3-3-1952, which the petitioner also admits in its Writ Petition. It is not comprehensible how the disputed property could be requisitioned when the LA. Case itself was started in 1959-1960. Annexure C also does not contain any date of issue of notice and as such, the very genuineness of Annexure-C is doubtful. Annexure-B, the official gazette dated 28-3-1968 filed with the affidavit-in-reply of the affidavit-in-opposition of respondent No.2, reveals that the entire land of CS Plot No. 177 along with the lands of other plots was acquired. The relevant portion of the Gazette notification is quoted below:

Dacca-No. DA-36/68/359-Reqn- 15th March 1968 Whereas by orders, dated the 28th September 1959 and 25th February ,1960, the properties described in the schedule below were requisitioned under section 3 of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 (East Bengal Act XIII of 1948);

And whereas the said properties continue to be subject to the requisition;

And whereas after considering the report made under sub-section (5) of section 5 of the said Act, Government have decided to acquire the said properties;

Now, therefore, in exercise of the power conferred by sub-section (7) of the section 5 of the said Act, it is hereby notified that the said requisitioned properties, as described in the schedule hereunder are acquired by Government.

Schedule

1. Full of cadastral survey plot Nos. 108, 109, 110, 177 and part of cadastral survey plot Nos. 100, 105,107, 172, 173 and 174 of mouza Begunbari, jurisdiction list No.279, Police, Station Tejgaon, District-Dacca. Area, more or less, 10.59 acres"

11. After publication of the Gazette notification the title of the original owner Mrs Madlena D Rozario was extinguished once and for all in the entire CS Plot No. 177.

12. Annexure-F, the -Gazette notification dated 20-5-1986, reveals that by Martial Law Order No. 128 of 1986, letter No.8-30/ 84-32/14 dated 23-2-1985, issued by Section Officer, Ministry of Land (Administration) and Land Reforms and the subsequent orders issued by the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka pursuant thereto were cancelled in LA Case No. 66/1957-1958. In the body of the MLO there is no reference of LA Case No. 16/1959-1960 in which the land of CS Plot No. 177 was acquired but in the schedule of the MLO, LA Case No. 16/1959-1960 as well as 1.04 acres of land of Plot No. 177 was mentioned. Interestingly, by the MLO, no order passed in LA Case No; 16/1959-1960 including the Gazette notification vesting the entire land of CS Plot No. 177 in the Government was cancelled. In this regard, Mr Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed submits that in order to show the land required in Dhaka- Tongi Diversion Road, 1.04 acres of land of CS Plot No. 177 were shown and that the said MLO has no bearing on LA Case No. 16/1959-1960.

13. We find substantial force in the submission of Mr. Ahmed. We are, however, of the view that by MLO No. 128 of 1986, the title of Mrs Madlena D Rozario was, not restored in 0.29 acre of land of CS Plot No. 177 after deduction of 1.04 acres of land required for Dhaka- Tongi Diversion Road because her title vested in the Government as per the Gazette, notification dated 28-3-1968. Therefore, Annexure-F is of no avail to the petitioner, Annexure-'D' to the Writ Petition reveals that Mrs Madlena D. Rozario executed and registered a general power of attorney on 14-1-1986 in favour of Edward Purification and her son Jacob Rozario empowering them to do all acts including sale in respect of the land of entire CS Plot Nos 163 and 177 corresponding to SA Plot Nos. 286 and 310 and RS Plot Nos. 5126 and 5121 measuring 1.23 acres of land. On the date of execution of the power of attorney, the attorneys entered into a contract with Md Saifur Rahman Khan to sell 0.19 acre of land of CS Plot No. 177. Md Saifur Rahman Khan, thereafter, filed a suit for specific performance of contract being Title Suit No. 84 of 1988 which was decreed on 15-8-1988, The petitioner is relying on' both Annexures-F and D. When 1.04 acres of land of CS Plot No. 177 were taken away by MLO No. 128 of 1986 (Annexure-F), it is not comprehensible how the original owner could appoint attorneys in respect of the entire land of CS Plot No. 177 and this has not been explained by the petitioner. It is remarkable to note that the date on which the two attorneys entered into a contract with Md Saifur Rahman Khan, the original owner (Mrs Madlena D Rozario) registered the power of attorney in favour of the attorneys. Therefore, the original owner herself could enter into the contract instead of her attorneys. Before the obtaining of the decree by Md Saifur Rahman Khan in the suit for specific performance of contract in respect of 0.19 acres of land of CS Plot No. 177, the entire land of that plot vested in the Government free from all encumbrances by the Gazette notification dated 28-3-1968. As such, the petitioner by its alleged purchase from Md Saifur Rahman Khan has not acquired any title in respect of 0.19 acre of land of cs Plot No. 177 on the basis of the decree dated 15-8-1988 passed in the suit for specific performance of contract because the title of Mrs Madlena D Rozario in 'that plot was extinguished on 28-3-1968. It is, of course, true that the Government was a party in the suit for specific performance of contract and that the Government failed to contest the suit. When the original owner, Mrs Madlena D Rozario had no title in the land of CS Plot No. 177, it is immaterial whether the Government contested the suit or not.

14. Annexure 1 to the Writ Petition shows that the Government filed Title Suit No. 5 of 1993 for setting aside the decree passed in Title Suit No. 84 of 1988 for specific performance of contract. The plaint of Title Suit No. 5 of 1993 was rejected by the Court on 16-5-1996. Mr TH Khan submits that since the rejection of plaint amounts to decree, the Government is bound by the decree passed in Title Suit No. 5 of 1993. We have already found that the petitioner has not acquired any title in the disputed land by the decree passed in Title Suit No, 84 of 1988 and, as such, the decree passed in Title Suit No.5 of 1993 is of no avail to the petitioner.

15. Annexure 'H' to the Writ Petition reveals that the entire land of CS Plot No. 177 vested in the Government and that the Government decided to release the same to the original owner Mrs Madlena D Rozario. Annexure 'H2' reveals that the land of the disputed plot was released from the list of vested property. Annexure-'H (6)' reveals that the possession of the entire land of the disputed plot measuring 1.23 (1.25) acres was restored to Abdus Sobhan Miah and others, the vendees of Mrs Madlena D Rozario. It is not comprehensible how the property acquired by the Government on 28-3-1968 was declared vested and even if the property was declared vested before publication of the Gazette notification dated 2S-3-1968, the property of a Christian lady could not be declared vested. Therefore, we find that Annexure-H (series) are mere paper transaction having no legal value. Therefore, the petitioner by its alleged purchase dated 30-4-1995 has not derived any interest in the land of CS Plot No. 177.

<u>16. Mr KZ Alam, learned Advocate appearing for respondent No.8, cites the decision in the case of Director of Housing and Settlement, Segunbagicha, Ramna, Dhaka vs Abdul Majid Howlader and others, 1 LG (AD) 64 = 9 BLC (AD) 51. In the case referred to above the Appellate Division found:</u>

<u>"....the law is now settled that once a property is acquired and vests in the Government, the person, whose property has been acquired, has no right to claim for release of the property from acquisition or, in other words, to have the acquired property released in his favour."</u>

<u>The Appellate Division also found as follows:</u>

<u>"In the background of the provision of law the suit filed by the respondents and decreed by the courts below was being totally non-entertainable by the civil Court, the High Court Division was required to exercise its discretionary jurisdiction to correct the gross error of law committed by the courts below."</u>

17. In the case referred to above, the decree was under challenge but here the decrees passed in the two suits, namely, Title Suit No. 84 of 1988 and Title Suit No.5 of 1993 were not under challenge even then the principle enunciated in the case referred to above applies in the facts and circumstances of the instant case.

<u>18. In the case of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of LA & LR and others vs Commercial Trust of Bangladesh Ltd and others, 1994 BLD (AD) 72 = 46 DLR (AD) 83. It was held:</u>

<u>"the Government's choice to withdraw any property from acquisition as conferred by section 8B of the Act must be exercised before the payment of compensation and not after it. Order of such withdrawal from acquisition must be done by a Gazette notification published in the official gazette."</u>

19. In the case of Brahmanbaria Pourashava vs Secretary, Ministry of Land Reforms, Government of Bangladesh and others reported in 51 DLR (AD) 8, a similar view was taken by the Appellate Division.

<u>20. In the instant case, we find that the Gazette notification vesting the disputed land in the Government was published on 18-3-1968 which was not cancelled by MLO No. 128 of 1986 and; as such, there is no scope to return the property to the original owner or any person claiming under him.</u>

21. In the light of the above, we do not find any substance in this Rule.

22. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

The interim order passed by this Court at the time of issuance of this Rule is hereby recalled and vacated.

End.

caseno: Appeal from Original Decree No. 502 of 2001.
lawyer:
Dr Rafiqur Rahman with Hashnat Quayum, Advocates ------ For the Appellant. 
JH Afric, Advocate ------For Respondent No.7.
parties:
Sultan Mahmud Chowdhury ------ Appellant
Vs
Secretary, Ministry of Public Works and Urban Development & ors ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Abdur Rashid J : Plaintiff presented the above appeal against the decree dated 12-3-2001 passed by the Subordinate Judge and Arbitration Court at Dhaka in Title Suit No. 3 of 2000, which dismissed the suit.

2. Plaintiff instituted the suit for a decree of declaration that memo dated 12-10-94 cancelling lease and that dated 29-10-94 granting lease of the suit plot in favour of defendant No. 7 were both illegal, collusive, forged, malafide and not binding upon the plaintiff.

3. Plaint case, in short, is that he got allotment of the suit plot measuring about 412.33 square yards by a letter dated 14-5-80. On payment of the requisite fees of Taka 68,581 a deed of lease was executed and registered on 4-4-84 leasing out the suit plot for 99 years. Same date possession was delivered to the plaintiff.

4. By raising semi-pucca structures, he established a factory under the name and style 'Mahmud Metal Corporation' to make rickshaw, steel body and other iron and steel products. He obtained necessary trade licence and got his name mutated in the office of the Assistant Commissioner (Land). He paid rents and taxes. He also obtained permission from defendant No. 3 to mortgage the land in order to collect fund. He applied to the Janata Bank for land and the Bank sanctioned a loan of Taka 13,00,000. But the amount of loan was not sufficient. So, he did not withdraw any money.

5. Suddenly, he got a notice dated 11-9-93 from the office of defendant No. 4 asking him to show cause within 7 days as to why his lease would not be cancelled. Against the notice, causes was shown with defendant No.4 of 26-9-93. At the time, the plaintiff went to Ajmeer. In the objection, it was categorically stated that on the demised plot, he established a factory, which was running. In the factory, all sorts of iron products and steel body of bus, minibus, truck, scooter, van, etc were made. Then, the plaintiff received another letter dated 12-10-94 issued under the signature of defendant No.4 cancelling his lease. On 9-11-94 he unsuccessfully saw defendant No.3. He came to know that by letter dated 29-10-94 the demised land was already allotted to Md Iqbal Ahmed Bhuiyan, so-called proprietor of 'the Little Industries'.

6. Defendant Nos. 1 to 5 jointly and defendant No. 7 separately filed written statements and contested the suit.

7. Case of the defendant Nos. 1 to 5 is that in accordance with the terms of the lease, the plaintiff failed to install any industry on the suit plot and on 11-8-88 and 11-9-93 notices were issued asking him to show cause. One Arifur Rahman, on behalf of the plaintiff, informed them there was a factory running on the suit plot. But on inquiry, no industry was found. Then after giving a notice to the plaintiff, a survey was held and the surveyor submitted his report. Having found the claim of the plaintiff false, the lease was cancelled. Subsequently, the plot was allotted to defendant No. 7 who already deposited the instalments. Plaintiff had no title or interest or right in the suit plot.

8. Defendant No. 7 adopting the case of defendant Nos. 1 to 5 stated that after payment of the instalments he became the lawful owner of the suit plot. In order to deprive him, the plaintiff instituted the suit on false claim.

On the pleadings following issues were framed:

1.	Whether the suit was maintainable in the form and manner as framed;

2.	Whether the plaintiff has got any cause of action for the suit;

3.	Whether the impugned letters issued from the office of defendant No.3 and under the signature of defendant No.4 were illegal;

4.	Whether the plaintiff was entitled to a decree as prayed for and

5.	What relief the plaintiff was entitled to.

9.	In support of his case, plaintiff examined 4 witnesses while defendants examined equal number of witnesses including defendant No.7. Papers and documents adduced on behalf of the plaintiff were marked as exhibit Nos. 1 to 9 and 10 series. While those of the defendants marked exhibit 'Ka' to 'Dha'.

10. Learned Subordinate Judge by impugned judgment and decree dismissed the suit. Hence, this appeal.

11. Mr Hashnat Quayum, learned Advocate for the appellant, submitted that plaintiff proved the existence of a running factory on the suit plot which was also admitted by the evidence of the defendants, but learned Subordinate Judge dismissed the suit on the wrong view of the matter that plaintiff failed to establish an industry on the suit plot.

12. He read sections 106, 111(g) and 114(A)of the Transfer of Property Act and submitted that the lease was for establishing a printing press which could not be said to be for any manufacturing purpose. None of the notices issued by the defendant was sanctioned by law as the breach alleged was not incapable of remedy.

13. He submitted that lease was cancelled malafide because before cancellation, the board of allotment already allowed the application of defendant No.7 dated 25-2-93. The decision dated 8-4-93 was taken at the instance of the then Works Minister. He also took us though the minutes of the board, exhibit 'Kha' adduced by the defendant No.7. He took us through the minutes that in similar cases of breach and cancellation of lease in respect of Ms Steelman Engineering, the Board after hearing the lessee revoked their earlier orders and allowed the lessee to continue but in the case of the plaintiff the board did neither consider the representation of the plaintiff nor give him any personal hearing before cancellation of the lease.

14. Lastly, he submitted that from the letter Exhibit 6 it was evident that it was issued without holding any enquiry and the knowledge of the prescribed authority at the instance of interested quarter including defendant No. 7 and learned Subordinate Judge failed to consider question of cancellation of the lease in the facts and circumstances of the case and on the evidence on record. In support, he cited Sati Prasanna Mukherjee and others vs Md Fazel, AIR 1952 Cal 320.

15. Defendant Nos. 1 to 5 did not appear in the appeal. Defendant No. 7 alone appeared. Mr JH Afric, learned Advocate for said defendant No. 7- respondent, took us through the record, particularly the deed of lease and submitted that as the plaintiff failed to make any industry on the demised plot within fourteen years the authority did not commit any illegality in cancelling the lease of the plaintiff for breach of the contract.

16. Main question before us is whether the trial Court was justified in dismissing the suit.

17. The facts are not disputed that the suit plot was allotted to the plaintiff. On receipt of requisite fees, a deed of lease was executed and registered on behalf of the President of the People's Republic of Bangladesh by one authorised officer of the Ministry of Works.

18. Said deed of lease stipulated, amongst others that the lessee applied for establishing a printing press and the lease was granted for the purpose of erecting thereon by the tenant a factory or workers quarter for manufacture of printing for a period of 99 years commencing from the first of April, 1984 on the terms, inter alia, 4. that the tenant shall start the industries concerned on the land within two years from the date of the commencement of the lease failing which the lease will be liable to be terminated under clause 16 but the lessor may for just and sufficient reasons extend the period. Clause 16 sub-clause (1), amongst others, provides that in the event of the tenant committing any breach of any of the covenants of this indenture otherwise than payment of rent, taxes, etc. the lessor shall be at liberty without prejudice to any other rights that he may possess after giving one calendar month's notice in writing to determine the rights of the tenant under these presents, re-enter into or upon the whole of the demised property or any part thereof and take possession thereof including all buildings, structures and erections, etc.

19. It appears that defendant No.4 issued a notice dated 11-9-93 asking the plaintiff to show cause within 7 days as to why the lease would not be cancelled after 30 days of service of the notice as per terms 16(1) and 42. In the notice, it was claimed that within 2 years of the lease as per terms 4, 7 and 8 no industry was established, and commenced.

20. Then, said defendant No.4 issued the letter dated 12-10-94 informing the plaintiff that his lease was cancelled and the Government would re-enter into the land under terms 16(9) and 42 of the lease document.

21. Whether the plaintiff committed any breach of the covenants of the contract of lease and. issue of the letter dated 12-10-94 cancelling the lease was permitted by law are the moot issues.

22. In support of plaint case, the plaintiff examined him as PW 1. He stated that he paid Taka 69,581 in 4 instalments. On 2-4-84 lease deed was executed and registered and possession was delivered to him by defendant No.4. The demised plot was 412.33 square yards. It was an industrial plot. But what sort of industry to be built was not fully described in the deed. After taking possession, he got the suit plot surrounded by walls and built semi-pucca structures thereon. He established a factory thereon. Name of the factory was 'Mahmud Metal Corporation'. Body of transport bus, tempo, baby-taxi, etc; iron grills, iron and steel products were made in the factory. He obtained trade licence. He renewed the trade licence time to time. He also applied for loan by mortgage of the suit plot. He also obtained permission of the Government for taking loan vide letter dated 22-4-84. Janata Bank sanctioned loan of Taka 13,00,000. As the amount was not sufficient, he did not withdraw any money. On 11-9-93 defendant No.4 issued a notice asking him to show cause within 7 days. At the time, he was out of the country in Ajmeer Sharif. His manager, Arifur Rahman received the notice and showed cause. On return back home, he went to the housing office and requested them to visit the plot personally and see whether there was any running factory or not. But without holding any enquiry, they cancelled the lease by letter dated 12-10-94. On 19-10-94 the Public Works Department asked him to vacate the land. He did not vacate the land. He came to know on 29-10-94 the land was allotted to defendant No.7.

23. He further deposed that he paid municipality taxes, rents, electricity bills. The factory was still running. He denied that he did not install any factory in the suit plot. Immediately after lease, he started a factory.

24. In cross-examination, he stated that he applied for the plot for establishing an industry but he did not mention the nature of the industry in the application. He also applied for loan for establishing an industry. Loan was sanctioned. He also prayed for enhancement of the loan. On 20-5-93 Arifur Rahman showed causes to the notice at the time he was in Ajmeer Sharif. On 10-7-99 there was an investigation as to whether there was an industry or not. Investigation was held in his presence. On 18-7-99 an advocate commissioner submitted his report in court. He got trade licence in 1985. He. submitted trade licence. Exhibits 10(a) and 10(e) were the receipt of payment of the money for renewal of the trade licence. Exhibit A was electricity bill for the year dated 25-9-99. He did not establish any industry for which plan was necessary. He did not take permission for construction from the Housing Directorate nor he obtained any sanction from Rajuk.

25. There was a tin shed in the suit plot. There was office room, store room, large room at front; various machineries were there in various rooms. The factory was running. Grill, Almirah, etc were made there. He took necessary permission. He again denied that he did not make any factory.

Raham Ali Khan was examined as PW 2. He stated that on the suit plot almirah, safe, etc are made. There are machineries. There was electric meter. The factory was running since 1984. At present it was also running.

26. PW 3 Md Habib stated that he used to work with paint. He knew the plaintiff. They work in the factory of the plaintiff. He was working since 1984. Body of bus, grill, etc were made there. There was electricity. There was electric meter. They work 24 hours. He used to paint with spray and hand.

27. Nirajan Mondal was examined as PW 4.

He stated that he got works done from the factory of the plaintiff. The plot number was 108. He got body of tempo made. Works of grill was also done there. He saw machineries in the factory. They were run by electricity. There was a meter.

28. In cross-examination, he stated that he saw the factory for 15/16 years. He got the works done since 1990.

29. Md Abu Zaher was a Court Assistant. He was examined on behalf of the defendant Nos. 1 to 5. He stated that as no industry was established under term 4 of the deed of lease the lease was cancelled. He produced the papers on behalf of the said defendants. He also filed the letter of allotment dated 29-10-94. Defendant No. 7 was given allotment on 29-10-94. He also submitted a survey report dated 13-9-93.

30. In cross-examination, he however, stated that the inquiry officer would not depose. He could not say how the inquiry officer went to the plot. Inquiry was held secretly.

31. Md Iqbal Ahmed Bhuiyan, defendant No. 7, was examined as DW 2. He stated that on 29-10-94 he got the allotment of the suit plot and deposited Taka 4,00,000 of the instalments. He claimed that the plaintiff had no industry on the suit plot nor he had any possession.

32. In cross-examination, he stated that his house is at Mirpur, and village home at Comilla under Muradnagar Police Station. House of Barrister Rafiqul Islam Miah was also in the same constituency. His industry was then closed for want of space. If he got land he would commence the industry again On 25-2-93 he prayed for allotment of an industrial plot. He got the plot of the plaintiff. There was nothing written, there was no signboard.

33. Badal Kumar Bhowmik was examined as DW 3. He stated that he was appointed Advocate Commissioner. On 10-7-99 he went to the suit plot. He found a semi-pucca tin shed 27' x 27' at the east of the suit plot. East of that was vacant. At the west side, there were 3 thatched huts. There was no factory on the plot but he saw 4/5 persons in the tin shed, two old almirahs. He saw them rubbing. He did not see any electric connection, the meter was hanging without connection.

34. In cross-examination, he stated that he could not say the distance of the suit plot from his house. He went to the suit plot. He could not say when he started from his house. He reached the suit plot at about 10-30 am. He saw the signboard of the name of the plaintiff at the suit plot. He did not remember, whether the signboard was in the name of Mahmud Metal Ltd. He did not see any gate. He saw 4/5 labourers were working in the 27 x 27 feet hut. He did not take any tape for measurement. He did not ask any question to them who are working. Gate of the plot might be towards the south. Signboard was to the south-east. He entered into the hut where the labourers were working. He denied that the factory was running on the suit plot since 1984 and he deposed at the instance of defendant No.7.

35. MA Rouf was examined as DW 4. He stated that he was Administrative Officer of DESCO. A bill was issued from their company to the plaintiff of plot No. 108 for Taka 85,327.40. Bill was not paid. For arrears of the bill the electric line was snapped. The plaintiff did not apply for re-connection of electricity.

36. On perusal of the above oral evidence along with the documents exhibited by the parties, it becomes clear that after lease the plaintiff established a factory under the name and style 'Mahmud Metal Corporation'. During the pendency of the suit, the Advocate Commissioner DW 3 also found the existence of 4 huts there including one of 27 x 27 feet semi-pucca hut and labourers working there.

37. It is true that in the lease deed, the plot was described to be industrial one and purpose of the lease was written to be for erecting of an industry or workers quarter for manufacture of printing. It was also stated that the lessor agreed to lease the demised property for modern press. We fail to understand how on earth on a small piece of land measuring 412.33 square yards only what modern printing press could be established. After close scrutiny of the lease deed, we are of the view that the parties intended that a small cottage industry would be established on the suit plot for provision of small scale entrepreneurs. Therefore, a factory for making small iron and/or steel products could not be said to be said intended by the parties.

<u>38. The land no doubt belonged to the Republic and on behalf of the Republic, the President transferred the land to the plaintiff by way of lease for 99 years. An authorised officer of the Ministry of Housing and Public Works as per the Rules of Business executed and registered the deed of sale on behalf of the President. Such lease of the suit plot was transfer of a right to enjoy the property and must be deemed to be in perpetuity within the meaning of section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act (Act IV of 1882), in short, the Act. Such lease could only validly be determined or terminated by a six months notice under section 106 of the Act. Where such lease is lawfully determined under section 106 or otherwise for breach of any express condition entitling the lessor to re-enter, such lessee could only be evicted by a suit after service of a notice under section 114A of the Act. Not otherwise.</u>

<u>39. In view of such legal position, the seven days notice dated 11-9-93 issued by defendant No. 4 to show cause or the letter dated 12-10-94 purportedly cancelling or determining the lease giving thirty days notice to vacate and intending to re-enter into the suit plot are not valid within the meaning of section 106 of the Act.</u>

<u>40. Moreover, such memo does not disclose any enquiry was held before the cancellation. A survey report was submitted but the author of such report did not come forward to take oath to support his opinion. Admittedly, the letter of cancellation was issued without giving any hearing to the plaintiff. Last, but not the least, an Assistant Commissioner, Settlement of the Office of the Commissioner, Settlement of the Ministry of Housing and Public Works was not definitely empowered to cancel a perm anent lease by such show of executive fiat.</u>

41. From exhibit 'Kha' it appears that there was a Board of Allotment in the Ministry of Housing Public Works comprising of a Joint Secretary and other officials to deal with the Government land. On the application of defendant No. 7 dated 25-2-93, the Board by its decision dated 8-4-93 allowed the application and decided to allot a plot of five 'Kathas' to him. By a letter dated 29-10-93 said defendant No.4 allotted the plot of the plaintiff to the said defendant.

42. So, before cancellation of the lease of the plaintiff decision was already taken to give the land to the defendant No. 7 as submitted by Mr Hashnat Quayum. When any action was actuated by no good faith that must be held to be malafide.

43.	In the circumstances, cancellation of the lease of the plaintiff and allotment of the suit plot to defendant No.7 must be held to be illegal, malafide and without jurisdiction. We are of the view that the learned Subordinate Judge missed the real issue in the suit and committed serious error in dismissing the suit.

44.	Appeal, therefore, succeeds.

45.	In the result, the appeal is allowed with cost. Impugned judgment and decree are set aside. The suit is decreed and the memo dated 12-10-94 cancelling the lease of the plaintiff of the suit plot and that dated 29-10-94 allotting said plot to defendant No.7 are declared to be illegal, collusive, without jurisdiction, malafide and of no legal effect.

Send down the LCR at once.

End.

lawyer:
Md Ibrahim Mollah, Advocate ----- For the Petitioners. 
Probir Halder, Advocate ----- For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Kala Chand alias Chand Mia &others ----- Petitioners
Vs
Karim Khan and others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule arises as against the judgment and decree dated 28-8-1997 and 3-9-1997 respectively passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, First Court, Narayangonj in Title Appeal No. 148 of 1994 allowing the appeal by reversing the judgment and decree dated 29-11-1994 and 30-11-1994 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Rupganj in Title Suit No. 16 of 1993 dismissing the suit on contest.

2. The opposite parties as plaintiffs have instituted a Title Suit being Title Suit No. 16 of 1993 in the court of Senior Assistant Judge, Rupganj under the District of Narayangonj for permanent injunction against the petitioners and the defendant- respondent opposite party Nos. 7 to 9. The further case of the plaintiff is that, one Akbar Bhuiyan was the owner of CS Khatian No. 15 with other land and Jonab Ali and others were the owners of the CS Khatian No. 243 including the disputed land and also other land. Before CS operation the CS Plot of CS Khatian No. 15 was owned and possessed by one Maizuddin and after a few years the said Maizuddin handed over the possession of the said Khatian to Akbar Bhuiyan. Thereafter, the whole of the CS Khatian Nos. 15 and 243 was sold out on auction and the said auction was purchased by the landlord Asliutosh Bandopadhaya and others. Thereafter, the said properties including the disputed properties were handed over to one Mohabbat Khan and the possession of the said properties was also given to him before 1940 and thus Mohabbat Khan became the owner and peaceful possessor of the said disputed land including other land by paying rent to the then Zaminder, Babu Ashutosh Bandopadhaya and others. Mohabbat Khan died leaving behind his three sons namely, Ayer Khan, Taiub Khan and Ala Box and the SA and RS parcha were prepared in the name of Ayer Khan, Taub Khan and Ala Box correctly and thereafter Ayer Khan died leaving behind two sons namely, Karim Khan, Salamat Khan and one daughter Tamarun Nessa and wife Sakhina, the opposite party Nos. 1-3 and 6 as his legal heirs and thus the plaintiff-appellant-opposite party Nos. 1 to 6 have been owning and possessing the suit land for more than 50 years within the knowledge of everybody including the defendant- respondents-petitioners and the plaintiff-opposite parties have been owning and peacefully possessing the suit land by growing seasonal crops and the defendant-petitioners have no interest and possession over the suit land including the schedule land. The defendant-petitioners with the malafide intention and to grab the properties tried to dispossess the plaintiff-opposite parties on 19-3-1993 from 9-00 to 10-00 AM but with the intervention of the local people the plaintiff opposite parties were saved from dispossession of the suit land. The plaintiff-opposite parties are compelled to file the suit for permanent injunction.

3. The case of the defendant-respondent- petitioners are that, one Akbar Ali Bhuiyan was the owner and possessor of CS Khatian No. 15. Janab Ali and others were the 16 annas owners and possessors of CS Khatian No. 243 and thereafter, Akbar Bhuiyan and Janab Ali and others handed over the possession of the said properties of Khatian Nos. 15 and 243 to one Maizuddin and Jasar Ali through Dao Sidda Bandak, thereafter the said properties were sold out on auction for want of rent. Thereafter, the father of Mahabbat Khan and Ismat Khan, that is Suja Khan, purchased the said sale of auction from the then Zaminder. Thereafter, Suja Khan and Ismat Khan died leaving behind two sons namely, Mohabbat Khan and Ismat Khan as his legal heirs and on amicable partition the disputed land has fallen in a saham of Ismat Khan and as a result he had been owning and possessing the said land.
