The RS parcha was prepared in the name of Ismat Khan and Mohabbat Khan correctly though the name of Ismat Khan shown in the RS Parcha as eight annas share and Mohabbat Khan also got eight annas share by amicable partition. Son of Mohabbat Khan had been owning and possessing the said land. Thereafter Ismat Khan sold out 0.45 acres of land out of 0.50 acres to Kala Chand from the plot No. 360 on 5-12-1997 vide registered Deed No. 35286 and handed over peaceful possession of the said land Ismat Khan also sold out 30 acres of land out of 36 acres from plot No. 361 on 12-3-1979 vide registered Deed No. 792 to one Mr Kala Chand, the petitioner No.1, and also handed over peaceful possession of the said plot. Thereafter Ismat Khan gifted the 0.04½ acres of land from plot No. 360 to his grandsons, Serajul Islam Khan and Md Dulal Khan on 12-3-1979 vide Registered Deed No. 795 and handed over the possession of the said land to his aforesaid grandsons. Thereafter, the rest portion i.e. 0.04-1/2 acres of land from plot No. 360. The disputed property was also gifted to his son Rup Chand on 12-3-1979 vide Registered Deed No. 794. Thereafter the said Rouf Khan, Serajul Islam Khan and the mother of Dulal Khan, Tara Bhanu sold out their 0.09 acres of land of plot No. 36 and 0.06 acres of land from plot No. 361 to Kala Chand on 27-8-1980 vide Registered Sub- Kabala deed being No. 794 and thus, this Kala Chand became the absolute owner and possessor of 0.54 acres of land from plot No. 360 and 0.36 acres of land from plot No. 361 for long more than 12 years and this Kala Chand mutated his name in separate Khatian and has been owning and possessing the schedule land by paying rents to the Government regularly. The plaintiff opposite parties have no right, title, possession and interest over the suit land in any manner and the claim of the plaintiff-appellant is false and a fabricated story and no occasion or occurrence took place. The plaintiff-opposite party have no right, title, interest and possession over an inch of the suit land. The defendant-petitioners are in possession of the suit land by way of cultivating the land and by recting houses over some portion of the schedule land. The plaintiff-opposite parties are not entitled to get decree of the suit land. The defendant-petitioner also stated in the written statement that while they were coming back from the Chamber of their learned Advocate of Upazila Court of Rupganj they lost the original deed including other valuable deeds on the way to their residence and they have filed a GD in the concerned thana, they are the owners and possessors of the entire suit land except 0.03 acres of land as the said 0.03 acres of land was acquired by the C&B Department for road.

4. The defendant-respondent-opposite party Nos. 7 to 9 also have filed written statement to the effect that they have been owning and possession the 0.54 acres of land from plot No. 360 by growing seasonal crops and they got the properties from the predecessors by way of inheritance and they have appointed one Md Moser Ali as their Attorney for maintenance of their property amounting to 3.23 acres of land including 0.52 acres of the suit land. But their names were not recorded in the SA Khatian for which they have filed another suit for declaration of title being Title Suit No. 54 of 1993 in the court of Senior Assistant Judge, Rupganj against the plaintiffs-appellant-respondent-opposite party and while this defendant-opposite party petitioner No. 1 came to know that suit for declaration has started this defendant-petitioner filed a petition under Order I rule 10 for adding them as party in the aforesaid suit and the learned court was pleased to add them as party in that suit being Title Suit No. 54 of 1993. After conclusion of the trial the learned Court was pleased to dismiss the suit on contest and plaintiff filed an appeal against the said judgment and decree which is now pending before the court of Additional District Judge.

5. The trial Court after taking deposition of 6 witnesses for the plaintiff and 2 witnesses for the defendant and Exhibits and after considering the exits have dismissed the suit for permanent injunction and against the said judgment and decree the plaintiff-opposite party Nos. 1-6 filed appeal before the learned District Judge and on transfer to the learned Court of Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Narayangonj for disposal, the court after considering the evidence on record allowed the appeal against which the defendant-respondent- petitioner preferred this revisional application and obtained the present Rule.

<u>6. Mr Ibrahim Mollah, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant-petitioner, submits that the trial Court after hearing the parties and the deposition and considering the Exhibits since found possession of the petitioner dismissed the suit which is very much in accordance with law against which the plaintiff-appellant-opposite parties have preferred appeal and the appellate Court without discussing the evidences allowed the appeal thus occasioned failure of justice. He further submits that both the plaintiff and the defendant though claimed the property by way of pattan but no pattan was produced before the court, RS was prepared in the name of the predecessors of the plaintiff and defendant. The petitioner has purchased by 3 registered deeds (Exhibits GH) on different dates and there was mutation case being No. 174 of 1986 and has been paying rent to the Government which are marked as Exhibit A series and paid rent up to 1991 and referred 28 DLR (AD) 61 and 32 DLR 252 wherein it has been stated Record of Right is not a document of title. It does not create or extinguish title to land. At best, along with other evidence it may support evidences of title. By itself, it is not an evidence of title "and it has been referred in 32 DLR 252 that Record of Right is evidence of present possession-Registered Kabala evidence of title. The records of rights of the Government which at best are evidence of possession at the time when such records are prepared and not an evidence of title as such this is a well-established principle of law. A registered Kabala is an evidence of title which will prevail over the other records of rights as such until and unless such kabala is canceled on a specific allegation of fraud by any civil Court in an appropriate civil suit." He has further referred 43 DLR 226 "There is no specific area or demarcation of the land allegedly encroached by the defendants- opposite parties, in such a case no order of temporary injunction can be granted" and in this connection he has referred schedule 'A' description of the plaint where the boundary was not specifically mentioned and where there was no specific demarcation of the plot. The plaintiff-opposite party cannot claim for an injunction or is not entitled to have injunction. The appellate Court while disposing of the appeal did not consider this very aspect rather considered the dakhilas as produced by the plaintiff (marked as Exhibit 6) and the rent receipt to the government (marked as Exhibit 5) in this connection. He has referred 30 DLR (SC) 41 "the private document made an exhibit on its formal proof, presumption as to its writing-question of its genuineness is a question of fact" and he submits that the Exhibit 6 are all private documents and the burden of proof is on him to prove his genuineness of the rent receipts which were not at all proved. Thus the appellate Court being the final court of fact should have considered all these aspects for which he is not entitled thus occasioned an error in the decision required to be interfered by this court.</u>

7. Mr Probir Halder, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-appellant- opposite parties, submits that though the pattan was not produced by the plaintiff but it is admitted fact that SA was prepared in the name of the sons of Mohabbat Khan, predecessor of the plaintiff, but name of the predecessor of the defendant has never been entered in the SA Khatian. Therefore, the chain of ownership could not be established and subsequent registration of documents; therefore does not create any title or ownership in the name of the defendant-petitioner and he has referred 2 BLC (AD) 92 that the High Court Division has no jurisdiction to disturb the final findings of facts on the ground mentioned in section 115 of the CPC without reversing the findings of the courts below and it cannot superimpose itself as a third Court for fresh application of evidence which is not its function and thereby it exceeded its revisional jurisdiction" and also referred in the same 2 BLC 134 (AD) Concurrent finding of fact. It cannot be sa.id that a finding of fact whether concurrent or not, arrived at by the lower appellate Court is binding on the High Court, as a revisional Court except in certain well-defined exceptional circumstances such :3.S non-consideration or misreading of material evidence affecting the merit of the case. Besides, the oral evidence the sale deeds and the SA Khatian on the basis of which the rents were alleged to have been paid by the plaintiffs though rent receipts have been duly considered by the appellate Court which is the final court of fact, the High Court Division was not correct in reversing the concurrent decisions of the Courts below." In this context he submits that the appellate Court has considered the dakhilas and the rent receipts Exhibits 6 and 5 from where it is established that the plaintiff-opposite party are in possession and title of the disputed property and further submits that as per schedule of the plaint, it has been specifically mentioned the total land which the plaintiff requires and sought for injunction thereby the suit plot is specifically demarcated and he is entitled to have injunction and submits that the registered deed by which the petitioner is claiming the property has got no basis as the petitioner could not establish the chain of ownership in the disputed property. Mr Halder further refers that though the petitioner was paying rent up to 1991, under a mutation case No. 174 of 1974 of 1986 that mutation case was dismissed against which the defendant preferred appeal and the appeal is pending before the learned ADC (Rev). Therefore though the petitioner has paid rent still they have not acquired any title in the disputed property.

<u>8. I have gone through the judgments of both the courts below and also Exhibits as filed by both the parties. Admitted fact is that the CS Khatian was prepared in the name of Jagadish and Ashutosh from where the plaintiff claims the ownership but the pattans were not produced by plaintiff and defendant before the court though RS was prepared in the name of the predecessor of the plaintiff and defendants. The plaintiff produced some dakhilas and also rent receipts i.e. Exhibit 5 which appeared to have been paid on 16-3-1980 and Exhibit 5 Ka is paid in 1969 in the name of Tayab Khan and Exhibit 6 series are the dakhilas given by the jaminder and the defendants have also filed rent receipts of the government which were marked as Exhibit A series and admitted position is that he paid rent up to 1991. The defendants have mutated and submitted some documents of that purchase deed of different dates i.e. 12-3-1979 and 5-12-1979. The dakhilas submitted by the plaintiff are the private documents and that are ie, to be proved by the scribe, the signatures are to be compared which were not considered by the lower appellate Court. These private dakhilas are yet to be proved and it is referred in 35 DLR 129 "that dakhilas are private documents and it would not carry any presumption of correctness as would be available in the case of any entry in the record of rights under the provisions of the Bengal Tenancy Act. It appears that both the parties have adduced rent receipts and the petitioner has paid rent up to 1991 and there was mutation though the mutation proceeding is under challenge in the appeal and, according to decision 35 DLR (AD) 216, rent receipts are evidence of possession, and may be used as collateral evidence of title. The petitioner has submitted certain rent receipts marked as Exhibit A series which were not considered by the learned appellate Court. Though it is a question of fact based on finding and is proved and this aspect since not discussed by the learned appellate Court, I find substance in this Rule. Since rent receipts are evidence of possession and collateral evidence of title and in a suit for permanent injunction where the plaintiff did not mention the boundary of the specific plot and there is no specific demarcation, in that view of the matter, granting injunction in favour of the plaintiff cannot be sustained.</u>

9. Accordingly, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to cost. The judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Narayangonj in Title Appeal No. 148 of 1994 is hereby set aside.

Send down the lower court records at once.

End.

lawyer:
Md Zakir Hossain Senior, Advocate ----- For the Appellants
Sheikh Razzaq Ali, Senior Advocate with Shamsul Haque, Advocates ----- For the Respondents
parties:
Shaikh Jahangir Hossain ----- Appellant
Vs.
Government of Bangladesh and others ----- Respondent
full_judgment:
A.B.M Khairul Haque, J: This appeal arises out of the judgment and order dated 20-2-1995 and decree dated 22-2-1995, passed by the Subordinate Judge, Third Court, Dhaka, in Title Suit No. 258 of 1952, in decreeing the suit.

2. One Sheikh Jahangir Hossain instituted the suit against the Secretary, Railway Division, Ministry of Communication, Government of Bangladesh and 7 others, praying for a declaration that the impugned order dated 4-8-1992 passed by the concerned Ministry, is illegal and not binding upon him with a further prayer for specific performance of contract contending, inter alia, that in response to a public notice for sale of the unused lands of the Railway Department through tender, the plaintiff submitted two tenders to the concerned authorities for two plots of lands along with the deposit of 25% of the price quoted by him against those two plots. On opening of the tenders, the plaintiff was found to be the highest bidder of the said two plots of land but subsequently the concerned authorities by their letter dated 4-8-1992 cancelled all the tenders for sale of the concerned plots of lands. Being aggrieved he instituted the present suit.

3. The suit was contested on behalf of the defendants contending, inter alia, that the suit is not maintainable in its present form and manner and there is no cause of action for the suit which was filed with a malafide motive, as such, liable to be rejected in limini. Besides, it is contended that the notice for tender specifically stated that the concerned authorities may cancel any tender without assigning any reason.

4. At the suit the learned Judge considered the following issues:

(i) 	Is the suit maintainable in its present form?

(ii) Is the suit barred by the law on limitation?

(iii) Is the impugned order dated 4-8-1992, rejecting the tender, without lawful authority?

(iv) Is the plaintiff entitled to purchase the disputed land and entitled to get the decree in such manner?

(v) What other relief the plaintiff is entitled to?

5. The plaintiff deposed himself as PW 1. He stated in his examination-in-chief that in response to a notice dated 8-12-1991 for selling plots through tender, he purchased two tender forms on 2-5-1992 for plot Nos. 15 and 18 at a price of Taka 750 each, having 12(twelve) kathas of lands in each plot, in total 25 (twenty-five) kathas, out of 74 plots for sale, that one Nur Ali Mollah submitted tender but it was changed because his tender being lower there would have been difficulties in accepting it, that he submitted tenders but failing to give any plot to Nur Ali, being angry with him, the defendant directed delivery of lands in favour of RAJUK in market price. He further stated that he in total deposited Taka 6,31,575, that, on the instruction of the defendant No.1 on 4-8-1992 the defendant No. 8 by the impugned letter deprived the plaintiff and illegally directed selling of the lands in favour of RAJUK. This witness prays for a declaration that the said memorandum is illegal, that in pursuance of the terms and conditions of the tender entered into an agreement on 3-5-1992 in respect of the 'ka' schedule land and that he submitted the relevant documents. These were marked as Exhibit 1 series. He also submitted the documents emboding an agreement dated 3-5-1992 in respect of 'kha' schedule land which was marked as Exhibit 2 series, that he deposited 25% as advance in respect of each of the plots, through bank drafts for Taka 3,93,070 in respect of 'ka' schedule land and Taka 2,37,505 in respect of ‘kha' schedule land on 3-5-1992. He further stated that he sent a representation on 3-6-1992 to the defendant No.1 in respect of the report dated 30-5-1992. He proved the report dated 30-5-1992 (Exhibit 3 series) and his representations dated 3-6-1992 were marked as Exhibit 4 series. He further stated that the defendants cancelled the allotment on the ground that realistic price was not offered in respect of the concerned plot of lands, as such, transferred the said lands in favour of RAJUK and cancelled the allotment in favour of the plaintiff (Exhibit 6), that he issued a notice on 8-9-1992 to the defendants demanding justice (Exhibits 7, 8, 9) but they did not reply. This witness as the plaintiff prays for a decree for execution of the deed in his favour on receipt of the rest of the money according to the agreement and for delivery of possession. In his cross-examination he denied that the tender was cancelled in public interest and stated that he did not know whether all the participants took back their money. PW 2 Sayed A Jalil is the father-in-law of the plaintiff. He stated in his examination-in-chief that the quality and the value of the plot of lands at Nikunja project are higher than that of the disputed lands. He was cross-examined but nothing of importance came out of it.

6. On behalf of the defendants Md Sirajul Islam deposed as DW 1. He stated in his examination-in-chief that they took initiative to sell the disputed lands through tender, that tender was invited in pursuance of the order dated 8-12-1991 in order to sell 74 plots, that the tenders were submitted on 3-5-1992, that the plaintiff also submitted his tender in due course. This witness submitted the tender notice and other relevant papers in connection with the tender which was marked as Exhibit Ka and Kha series. He also stated that the concerned authorities reserved their right to cancel/reject any of the tenders without assigning any reason, that the tenders were rejected in pursuance to a memo dated 9-8-1992 because the tenders did not fetch acceptable price for the concerned plots and all the other participants received back their money except the plaintiff. He further stated that the disputed lands are situated by the side of Nikunja Project of RAJUK, that the defendant was not bound to allot the plot of land in favour of the plaintiff according to the tender. In his cross-examination he stated that he does not know whether the plots in Nikunja have got better facilities than the concerned disputed lands.

7. The learned Judge after hearing, by his judgment found that the plaintiff duly submitted two tenders, for the plot No.15 and plot No.18, and also deposited 25% of his quoted price in favour of the defendant and both of his tenders were found to be the highest, that in such circumstances the decision to cancel the tender was not proper only on the ground that realistic price for the plots was not offered and the decision to transfer the disputed lands in favour of RAJUK at market price because those fetched lesser price was not justified, rather, was without any reason, that the reasons given by the defendant for canceling the tender was not correct since the plaintiff in exercise of his constitutional rights, on payment according to the market price, performed his part of the terms and conditions of the tender. In this respect learned Judge relied on a decision reported in 27 DLR 382. In considering the contention made on behalf of the defendant that the Bangladesh Railway reserved the right to reject any tender without assigning any reason the learned Judge on the basis of the observation made in the decision reported in 27 DLR 62 held that the defendant Railway Authority acted illegally in canceling the tender on an illegitimate reason and without any ground. The learned Judge further held that since the plaintiff did not to the decision in the case of Associated Provincial yet take back 25% of his offered price for the plots, he is entitled to have the disputed properties registered in his favour on payment of the rest of the money.

8. Being aggrieved the defendants filed the instant appeal.

9. Mr Zakir Hossain, Advocate, appears on behalf of the appellants while Mr Sheikh Razzaq Ali, Senior Advocate, appears with Mr Shamsul Haque, Advocate, for the respondent.

10. Mr Zakir Hossain, the learned Advocate, appearing on behalf of the appellants submits that it is true that the Railway Authority published a notice inviting tender from the public at large to sell some unused lands of the Railway Department and the plaintiff duly submitted two tenders offering to purchase two plots of the land as mentioned in the plaint itself but since his tender was not accepted by the concerned authorities, no contract came into existence between the parties, as such, there was nothing to enforce by way of specific performance of contract. The learned Advocate also drew our attention to the last part of the tender (Exhibit ka-1) where it was specifically mentioned that the Railaway Authorities reserved their right to cancel/reject any tender without assigning any reason, as such, the concerned authorities in exercise of their lawful right rejected all the tenders including those of the plaintiff and in exercise of their lawful discretion decided to transfer the entire unused lands in favour of RAJUK at the market price. As such, he prayers for allowing the appeal and dismissed the suit.

<u>11. On the other hand, Mr Sheikh Razzaq Ali, the learned Advocate, appearing on behalf of the respondent candidly admits that this suit was not properly framed and there cannot be any suit for the specific performance of contract because there was no contract at all but he submits that although the Railway Authority has got the right to reject and cancel any tender but they are obliged to act fairly and reasonably in rejecting such a tender that Government authorities cannot act arbitrarily or capriciously. In support of his contention he refers Picture Houses vs Wednesbury Corporations 1948 1 KB-223 CA.</u>

12. It appears that the railway authorities wanted to sell some of their unused lands by public auction and for that purpose they invited tenders from the interested persons for purchase of those lands. It is also admitted that the plaintiff submitted two tenders for plot No.15 and Plot No.18 and also deposited 25% of the price of those two plots quoted by him. It is also admitted that he was the highest bidder in respect of those two plots, but it appears that the railway authorities in evaluating the entire project came to resolve that the tenders submitted to them do not come up with the expected price for the concerned plots notified to be sold. As such, the concerned authorities of the railway department by their Memo dated 4-8-1992 decided to reject/cancel all the tenders including those of the plaintiff.

<u>13. An advertisement in the newspapers inviting tenders, as in this case, to sell lands, was not an offer made by the Railway Department, but a mere invitation to treat, an invitation to the people at large for making offers. In response to such an invitation, when the plaintiff and many others submitted their tenders with their own quoted price, they were making offers to purchase the plot of lands for which they submitted their tenders. Those tenders which were mere offers to buy the plot of lands did not constitute any agreement, enforceable under the law. We have considered the papers marked as Exhibits 1 and 2 series. There are applications of tender and other incidental papers. Those papers do not constitute any contract. There the learned Subordinate Judge committed an error of law in thinking that those tenders created rights, those did not. Even without the exception clause as embodied in the tender that the authorities were entitled to reject any tender without assigning any reason, the concerned authorities before acceptance were absolutely within their rights to reject any tender simply because there were no agreement or contract, so long they acted reasonably within the meaning of Wednesbury principle (Associated Provincial Picture Houses Ltd vs Wednesbury Corporation (1948) I KB 223) since they were public authority. In this case although in response to the public notice the plaintiff submitted two tenders and also deposited the required 25% deposits but since those tenders were not accepted by the railway department, no agreement came into existence and they had no obligation, legal or otherwise, to allot any plot of land in favour of the plaintiff.</u>

14. In this case, the concerned authorities on proper consideration abandoned the scheme to sell their lands through tender and resolved to sell through RAJUK, another Authority who generally deals with allotment and sale of lands to the public at large, thereby satisfied the reason-ability test propounded in the Wednesbury decision.

<u>15. A Court of law is to see whether the concerned Authority considered the issue or not but it is always for them to take the decision on the particular issue; a Court of law shall never impose its own discretion over the concerned authorities and abdicate their functions. It is for them and for them alone to take the decision and not for a Court of law. An action of an authority can be challenged if they act without jurisdiction or illegally or unreasonably, otherwise not.</u>

16. In the instant case, the Railway authorities addressed themselves on the issue and on due consideration they abandoned the idea of selling lands through tender and cancelled the tenders, not only of the plaintiff but of all the tenderers and, as such, it cannot be said that they were guilty of discrimination. They were not.

17. True it is that the plaintiff has got constitutional right to submit a tender, similarly, the Railway Authorities had also legal right not to accept it.

18. In this case, the plaintiff merely submitted his tenders but those even with 25% deposit of his own quoted price did not clothe him with any right to property, as such, his suit for declaration was not maintainable. Since there were no agreements, his suit for specific performance of contract had also no basis and was liable to be dismissed.

19. The plaintiff, however, is entitled to take back his money deposited with his tenders.

20. Before parting with the case we are constrained to observe that the learned Judge lacks basic concepts on the law on contract and the applicability of the provision of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act.

21. Let a copy of this judgment be forwarded to the learned Judge wherever he is posed now, for his future guidance.

Send down the lower Court records at once.

End.

lawyer:
Rafique-ul-Huq with M A Samad, Senior Advocates and MGH Ruhullah, Ahsanul Karim, Mizan Sayeed and Faheemul Huq, Advocates ----- For the Petitioner. 
Dr Kamal Hossain with Rokanuddin Mahmood, Senior Advocates ----- For Contemner-Opposite Parties.
parties:
Akhteruzzaman Chowdhury ------ Contempt Petitioner
Vs.
Hamidul Huq, MD, UCBL and another ------ Contemner Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This contempt Rule was issued calling upon the contemner opposite parties to show cause as to why they shall not be committed for contempt of court for dishonouring, disregarding and non compliance of the direction given in the judgment and order passed by this court on 15-4-2002 and the subsequent order dated 17-5-2003 in Company Matter No.2 of 2000 and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The facts which led to the issuance of this Rule are that, the present petitioner is a sponsor shareholder of the United Commercial Bank Ltd. (hereinafter called "the Bank") and he was the first elected Chairman of the Board of Directors of the said Bank and the present contemner-opposite parties are the Managing Director and the Secretary respectively of the said Bank. It appears that on 18-1-2000 one Jahangir Alam Khan, a shareholder and a Director of the Bank, filed an application under section 81(2) of the Companies Act, 1994 for holding of Annual General Meeting (hereinafter called "the AGM") for the years 1998 and 1999, being Company Matter No. 2 of 2000. In that application the present petitioner was added as respondent No.3 and he filed an application under section 85(3) of the Companies Act, 1994 (hereinafter called the Act) and also prayed for calling, holding and conducting the AGM for the years 1998-2000 under the Chairmanship of a neutral and independent person and the Company Court after hearing the parties by its order dated 15-4-2002 was pleased to allow the application of the present petitioner after invoking its jurisdiction under section 85(3) of the Act in view of the facts and circumstances of the case and condoned the delay in holding the AGM for the aforesaid years and enlarged the time for holding the same under the Chairmanship of a neutral person and Mr KZ Alam, Barrister-at-Law and a Senior Advocate of this Court was appointed as Chairman designate to call, hold and conduct the AGM for the aforesaid years. By that order this court also directed the management of the Bank to extend all co-operation to the Chairman designate in the matter of holding the AGM. It further appears that against the aforesaid judgment the Bank preferred Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1049 of 2002 before the Appellate Division and the Appellate Division by their judgment and order dated 22-4-03 dismissed the aforesaid Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal. After the dismissal of the aforesaid leave petition, the present petitioner filed an application before this Court for further extension of time for holding AGM which was allowed by this Court and time was extended for holding the AGM for the aforesaid years up to 17-8-2003 by its order dated 15-4-2002 and Mr KZ Alam, the Chairman designate, was directed to hold the AGM within that time frame.

3. It appears that in the meantime a change was brought about in the Bank Company (Amendment) Act, 2003 and section 15 ka ka was inserted in the original Bank Company Act, 1991 and in view of the new section introduced in the Bank Company Act, the contemner No.2 vide letter dated 17-7-2003 posed three questions to Mr KZ Alam and sought his guidance on those matters. Upon receipt of this letter, Mr KZ Alam held a meeting with the Managing Director, that is, the contemner opposite party No. 1, on 18-7-2003 and pursuant to the said meeting Mr KZ Alam issued a letter dated 19-7-2003 asking the contemner-opposite party No. 1 to make necessary arrangements for holding the AGM of the Bank within the time fixed by this Court and to do the needful for holding the meeting which is evidenced by Annexure 'X' to this application. It appears that in spite of that request no steps were taken by the contemner-opposite parties to hold the AGM as per order of this Court and on receipt of the letter dated 17-7-2003 from the contemner-opposite party No.2 Mr KZ Alam referred to this earlier letter dated 19- 7-2003 and talked to the contemner-opposite party No.1 over telephone regarding holding of the AGM and again by his letter dated 22-7-2003 requested the contemner-opposite party No. 1 not to waste any further time and to complete all formalities for holding of AGM of the Bank. This letter is annexed as Annexure-'X-2' to the application. It is contended that in spite of such repeated requests no step whatsoever was taken by the contemners for holding the AGM whereupon Mr KZ Alam again by his letter dated 26-7-2003 requested the contemner opposite party No. 1 to inform him at the earliest as to what the contemner-opposite parties are contemplating in respect of holding of AGM of the Bank as per order of this Court and reminded the contemner opposite party No. 1 that his such inaction in holding the AGM of the Bank is, in effect, violation of the order of this Court and amounts to disregarding the order of this court and this may be brought to the notice of this court and the contemner opposite parties may be held liable for defiance of the order of this court. It is further contended that the contemners did not pay any heed to the repeated requests, of Mr KZ Alam, the Chairman designate, rather the contemner opposite party No.2 by his letter dated 27-7-2003 expressed their inability to proceed with the formalities for holding of AGM of the Bank. It further appears that after the introduction of section 15 ka ka to the Bank Company Act, 1991 one of the shareholders of the Bank filed a Writ Petition challenging the legality of the aforesaid Act which is registered as Writ Petition No. 4809 of 2003 in the High Court Division and another shareholder of the Dhaka Bank also challenged the aforesaid new law in Writ Petition No. 3482 of 2003 and it was brought to the notice of the Chairman designate that the latter writ petition is a part-heard matter and the hearing will resume from tomorrow and the judgment of the said writ petition is expected to be delivered very soon and that judgment will also help them resolve all the legal issues and it was further stated that they do not think that there will be any violation of the court's order under the circumstances as the difficulties in holding the AGM has not been caused by them. On receipt of the said letter dated 27-7-2003 issued by the contemner opposite party No.2, the Chairman designate, Mr KZ Alam, expressed his dissatisfaction for non-cooperation in making necessary arrangement for holding the AGM as per direction of this Court and the unreasonable and uncalled for activities of the contemner-opposite parties and again wrote to the contemner-opposite party No. 1 stating that he is appointed Chairman for the purpose of holding the AGM of the Bank for the years in question and he requested them to publish and notify the date for holding the AGM giving details of the time and place but neither of the contemner opposite parties had taken any steps in that behalf and instead was advising the Chairman designate as to what is his function and as to how he should conduct himself. It further appears that in that letter it was also mentioned that after disposal of Company Matter No.2 of 2000 by this court and also after the dismissal of leave petition by the Appellate Division a shareholder of the Bank filed Company Matter No. 60 of 2003 which is pending before this Court and the contemner opposite party No.2 informed the Chairman designate that in the circumstances, if the time frame for holding the AGM cannot be met, they will ask for further extension of time to hold the AGM which clearly shows that the contemner-opposite parties deliberately flouted and disregarded the order of this court which amounts to contempt of court.

4. As against that the contemner opposite parties by filing an affidavit of explanation contended, inter alia, that the bank is run and managed by a Board of Directors. According to Article 131 of the Articles of Association, its business is managed by the Directors who exercised all such powers and do all such acts as authorised by the Memorandum of Association and Articles of Association. It is further contended that the Managing Director is the Chief Executive of the Bank who is appointed by the Board of Directors with the approval of the Bangladesh Bank and the Managing Director is also ex-officio Director of the Bank and he does not have any power for holding any meeting of the Bank under the statute and the law. Similarly, the contemner No.2 is the Secretary of the Board of Directors whose functions and duties are similar to those of companies secretaries and nothing more. He is an officer of the company and does not have any power to hold any meeting of the company under the law. It is further contended that by order dated 15-4-2002 this court appointed Mr KZ Alam as Chairman designate to call, hold and conduct the AGM for the aforesaid years in accordance with law and the Articles of the Bank and this court further directed the management of the Bank to extend their all co-operation in the matter of holding AGM. Therefore, it is contended that by the impugned order no direction whatsoever was issued upon the contemner-opposite parties to call, hold or conduct any AGM for the years in question. It is further contended that they cannot be said to have committed any contempt of this court in view of the fact that these two contemner-opposite parties were not parties in Matter No.2 of 2000 nor the contemners have any power to call the AGM or to issue notice for holding AGM under the Articles of Association or the Act. Therefore, in the circumstances, the contemners cannot be said to have violated the order issued by this court in the matter of holding AGM. It is further contended that as officials of the Bank the contemner opposite parties have extended all possible co-operations to the Chairman designate in the matter of holding the AGM and there was no such instance of non-cooperation with Mr KZ Alam, Chairman designate. It is further contended that they, out of their sincerity, brought to the notice of the Chairman designate about the change brought about in law by section 15 ka ka and sought clarification in view of the amendment to Bank Company Act so that they can get guidance for holding AGM but the Chairman designate without giving any guideline to them replied that he was not concerned with the amendment and the Bangladesh Bank Circulars and that it should be legally dealt with by an aggrieved person. They also out of their sincerity brought to the notice of the Chairman about the pendency of two writ petitions challenging the legality and propriety of the new legislation and one of the writ petitions was being heard by this court. Therefore, they out of their sincerity informed that in the circumstances they would pray for extension of time in matter No. 60 of 2003 or in the alternative they would apply for extension of time in Matter No.2 of 2000 for holding the AGM. Therefore, by no stretch of imagination it can be said that they have committed any contempt of this Court by disregarding or violating any order of this court.

5. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, submits that from the materials on record as evidenced by annexures and the conduct of the contemner-opposite parties it is crystal clear that the contemner-opposite parties in the name of seeking advice or guideline from the Chairman designate in the matter of interpretation of section 15 ka ka flouted the order of this court for not holding the AGM of the Bank. The learned Advocate has taken me through all the annexures, that is, the letters written by the contemner-opposite parties from time to time and the letters written by Mr KZ Alam, the Chairman designate and referring to those letters the learned Advocate emphatically submits that it was repeatedly pointed out to the contemner-opposite parties by the Chairman designate that he is entrusted with the sole duty of holding the AGM of the years in question in accordance with law and the Articles of Association and, with that end in view, he repeatedly asked the contemner-opposite parties to give all assistance to call, hold and conduct the AGM for the years in question but, on this plea or that and taking undue advantage of introduction of section 15 ka ka which has nothing to do in the matter of holding the AGM, they repeatedly obstructed the course of justice by not extending their cooperation to call, hold and conduct the AGM for the years in question. The learned Advocate further submits that it was the duty of the Chairman to handle the question if at all it was raised on the floor of the meeting but that cannot be a ground for non-issuance of the notice of the AGM more so when they were repeatedly asked by the chairman designate to do so. The learned Advocate further submits that the contemners have flouted this Court's order by taking a stand that unless the situation is clarified by the chairman they cannot issue the notice. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq, the learned Advocate further submits that, no doubt, by the impugned order dated 15-4-2002 the Chairman designate was entrusted with the duty of calling, holding and conducting the AGM for the said years but nevertheless, a duty was cast upon the management of the Bank to extend all co-operation to him to hold the AGM. The learned Advocate referring to' section 2(m) of the Companies Act, 1994 and section 5(ঢ) of the Bank Companies Act, 1991 submitted that definition of Managing Director has been given in those two sections and contemner opposite party No. 1 is admittedly the Managing Director of the Bank and from the definition itself it is clear that the Managing Director does form part of the management of the Bank. Mr Huq further submits that the powers which are vested in the Managing Director by the Articles of Association also clearly indicate that he is a part and parcel of the management of the Bank. Mr Huq then refers to section 2(u) of the Companies Act, 1994 and submits that secretary as defined in that sub-section also clearly indicates that the secretary of a company holds a vital position in the company and is a part of the management. The learned Advocate then submits that those two most important persons carry on the day-to-day affairs of the Bank and the Bank is run by those two officials. As there is a duty cast upon the management of the Bank to take all necessary steps for holding the AGM as per direction of this court under the Chairmanship of the Chairman designate it was the bounden duty and legal obligation on the part of those two officials to wholeheartedly co-operate with the designated chairman but from the letters issued by the Chairman designate it is clear and obvious that repeatedly these two officials of the Bank had deliberately and willfully violated this court's order on the plea that a clarification of section 15 ka ka is necessary with which they were not at all concerned as Managing Director and Secretary of the Bank in holding the AGM for the years 1998-2000. It is further submitted by Mr Huq that the contemner-opposite parties with full consciousness had flouted the direction of this court and with malafide motive and intention has undermined the position and authority of this court and, as such, they are liable to be punished for contempt of court in accordance with law. He further submitted that the contemner-opposite parties wilfully and intentionally disregarded and disobeyed the direction given by this court in Company Matter No.2 of 2000 on 15-4-2002 and 17-5-2003. Mr Huq referring to the order dated 17-5-2003 also submitted that the so-called legal question which is posed by the contemner-opposite parties through their communication to the Chairman designate was also brought to the notice of this court and this court after full-fledged hearing by order dated 17-5-2003 extended the time for holding the AGM by 17-8-2003 and against that order neither the Bank nor any shareholder filed any petition challenging the same before the Appellate Division and thus the order dated 17-5-2003 has attained its finality and therefore, it does not lie in the mouth of the contemner opposite parties to say that due to want of clarification from the Chairman designate about the interpretation of section 15 ka ka of the Act it was not possible on their part to hold the AGM for the years in question. Mr Huq also submitted that the two writ petitions which have been mentioned by the contemner-opposite party No. 2 in his communication to the Chairman designate clearly shows that the contemner-opposite parties are bent upon obstructing the holding of the AGM and, in this way, the contemner opposite parties are flouting and disregarding the specific direction of this court. He further contended that all the attempts of the contemners were designed not to help and cooperate with the Chairman designate and not to hold the AGM under the Chairmanship of Mr KZ Alam and this is a gross contempt of court.

6. Mr Rokanuddin Mahmud, the learned Advocate, initially argued the case on behalf of the contemners. Thereafter Dr Kamal Hossain also advanced arguments on behalf of the contemner-opposite parties. The submissions made by both the learned Advocates are one and same in substance. The main contention raised by the learned Advocates for the contemner-opposite parties is that in the facts and circumstances of the case it cannot be said by any stretch of imagination that in any way the opposite parties have violated or disregarded that court's order rather they were keen to obey the order of this court and they, out of sheer sincerity and sense of duty of this Court and the Chairman designate, have brought to the notice of the Chairman designate about change in law introduced by section 15 ka ka of the Companies Act. Dr Kamal Hossain has also taken me through the letters written by the opposite parties from time to time of Mr KZ Alam, the Chairman appointed by this Court for holding AGM, and referring to those letters be submitted that very pertinent and important question of law centering round the holding of the AGM was brought to the notice of the Chairman designate and waiting for this guideline so that the AGM can be held smoothly and as per provisions of the Act but at no point of time the Chairman designate did co-operate with them nor did he ever give, at any point of time, the guideline which was essentially required to resolve the matter in the light of introduction of section 15 ka ka to the Act and the Chairman designate was required to give his opinion or guideline on the questions raised by the opposite parties to the Chairman designate. Dr Hossain further submitted, referring to the order dated 15-4-2002, that a direction of this Court was upon the Chairman designate to call, hold and conduct the AGM and at no point of time these contemner-opposite parties were ever directed by this Court to hold the AGM nor they have any statutory power under the Articles of Association of the company to do so. Dr Hossain submitted that it was not within the power of any of the contemner opposite parties and it was absolutely within the power of Chairman designate to issue any notice for calling the AGM for those years and from the correspondence it is clear that these contemner opposite parties were very much sincere to extend their cooperation to hold the AGM for the years in question. Dr Hossain further emphatically submitted that if the facts and circumstances of the case are examined by keeping the background of the case in mind it would be found that the contemner-opposite parties had never any intention to disobey the order of this court nor there was any disregard or violation of this Court's order rather they, in their own way, always tried to help the Chairman designate to call, hold and conduct the AGM for the years in question and when it appears that the Chairman designate could not or did not give any guideline on the complicated question of law and the time-frame fixed by this court expired on 17-8-2003 they thought it fit to refer this matter to the Legal Adviser of the Bank to pray for extending time either in Matter No.2 of 2000 or in Matter No. 60 of 2003 Dr Hossain then argued that from the materials on record it is apparent that the contemner-opposite parties rendered all co-operations to the Chairman designate to hold the AGM. He also submitted that at no point of time the Chairman has ever directed the opposite parties to call for the AGM. Therefore, by no stretch of imagination it can be said that they have, in any way, disregarded or flouted this court's order of either of the dates. It is also submitted by Dr Kamal Hossain that the contemners were not parties in Matter No.2 of 2000 and there was no allegation whatsoever against them in respect of the holding or delaying the holding of the AGM and he emphasised that there was no direction upon these contemners to issue any notice for calling the AGM, rather it was the duty of the Chairman designate to call, hold and conduct the AGM. Dr Hossain further submitted that under the statute and the Articles of Association of the company the opposite parties do not have any power to call the AGM of the company. Dr Hossain finally submitted that from the impugned order it is clear that the Chairman designate was entrusted with the duty to call, hold and conduct the AGM for the years in question but from the materials on record admittedly at no point of time the Chairman had ever issued any notice calling for the AGM. Therefore, in these circumstances, the opposite parties cannot be said to have violated this court's order. It is also contended by Dr Hossain that due to introduction of section 15 ka ka to the Act, and for the inaction of the Chairman designate the AGM for the years could not be held and also for pendency of Matter No. 60 of 2003 before this Court.

7. Perused the application, affidavit of explanation filed by the contemner opposite parties and affidavit-in-reply thereto filed by the petitioner. In this Rule the only question that calls for determination is, as to whether under the facts and circumstances of the case, the action/inaction of the contemner-opposite parties did amount to disregard to the order of this court dated 15th April 2002 and 17th of May, 2003 passed in matter No. 2 of 2000.

8. The bone of contention raised by Mr Rafique-ul-Huq is, that after passing of those orders the contemner opposite parties being integral part of the management of the Bank and being instrumental to holding the AGM repeatedly, deliberately and consciously avoided to cooperate with the Chairman designate for issuing the notice for holding of the AGM for the years in question. On the other hand, the contention of the opposite parties are that they had extended their whole-hearted cooperation to the Chairman in this regard.

9. The admitted position is that the contemner opposite party No.1 is the Managing Director and contemner opposite party No.2 is the Secretary of Bank. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, referring to section 2(m) of the Companies Act, 1994 submitted that the Managing Director of the company as defined in sub-section (m) of section 2 does form part of the management of a. company and referring to sub- section (u) of the said section he submitted that the Secretary, that is, the opposite party No.2, also holds a pivotal position in the Bank as Secretary of the company who plays the vital role and both of them play a vital role in running the day-to-day affairs of the Bank as part of the management. Mr Huq also referred to section 5(ঢ) of the Bank Companies Act, 1991 wherein Managing Director of a Bank Company has been defined and submitted that the contemner opposite party No. 1 does form part of the management of the company is not even denied by the contemner opposite parties in their affidavit of explanation wherein they have candidly admitted that the opposite party No. 1 is the Managing Director and, as such, he is the Chief Executive who is appointed by the Board of Directors and also admitted that the opposite party No.2 is the Secretary of the company. Drawing my attention to the order dated 15-4-2002, Dr Kamal Hossain most emphatically argued that this court directed the Chairman designate Mr K Z Alam, Bar-at-Law and Senior Advocate of this Court, to call, hold and conduct the meeting in accordance with the provisions of the Act and the Managing Director and the Secretary of the company have no statutory power for calling such meeting. It is true that the contemners have no powers to call the AGM but nevertheless it is found beyond any hesitation that these two persons are most integral part of the management of the Bank and instrumental to holding the AGM of the Bank and none can hold the AGM without their assistance and cooperation. All the records of the Bank are in exclusive possession of these two persons and it appears that Mr KZ Alam, the Chairman designate, repeatedly hammered upon these two contemners to publish a notice fixing time and place for holding the AGM. He has also requested the contemner opposite party No. 1 to get the notice approved by him before publication of the same but these two persons holding such key positions in the Bank totally non- cooperated with Mr KZ Alam. It appears to me, beyond any doubt, that in a very subtle and sophisticated way the contemners violated this court's order in the name of extending their so-called co-operation to the Chairman designate by raising some irrelevant and unwarranted questions centering round the introduction of section 15 ka ka to the Bank Company Act, 1991 by Bank Company (amendment) Act, 2003. During the course of argument Mr Huq has urged upon me that neither this new section 15 ka ka nor the writ petition challenging the legality and propriety of the legislation has any bearing upon this matter as the holding of the AGM is for the years 1998-2000. He further emphatically submitted that this question could be raised by the shareholders if they wanted to in their general meeting and it is the responsibility of the Chairman to handle the issue on the floor of the meeting and the contemners as employees of the Bank have nothing to do though they are holding key positions. No doubt, they do form part of the management but nevertheless both of them as employees of the Bank are answerable for their actions to the Board of Directors. But this does not absolve them of their legal obligation to assist the chairman designate to call, hold and conduct the AGMs in question and the contemners opted for not to co-operate with the designated Chairman. That the contemner-opposite parties have violated this court's order intentionally and deliberately is evident from their own correspondence. It appears from Annexure-X(2), a letter dated 22-7-2003, written by the Chairman designate to the Managing Director wherefrom it appears that he urged upon them to call the AGM for the three years in question pursuant to the order of this Court dated 17-5-2003 and he requested them to make all arrangement for holding the AGM within August 17, 2003 at the latest and also requested them to ensure that the accounts for the years in question are sent to the shareholders and also directed them to publish the notice in the two major national dailies, one in English and the other in vernacular, within the next two/three days and he requested them to send a draft to him for approval prior to publication of the notice with a clause that the notice will be an information to all shareholders and no objection could be taken as to non receipt of the annual report by any shareholders. On receipt of the letter dated 17-7-2003 written by the Secretary of the company, the Chairman designate Mr KZ Alam again wrote another letter wherein he, in clear terms, spelt out that his prime responsibility is to hold the Annual General Meeting of the Bank for the three years in question and the meetings must be held by the 17th of August, 2003 at the latest. But in spite of that the contemners took diametrically opposite stand in the matter which is evidenced by the letter dated 27-7-2003 written by the contemner No.2, (Annexure-'5' to the affidavit of explanation) wherein they have taken the firm stand that the AGM cannot be held unless the new section 15 ka ka is interpreted by the Court and therefore, they will apply for further extension of time. This stand taken by them clearly shows that they were determined not to hold the AGMs in question as per direction of this Court, it has already been indicated that new section 15 ka ka is prospective and it will have effect from 2003. But the AGM in question is for the years 1998-2000 and the newly introduced section 15 ka ka has no manner of application. In spite of that to delay the holding of the AGM they have raised the irrelevant question with ulterior motive. The contents of the aforesaid letter clearly show that right from the beginning these two persons were bent upon not to hold the AGM of the Bank pursuant to the order of this court and tried best to delay the calling, holding and conducting of the AGM and holding of the election of the Board of Directors. The contemners knew it well that the new section 15 ka ka is not applicable to the instant case as the same contention was, in fact, repelled by this Court on 17-5-2003 when further extension of time was allowed for holding the AGM. Thus I do not find any reason for raising that question before the chairman designate. The purpose is nothing but one i.e. to delay the holding of the AGMs. By taking the present stand in their letter dated 17-7-2003 (Annexure '5') to the affidavit of explanation) the contemners have flouted this Court's order dated 17-5-2003. The contemners again violated this Court's order by not co-operating with the chairman designate to call, hold and conduct the AGMs in question. Not only that, taking the plea of pendency of Writ Petitions , challenging the validity of section 15 ka ka they refused to co-operate with the Chairman in the matter of holding the AGMs. The evil design of the contemners is clear from yet another incident. The contemner No. 2 in his letter dated 17-8-2003 informed the chairman designate that they will pray for a further extension of time for holding the AGM but it has not been stated either by the present contempt petitioner or by the contemner opposite parties as to what further steps have been taken by them in getting the time extended for holding the AGM. But the admitted position is that after the expiry of original time for holding the AGM it is the present petitioner who filed an application for extension of time for holding AGM and on his application this Court by its order dated 17-5-2003 extended the time for further three months which expired on 17-8-2003. Neither the petitioner of Matter No. 2 of 2000 nor the Bank, as it appears, took any step till today for extending the time for holding the AGM and this clearly proves their ill motive of flouting the Court's order. It further appears that till today the Bank has not filed any application for further extension of time for holding the AGM for the years in question. Therefore, it appears that these two contemners who are now running the affairs of the Bank to help the persons who are at the helm of the affairs of the Bank did not extend their cooperation to the Chairman designate for holding the AGM for the years in question and these kinds of activities of the contemner-opposite parties are most unbecoming of them and their in actions are detrimental to the interest of the Bank. It further appears that these two contemners deliberately and intentionally to frustrate the orders passed in the Matter No.2 of 2000 have obstructed the holding of the AGM on lame excuses one after another. In their letter dated 27-7-2003, the Secretary told that they have decided to wait for the judgment of Writ Petition No. 3482 of 2003 but neither the Managing Director nor the Secretary took the step to extend the time for holding the AGM. It further appears that the contemners outstepping their authority have themselves decided to wait for the judgment of the aforesaid Writ Petition. They have no legal authority to do so. It indicates that they were acting at the instance of someone who is behind the screen. It is clear that right from the beginning till today they are desperately non-cooperating with the Chairman designate in the matter of holding the AGM though the chairman designate repeatedly requested the contemners to make arrangement for holding the AGM within the time fixed by this Court. The contemners raised so many questions centering round the interpretation of section 15 Ka Ka of Bank Companies Act but the new legislation has no manner of application in the instant case inasmuch as in Matter No. 2 of 2000 this court has condoned the delay and ordered for holding the AGM for the years in question. In spite of that with the sole motive of delaying the holding of the AGM and flouting this Court's order the contemners consistently raised, the irrelevant questions to the Chairman designate and tried their best to confuse him in holding the AGM and the Chairman designate rightly pointed out that if anyone is aggrieved by the new legislation he can resolve the question in an appropriate court but his prime duty was to hold the AGM as per direction of this Court. In spite of his repeated requests and reminders the contemner-opposite parties did not extend their co- operation for holding the AGM for the years in question. It appears that the Bank is not interested in holding the AGM as evidenced from the fact that they have challenged the order dated 15-4-2002 passed in Matter No.2 of 2000 before the Appellate Division and on their failure to get a favourable order from the Appellate Division these two contemner-opposite parties who are the key position holders in the Bank tried their best to obstruct the holding of the AGM on flimsy grounds and they, overstepping their authority, raised some illegal and irrelevant questions before the Chairman designate without coming to this Court for seeking any guidance. This fact also indicates that right from the beginning these two contemner-opposite parties were consistently and deliberately trying their best to frustrate the Court's order in holding the AGM for the years in question. By their aforesaid actions and inactions the contemner-opposite parties have willfully and intentionally flouted and disregarded this court's order dated 15-4-2002 and 17-5-2003 passed in Matter No.2 of 2000.

<u>10. On a perusal of Bank Companies (Amendment) Act, 2003 it appears that this new legislation has been introduced prospectively. Therefore, they will have no bearing upon the AGMs for the years in question but ignoring this aspect the contemner opposite parties repeatedly hammered upon the Chairman designate to give his opinion as to the interpretation of this new section and the circular of the Bangladesh Bank. Therefore, it appears to me that in the name of seeking advice or guideline from the Chairman designate on an issue which has no relevance with the holding of the AGMs for the years in question they have obstructed the course of justice and flouted this court's order.</u>

<u>11. In dealing with this case, I am not in oblivion of the fact that the power of contempt is an extraordinary power where this court acts both as prosecutor and arbiter and it is well settled that this power should be used sparingly in an extraordinary situation which warrants intervention from this court. I have also not lost sight of the fact that the contempt proceeding is a quasi-criminal proceeding and like any other criminal proceeding the contemners are also entitled to get the benefit of doubt. Therefore, to warrant conviction in a contempt proceeding allegation leveled against the contemners must be proved beyond reasonable doubt. Keeping these principles of law in mind I have weighed the materials on record and I find that in the instant case the petitioner has been able to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the contemners have willfully and deliberately violated this court's order dated 15-4-2002 and the subsequent order dated 17-5-2003 passed in Matter No.2 of 2000. In the affidavit of explanation the case of the contemners is, that they have no authority to hold the AGM of the Bank but I have already pointed out that the letter dated 27-7-2003 written by the contemner No.2 to the Chairman designate Mr KZ Alam, contemner No. 1, informed him that they have decided to wait till the disposal of the Writ Petition No. 3482 of 2003 and this fact alone establishes beyond doubt that the contemners have no or any regard for this court and they, at the instance of the persons in authority of the Bank to help them cherish their goal, flouted this court's order acting beyond their jurisdiction and therefore they have exposed themselves to be liable for contempt of court for willful violation and disregard of this court's order. It appears that right from the beginning the contemners in the name of helping the chairman designate obstructed the holding of the AGM on various baseless pleas.</u>

<u>12. In view of aforesaid discussions. I find them guilty of committing the offence of contempt of this court by disobeying and flouting this Court's orders dated 15-4-2002 and 17-8-2003 passed in Matter No.2 of 2000.</u>

<u>In the result the Rule is made absolute. Both the contemners namely, Hamidul Huq, Managing Director, and Mirza Mahmud Rafiqur Rahman, Secretary of the Board of Directors, both of United Commercial Bank Limited, having its Head Office at Federation Bhaban, 60. Motijheel Commercial Area, Dhaka, are guilty of committing contempt of this Court for violating the court's orders dated 15-4-2002 and 17-5-2003 passed in Company Matter No.2 of 2000 and sentence each of them to pay a fine amounting to Taka 2000 to be paid within one month from date, in default, each of them to suffer simple imprisonment for 15 (fifteen) days.</u>

End.

Mahmudul Islam, Attorney-General, instructed by Sufia Khatun, Advocate-on-Record------For the Respondents.

case_source: (From the Judgment and order dated 10 April 1997 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition Nos. 452 and 564 of 1994).
full_judgment:
M Reza Chowdhury J: This civil petition for leave to appeal is against the judgment and order dated 10-4-1997 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 452 of 1994 and Writ Petition No. 564 of 1994 discharging the Rules.

2. The petitioners in the said writ petitions challenged the respondent's action of challenging the original layout plan No. 53 dated 16-4-1980 and dividing 60 feet wide road on the southern side of the petitioner's plot No. 21 Road No.1, Block KA of Section 6, Mirpur and Plot No. 18 of Main Road 1 Block-KA of section 6, Mirpur. It was alleged that the action of the respondent in dividing southern Road No. 1 adjacent to the plots allotted to the petitioners into sub-plots and allotting the same to different persons blocking access from the southern road to the said plots allotted to the petitioners in violation of the original layout plan was illegal. The petitioners of the Rules having constructed building on the allotted plots with approved plan and having taken gas, water, electricity, etc connections from the said southern road, the creation of sub-plots out of the said road and allotting those to others adversely affect those connections and is illegal. It was also submitted that respondent could not violate the covenant in the lease deed and was thus estopped from creating new sub-plots depriving the petitioners from enjoying the existing facilities.

<u>3. The High Court Division examined the layout plan annexed with Writ Petition No. 452 of 1994 which showed that towards the north of commercial plot Nos. 18 and 21 and other plots was the Main Road No. 1 and in between the commercial plots and the said Main Road No.1 was a large strip of vacant land and in front of those commercial plots and part of the vacant strip of land in front of those commercial plots which had been earmarked for car parking. There was another strip of vacant land to the south of said commercial plots and to the further south adjacent to that vacant strip of land was Road No.1. It further appeared from the layout plan dated 29-10-1981 attached to Writ Petition No. 564 of 1994 that to the north of commercial plot Nos. 18 and 21 in question and other commercial plots was main road No. 1 and in between the main road No. 1 and those commercial plots was wide strip of vacant land and in front of those commercial plots towards the north part of the said vacant land there was footpath. It further appeared from the said plan that to the south of aforesaid commercial plots there was another strip of vacant land and to the further south of that strip of vacant land there was a car park and to the further south of the car park was Road No.1. From the schedule of respective lease deed of the petitioners it appears that commercial plots in question were allotted to each of the petitioners from Main Road No. 1 which is to the north of those plots and there was no mention of southern road No. 1 in the lease deeds. It is the strip of vacant land to the south of those commercial plots including plot Nos. 18 and 21 in question which has been divided into sub-plots. It was also noticed in the respective lease deeds that there was no mention of Road No. 1 in the south. The said road was not contiguous south of the concerned plot of the respective petitioners but in between the said south Road No. 1 and commercial plots in question which was a strip of vacant land. It was therefore clear that the petitioner had no access to the said southern road. Direct access of the petitioner of each of the Rules is to the main road towards the north. The High Court Division therefore found no merit in the contention of the petitioners that access to the road towards the south had been blocked by creation of sub-plots to the south of those commercial plots including the plots in question. The High Court Division also found there was nothing in the lease deed of respective petitioner to show that each of the petitioners was allowed use of the southern road. There was no assurance on the part of the lessor government respondent allowing the petitioner use of the said southern road or access thereto and, as such, the petitioner's construction of building with approved plan showing access to the south cannot be a ground for stopping the government from converting the vacant strip land to the south of those commercial plots into sub-plots and leasing out the same to others. Item 23(1V) of the lease deed says that the lessor shall always have the right and be entitled, without obtaining any consent from or paying any compensation to the tenant to deal as it may think fit with any of the lands adjoining or opposite or near to the demised property and to erect or permit to be erected thereon any building, structures, etc notwithstanding that such constructions, etc affect or diminish the light or air which might have at any time during the currency of the indenture been enjoyed by the demised property or any part thereof. In the writ petition there was no allegation of adversely affecting or diminishing light or air of the petitioner by creation of sub-plots and allotment of the same to others. Further, the allottees of the plots had not been impleaded in the two Rules and so those are bad for defect of parties.</u>

4. In those facts and circumstances the High Court Division discharged the Rule.

5. We do not find any illegality in the judgment and orders passed by the High Court Division.

The petitions are therefore dismissed.

End.
