full_judgment:
This Rule has been obtained by the defendant of a Small Cause Court suit on an application under section 25 of the Small Cause Court's Act against a decree of ejectment in favour of the opposite party No 1. The said opposite party instituted the suit for ejectment of the petitioner in the Court of Second Munsif, Rangpur sitting as a Small Cause Court Judge.

2. The plaintiff's case in brief is that the suit premises as described in the schedule to the plaint formerly belonged to Abbas Ali who has been made opposite party No. 2 in the present proceeding Abbas Ali acquired the premises in the suit from Bhupendra Narayan Roy Chowdhury, a Zamindar of Mathana Bara Taraf Estate and the land has been correctly recorded in the name of said Abbas  Ali in the recent Khatian, Abbas Ali constructed a house upon the disputed land and inducted the petitioner as a monthly tenant at a rent of Rs. 16/- per month according to Bengali Calendar. The petitioner paid rent unto Aswin 1372 B. S. to Abbas Ali on proper receipts but thereafter he defaulted in making payment of rent whereupon House Rent Control Case No. 30/55-56 was brought by Abbas Ali and the same ended in a compromise. Abbas Ali having been in need of money subsequently sold the disputed property to the plaintiff by a registered kabala dated 24-7-1967. After the purchase the plaintiff demanded rent from the petitioner who with an evil design approached the Enemy Property Authority and on misrepresentation of facts succeeded in taking settlement of the disputed premises from the Asset Custodian Enemy Property. However, on the plaintiff's representation the property was ultimately released, Grounds for ejectment are habitual default of the petitioner in regard to payment of rent as well as bonafide requirement of the suit premises for the personal use and occupation of the plaintiff. The tenancy in question has been terminated by service of notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act with effect from the 1st Baishakh, 1377 B. S.

3. The suit has been contested by the petitioner by filing a written statement in which it is contended that the suit is not maintainable in the present form, that the suit is bad for defect of parties, that it has not been properly valued that service of the notice under section 106 of the T.P. Act was not legal and valid and that there is no relationship of landlord and tenant between the plaintiff and the defendant. A contention has also been raised that the plaintiff has acquired no right, title and interest to the property inasmuch as Abbas Ali had no such title. It is the defence case on the question of title that the suit premises did not belong to Bhupendra but to Sarojini Debya from whom the defendant No. 1 have obtained a settlement of the premises in question.

4. Apart from examining himself, the plaintiff examined Abbas Ali as P.W. 1 and Aftabuddin Sardar an officer of Bhupendra Narayan Roy Chowdhury as P. W. 3 and the petitioner examined himself as a witness as well as Jitendra Nath Chakrabarty and Jitendra Nath Sarkar as two other witnesses on his behalf. A number of documents also have been proved on behalf of both parties in support of their respective contentions.

5. The learned S.C.C. Judge on consideration of the evidence on record has come to the finding that it has been sufficiently proved that defendant No.1 was induced in the suit premises by Abbas Ali, that the petitioner was a defaulter and also a refractory tenant, that the house is required bonafide by the plaintiff for his own use and occupations and that the tenancy of the petitioner has been determined by a valid and legal notice. On the basis of the aforesaid finding’s the suit has been decreed against the petitioner.

6. As against the said decree of the learned S.C.C. Judge, the present rule has been obtained on him half of defendant No. 1 under section 25 of the S. C. C. Act.

7. Mr. Ismailuddin Sarkar, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner has argued mainly two points namely, the suit is not maintainable because it involves a complicated question of title and secondly the finding of the S C. C, Judge as to the existence of the relationship of landlord and tenant between Abbas Ali and defendant No. 1 is bad in law.

<u>8. With regard to the first submission. Mr. Sarkar the learned Advocate for the petitioner, has contended that the question involved is the conflicting claims of title by Bhupendra Narayan Roy Chowdhury from whom Abbas Ali is said to have taken settlement on the one hand, and Sarojini Debya from whom defendant No 1 has asserted in this case to have obtained settlement of the disputed premises, on the other hand. As a matter of fact, a number of documents have been proved in this case in support of the rival claims of the parties. In my opinion, there has been a contusion of thought as to the nature of the present litigation, which also is responsible for the strenuous argument in the Court below as well as before this Court on the question of validity of the alleged title of the predecessors of the two parties. The suit being one between an alleged landlord and an alleged tenant for encirclement of certain rights of a landlord, the simple question which is to be tried in this suit is whether there is existence of any relationship of a landlord and a tenant. In such a case, the question of title to the premises in question is not relevant at all. If the relationship is proved in favour of the landlord, the landlord's claim cannot be resisted whatever may be the state of things regarding his title to the property. On the other hand, if the landlord fails to establish the relationship as alleged by him he cannot succeed in such a suit even if he proves his title to the property. This position of law is based upon the rule of evidence regarding the doctrine of estoppel as embodied in section 116 of the Evidence Act. If the landlord can prove that the defendant was inducted by him on the disputed premises or that the defendant has attorney to him and has continued in possession on payment of rent after recognizing him as the landlord he cannot turn round and deny the title of the said landlord at the inception of the tenancy. The question of title is thus beyond the scope of such kind of litigation and that is why Mr. Justice Chowdhury (as he then was) in the case of Ahmed Shah Vs Abdul Barkat reported in 11 DLR. Dacca, 427 has held that in a Small Cause Court suit between a landlord and a tenant, the Court has got no business to go into the question of title except incidentally for the purpose of deciding the question raised in the suit which is absolutely necessary for a decision in the case and that the tenant inducted by the plaintiff landlord cannot deny the title of the landlord during the continuance of the tenancy. Mr. Sarkar has submitted that this view of law is not correct and has cited the case of Habibur Rahman & ors. Vs Md Mansur reported in 22 D.L. R , Dacca, page 505 and has drawn my attention to the observation of the learned Simile Judge, Maksum-ul Hakim, J. who after quoting the observation of Chowdhury. J. in 11 D.L. R. 427 to the effect that a Small because Court Judge has got no business to go into the question of title except incidentally made the following comments:</u>

<u>"I regret to say that I am not in a position to accept this proposition as sound. Even in a case where the principal point is one relating of the question of determination of title, the same can be cantered and decided by a Court of Small Cause, provided the suit is otherwise friable by such a Court and does not fall outside the ambit of its jurisdiction in view of the subject-matter being included within the list of the articles mentioned in the Second Schedule of the Small Cause Courts Act".</u>

<u>9. I may say with respect that there is in fact no actual difference of opinion between the two learned Judges and those they were saving almost the same thing in two different languages. What was meant by Chowdhury, J. was that the question of title with which a Small Cause Court Judge might be faced was only incidental and not that he was never to try any question of title. In order to decide the principal cause is may have to go into the question of title and then determine a particular right, the infringement of which provides the cause of action of such a suit. From a reading of section 23 of the Provincial Small Cause Court Act, it is clear that when the determination of any right before the Small Cause Court is dependent upon proof or disproof of a title to immovable property, he may return the plaint to be filed in the Court having jurisdiction to deter mine title for a proper determination of the said question. This power is, however, discretionary, and it clearly indicates that a small Cause Court has the power to decide an incidental question of title in a suit which is essentially of Small Cause nature, in case it chooses not to return the plaint. Its decision on the question of title will not, of course, be final and therefore will not be res judicata in a suit brought before a Civil Court because, as will appear from the list of the articles mentioned in the Second Schedule of the Provincial S. C. C. Act, an S. C. C. Judge has no jurisdiction over any suit for possession other than a suit for ejectment of a tenant or a suit for determination or enforcement of any other right to or interest in immovable property.</u>

10. The determination of the issue in the present case is dependent upon a decision as to the existence of the relationships of landlord and tenant between Abbas Ali, proforma defendant No. 2 and defendant No. 1, the present petitioner and also the subsequent acquisition of the right, title and interest of the said Abbas Ali by the plaintiff, the opposite party No.1. If the relationship of landlord and tenant between Abbas Ali and defendant No. 1 is established by the evidence on record, the question of subsequent acquisition of the title of Abbas Ali by the present opposite party No. 1 can certainly be raised in this case because the claim of the plaintiff that he has stepped into the shoes of Abbas Ali depends upon the determination of the derivative title of the plaintiff from Abbas Ali which is not hit by section 116 of the Evidence Act. As a matter of fact, in the case resorted in 22 D.L R pages 505, Muksum-ul-Hakim. J. dealt with such a question. It as alleged in the said case that the defendant No.1 was a tenant under the Shebayet who was the original landlord and  the plaintiff of that suit claimed to have acquired title if the said Shebayet by a registered deed of lease coupled with a kabala in respect of the rent receiving interest and thereby acquired the right to treat the defendant No. 1 as a monthly tenant of the premises in question. Now the question of the acquisition of title by the plaintiff from the said Shebayet was challenged on the ground that the dead of title was void and ineffective and did not confer any title on the plaintiff. The learned Judge, however, did not consider the question to be a complicated one and therefore held that this, could be decided by a Small Cause Court Judge.

<u>11. In this case also the dispute as to the title of the plaintiff, i.e., the question of acquisition of title of Abbas Ali by the plaintiff might very well have been raised and such a question would have been within the competence of the Small Cause Court Judge but the dispute as to the title of Abbas Ali. i.e. the question of acquisition of title of the superior landlord by Abbas Ali need not be tried by the said Court, because if the relationship of landlord and tenant could be established between Abbas Ali and defendant No.1 the latter was stopped item challenging the existence of title of Abbas Ali. In that view of the matter I do not think that there is any question of title in this case which is beyond the jurisdiction of a Small Cause Courts Judge and I am therefore of opinion that it cannot be contended that the suit is not maintainable in a Small Cause Court. The provision of section 23 of the Small Cause Court Act does not lay down that an issue as to title renders an S C.C. suit non-maintainable as tuck, but enacts that the authority of an S.C.C. Judge to hear such a suit is discretionary. In this case the derivative title of the plaintiff does not appear to have been challenged at all. Therefore, the only question of importance before the Small Cause Court Judge was whether the relationship of landlord and tenant was established by satisfactory evidence. I may however refer to the case of Chengtue Sardar Vs Jaheruddin reported in A.I.R. 1926 Cal. 723 which has been cited by Mr. Sarkar, the learned Advocate for the petitioner. In that case it has been held that the defendant can get over title Rule of estoppel if he can show that the attorney to the landlord under some mistake or en account of some fraud. It should further be pointed out that such a mistake of fraud is to be specifically pleaded. No such case has been made out either in pleading or in evidence. Therefore, I do not find any substance in this contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioner.</u>

12. So far as the second contention is concerned, the learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the finders as to the relationship of land id and tenant is bad because it baa been arrived at in disregard of the evidence en record which is to the street that defendant No. 1 did not recognize Abbas Ali as a landlord but rather treated him as an officer of the owner, Sarojini Devi.

13. The finding of the S. C. C. Judge as to the existence of relationship of landlord and tenant is based upon Ext. 1, a certified copy of the petition filed by Abbas Ali against defendant No. 1 in the Court of the Rent Controller being House Rent Control Case No. 30 of 1955-56 for permission to bring a suit for ejectment and for arrears for rent amounting to Rs. 246/- Ext. 3, a petition of compromise filed on behalf of said Abbas Ali and the defendant No. 1 in which the dispute was compromised on condition that the defendant would pay off all arrear rent by the end of month of Flagon, Exts. 4 and 4 (a), two books containing counterfoils of rent-receipts covering the period from 7-7-56 to 29-11-65, the signature of Defendant No. 1 in these rent receipts having been marked Ext. 5 series and also a letter Ext. 6 dated 13-4-61 written by defendant No. 1 to Abbas Ali in which he was beseeching Abbas Ali to repair the but in which he had been living and also requested for an adjustment of arrear rent against construction or repair costs of the huts in case Abbas Ali himself did not arrange to effect the repair. I have looked into all these document, from which it is clear that defendant No. 1 had accepted Abbas Ali as the landlord of the premises and had been making payment of rent to him continuously for a number of years. The genuineness of these documents have never been challenged. The only case defendant No. 1 tried to make out at the time of the trial was that he took Abbas Ali as an officer of Sarojini Debya. In support of this case, he pledged merely his oral testimony at the time of the trial. He deposed in his examination in chief in the following manner:—

"Later in 1961 Abbas claimed himself as landlord I reported this to Sarejini. She asked me not to pay rent to them. So I did not pay. They tiled case under Rent Control. I appeared but had no lawyer. The case was compromised. But I compromised with a view that Abbasuddin would be merely a collector and not a landlord. They used to write names such as Abbas Ali, Arojuddin as landlords in the receipts".

In cross examination, he further said: "I can read and write English. I got counter-parts of the Murri Books Bled by the Plaintiff. I have signed the Murri Hooks (counterfoils). I signed the compromise petition Ext. 3".

14. from a consideration of the testimony of this witness along with Exts. 1, 3, 4, 4 (a), 5 series and 6 it does not appear that there is any basis for the contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioner that Abbas Ali was treated as an officer of Sarojini Debya in the contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioner that the finding which has been arrived at by the learned S. C. C. Judge is contrary to the evidence on record.

15. I should, however, mention here that the observation made by the learned S. C. C. Judge with regard to the partition deed Ext. 18 that Sarojini had already given the suit plot to Bhupendra Group is based on a misreading of the said deed. No such thing was proved by the said partition deed. But in my opinion reference to the title of the respective parties was not at all called for. I do not find any substance in any of the contentions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner and the Rule is therefore discharged with costs.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and Order dated 11-7-1969 passed by the Dacca High Court in petition No. 311 of 1967)
full_judgment:
Muhammad Abdullah Jabir J.—This appeal, by special leave, arises out of judgment and order passed by the erstwhile High Court of East Pakistan dismissing an application filed under Article 98 of the Constitution of Pakistan of 1962 by the appellants challenging the legality of an order of requisition of some plots including plot Nos. 732, 733, 734, 694 and 737 of Mouza Shahar Khilgaon, P. S. Tejgaon in L. A. Case No. 91 of 1962-63, under the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 (hereinafter referred to as "The Requisition of Property Act") and praying for a direction to derequisition certain other lands including plot Nos. 713 and 714 of the said Mouza which were also requisitioned under the said Act in L. A. Case No. 142 of 1961-62.

2. The appellant's case was that in L. A. Case No. 142 of 1961-62 an area of 4.43 acres of lands belonging to Harilal Goswami, the predecessor of the appellants and their co-sharer Motilal Goswami was requisitioned for the purpose of constructing quarters for the residence of the staff of D.I.T. (Dacca Improvement Trust) but ultimately some portions of the plots in question were only utilised for the construction of staff quarters while some others were utilised for the purpose of construction of North-South Road and the remaining portions including plot Nos. 713 and 714 were not at all utilised nor were they required for the purpose of constructing staff quarters. It is their further case that a although the scheme of the D.I.T. for construction of staff quarters had been completed and the area utilised for the purpose had been bounded and demarcated by pucca walls and the remaining vacant portions of the plots lying outside that boundary, an area of 2.39 acres of lands of some plots including plot Nos. 732, 733 and 734 belonging to Harilal Goswami and his co-sharer was requisitioned in L. A. Case No. 91 of 1962-63 for the purpose of D.I.T. staff quarters as additional lands under the Requisition of property Act and that plot No. 694 along with other lands were shown in the notice issued under section 5(1) of that Act in L. A. Case No. 91 of 1962-63. Harilal Goswami made a representation to Mr. G. A. Madani, the then Chairman of the D.I.T. who, after holding some enquiry, passed an order on 16-2-66 on the body of the sketch man, annexed to the petition, directing that the triangular plot marked 'A' therein be derequisitioned but since no action was taken in pursuance of that order, he made a representation to the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Requisition) Dacca who on the basis of the direction of Mr. Madani took the view that the area marked 'A' in the sketch map covering plots Nos. 732, 733, 734, 694 and 737 which were not required for the purpose of D.I.T. staff quarters should be derequisitioned and that plot No. 714 which was also not required for the said purpose but was sought to be used by the D.I.T. for providing alternative accommodation to the affected persons should also be derequisitioned and sought approval of the Government in this behalf. As regards the other plot, namely, plot No. 713 an observation was made that this plot which was also not required for the purpose of D.I.T. staff quarters had been irregularly allotted to a private individual, namely, Mr. Wahab, an Engineer for construction of his private house.

3. The learned Judges of the High Court dismissed the application on the findings, inter alia, that though Mr. Madani and the Additional Deputy Commissioner had expressed the views in favour of derequisition of the plots in question, the G6vernment did not accept their recommendations and, therefore, the requisition continued and there was no question of derequisitioning the same. The learned Judges also came to the finding that there was no bar against utilization for a public purpose of lands which were requisitioned for another public purpose. Thereafter the appellant filed a petition for special leave to appeal before the erstwhile Supreme Court of Pakistan which granted the leave prayed for to consider the following contentions —

(a) Since the requisitioning body came to definite findings that some portions of the requisitioned lands were nor required for the purpose for which they were requisitioned, the learned Judges should have given a direction to derequisition those portions.

(b) The lands requisitioned for a public purpose within the meaning of the Requisition of Property Act cannot be utilised for a public purpose which comes within the purview of the Town Improvement Act.

4. In order to appreciate the validity of the contentions raised in this appeal, it is necessary to state at the outset that the plots in question were requisitioned by the Additional Commissioner, Dacca under Section 3 of the Requisition of Property Act for a public purpose viz. construction of D.I.T. Staff Quarters. Upon representation of Harilal Goswami, the then Chairman of the D.I.T. passed an order on 16-2-66 directing that the triangular plot in the sketch map, marked 'A' which covered plot Nos. 694 and 734 and parts of plot Nos. 732, 733 and 737, be derequisitioned. Thereafter some of the interested persons filed petitions before the requisitioning authority for derequisition of their lands and on 19-8-66, the Additional Deputy Commissioner, Dacca recorded an order, the relevant portion of which is as follows:—

"It appears that the then Chairman D.I.T. categorically ordered that the triangular plot at 'A' in the Photostat copy be derequisitioned immediately. Plot 'A' marked in the sketch consists of plots Nos. 732, 733, 734, 694 and 737 only. As per order of the Chairman, the above plots be derequisitioned....please communicate decisions to Government for approval and endorsement. Derequisition notice be issued after obtaining Government's approval."

5. As already stated, the requisition of the plots in question were made in exercise of powers conferred under Section 3 of the Requisition of Property Act, the relevant portion of which is as follows :—

"3. When any property is required for a public purpose or in public interest, the Deputy Commissioner may requisition it by an order in writing:

Provided that the projects covering more than one district or the projects of which the requiring body is the Dacca Improvement Trust, the Chittagong Development Authority or the Khulna Development Authority, the proposal shall require the approval of the Provincial Government before proceedings under the Act is started."

6. Mr. S. R. Pal appearing for the appellant contended that the approval of the Government contemplated under the proviso of Section 3 is necessary for the purpose of initiation of proceedings for requisition of property in a case where the requiring body is the D.I.T., C.D.A., or K.D.A. but after the proceedings are initiated and the property has been requisitioned, the Government has nothing further to do and if subsequently the requisitioning authority decides to derequisition the property or any part thereof, it can do so itself without seeking approval of the Government in the mailer. In this connection he has invited our attention to the provision of sub-section (1) of Section 8 of the Requisition of Property Act which presupposes a decision to derequisition. Sub-section (1) of Section 8 is as follows:—

"8. (1) Where any requisitioned property is to be released from requisition, the Deputy Commissioner may restore it to the persons from whom the property was requisitioned or to his successor in interest or to such other person as may appear to the Deputy Commissioner to be entitled to such restoration".

7. According to the learned Counsel for the appellants, the term "project" in proviso of Section 3 of the Requisition Act is synonymous with the term "Scheme" in Sections 38, 42 and 50 in Chapter III of the Town Improvement Act, 1953 and that since the provision for construction of staff quarters, for the purpose of which the plots were requisitioned, is an "improvement scheme" contemplated under clause (e)(i) of Section 38, and which may have been sanctioned by Government under Section 50, the D.I.T. was competent to abandon under Section 92 of that Act, the plots which were not required for that improvement scheme. It is, therefore, contended that since the requiring body, namely, D.I.T. and the requisitioning authority, namely, the Additional Deputy Commissioner decided upon derequisition of the plots, the latter should have passed orders in the matter without seeking approval of Government, which was unnecessary. Reference in this connection has been made to the decision in the case of Mst. AH Begum and ors. Vs. Badrul Islam Ali Khan and others reported in A.I.R. 1938 Privy Council 184. As regards the powers of a statutory body, such as D.I.T. reference was made to para 129 at page 62 in Halsbury's Laws of England, Third Edition Vol. 9, which was as follows :—

"129. Statutory corporations.- The powers of a corporation created by statute are limited and circumscribed by the statutes which regulate it, and extend no further than is expressly stated there in, or is necessarily and properly required for carrying into effect the purpose of its incorporation, or may be fairly regarded as incidental to, or consequential upon, those things which the legislature has authorized. What the statute does not expressly or impliedly authorize is to be taken to be prohibited."

8. The learned Attorney-General appearing for the respondent contended that upon the proposal sent by the D.I.T. for requisition of lands for the construction of staff quarters, the Government under the proviso to section 3 of the" Requisition of Property Act accorded its approval to the proposal and hereafter the order of requisition was passed by the requisitioning authority under section 3 read with section 9 of the Requisition of Property Act. According to him a project contemplated under the proviso to section 3 of the Requisition of property Act is not the same thing as an improvement scheme under the Town Improvement Act because whereas an "improvement scheme" has been defined in clause (f) of section 2 of the Town Improvement Act as meaning any scheme under Chapter III but not including a rehousing scheme or a projected public street referred to in Section 69, the term "project" has not been defined in the Requisition of Property Act and a project for constructing staff quarters is not a scheme as mentioned in section 38 and other Sections under Chapter III of the Town Improvement Act. According to the learned Attorney-General, therefore, since the requisition was made, in the instant case, upon obtaining approval of the Government, in seeking approval of the Government for derequisition, the requisitioning authority cannot be said to have committed any illegality.

<u>9. The term "project" which occurs in proviso to section 3 of the said Act does not occur in section 38 or any other section under Chapter III of the Town Improvement Act which deals with an improvement scheme as defined in clause (f) of section 2 of that Act. According to clause (e)(i) of section 38 of the Town Improvement Act the Board of D.I.T. may pass a resolution to provide for, among others, "housing accommodation" and may then proceed to frame an improvement scheme and section 50 of that Act lays down that when such a scheme is submitted under Section 49 thereof, the provincial Government may sanction the same either with or without modification or may refuse to sanction the same. It does not appear nor has it been contended on behalf of the appellants, that the question relating to the construction of staff quarters was considered by the Board as a question of "housing accommodations" and an improvement scheme in respect of it was prepared by the Board under Section 38, or that it was submitted to the Government under Section 49 or that the Government sanctioned it under Section 50 of the Town Improvement Act. There is no dispute that the plots in question were requisitioned in accordance with the provisions of the Requisition of Property Act after obtaining the approval of the Government on the proposal of the D.I.T. for utilization of the same for a project contemplated under the proviso of section 3 of that Act. In the circumstances, the attempt made on behalf of the appellant to import the provisions of section 38 and other sections under Chapter 111 of the Town Improvement Act to the proceedings taken under the Requisition of Property Act and to make the term ''improvement schemes occurring in the former Act as synonymous with the term "project" occurring in the latter appears to be in exercise in futility.</u>

10. The statement of law in Halsbury's Laws of England at page 62 of Volume 9 referred to by the learned Counsel for the appellant does not come in conflict with the action of the D.I.T. in seeking approval of the Government for the construction of D.I.T. staff quarters. There is no dispute that the project in question was a public purpose for which the plots in question were requisitioned, and proviso of section 3 of the Requisition of property Act, contemplates, that for the purpose of requisition, the approval of the Government should be sought.

11. The learned Counsel for the appellants invited our attention to the following observations of the Privy Council in the case reported in AIR 1938, Privy Council, page 184, in support of his contention-

“Where the Consent in writing of the Advocate-General or Collector has been given to a suit by three persons as plaintiffs the suit cannot validly be instituted by two only. The suit as instituted must conform to the consent. On the other hand if the three persons join as plaintiffs and two of them die pending suit, the suit does not become defective or incompetent. There is no provision whatever in the Code for recourse being had to the Advocate-General or Collector during the course of a suit or of any proceedings in appeal. As subsection (2) of section 92 sufficiently shows, the consent in writing is a condition of the valid institution of a suit and has no reference to any other stage."

The appeal before the Privy Council arose out of a suit brought by respondents 1-5 with the sanction of the Collector under Sections 1 and 93 of the Civil Procedure Code for removing the appellant Mst. Ali Begum as defacto Mutwalli and for other reliefs. The suit was dismissed and 4(four) out of 5 (five) appealed to the High Court making the reaming plaintiff a respondent to the appeal. The High Court at the time of hearing made that plaintiff an appellant instead of a respondent, set aside the decree of the trial Court remanded the case to that Court for decisions whether Mst. Ali Begum should be Mutwalli and gave certain other directions whereupon she Appealed to the Privy Council and the question arose whether the appeal as brought to the High Court was competent and if not whether the defect was cured by making the respondent plaintiff an appellant. It does not appear whether the question as to the necessity of obtaining the consent of the Advocate-General or Collector in the proceedings in appeal came up for consideration. Be that as it may, the said observations do not appear to have any relevance in relation to the facts and circumstances and the law under consideration.

<u>12. The question relating to the release of requisitioned land, it is not disputed, falls within the administrative function of the requisitioning authority and if the said authority, having regard to the facts in the instant case that the order of requisition of the plots was passed by it upon approval of the proposal of the requiring body by the Government considered it necessary to seek approval of the Government before passing an order of release of the same, it does not appear how that discretion called for interference by the High Court and how the High Court could pass an order of release under the Requisition of Property Act.</u>

13. The next question that appears from the order granting leave to appeal calling for consideration was whether lands requisitioned for a public purpose within the meaning of the Requisition of property Act can be utilised for a public purpose which comes within the purview of the Town Improvement Act. This contention relates to plot No. 714, which was also requisitioned for the purpose of D.I.T. staff quarters but on account of the said plot not being required for that purpose, was sought to be utilised by the D.I.T. for another public purpose, namely, to rehabilitate persons who were displaced from their lands on account of the implementation of the project of construction of D.I.T. staff quarters. Mr. S. R. Pal contended that a public purpose under the Requisition of Property Act is not the same as a public purpose under the Town Improvement Act and since the plot was requisitioned for a public purpose under Section 3 of the former Act, it cannot be utilised for rehabilitation of the displaced persons which is a rehousing scheme contemplated under section 42 of the latter and he sought support from the decision of an English Court in the case of Gordon, Dadds & Co. Vs. Morris and others (1945) 2 A.E.L.R., 616 at 622. The learned Attorney-General, on the other hand, contended that once land is requisitioned for a public purpose under a project under the Requisitioned of property Act, it can subsequently be utilised for some other public purpose, if the project for which the requisition was made is a composite one. According to him the plan for rehabilitating the displaced persons was contemplated in the project for the implementation of which the plot along with other plots were requisitioned and that plan does not fall within the ambit of the Town Improvement Act. He has also relied upon the decision cited on behalf of the appellant.

The question that was formulated for consideration in the order granting leave to appeal was based upon the contention that the plan of the D.I.T. to utilize the plot in question for rehabilitation was a public purpose within the purview of the Town Improvement Act. The contention is based upon a presumption that the plan to rehabilitate the displaced persons was also a scheme, namely, rehousing scheme contemplated under the Town Improvement Act, we have already indicated that there is no basis for the presumption that the project relating to the construction of D.I.T. staff quarters was an improvement scheme under the Town Improvement Act. So also there is no basis for the presumption now sought to be advance. We have no material before us to hold that for the rehabilitation of the persons, who were affected, the Board prepared any rehousing scheme under section 42 of the Town Improvement Act.

<u>14. In the case of Gordon, Dadds & Co. Vs. Morris and others on which reliance has been placed by the parties, certain premises were requisitioned by an order dated September, 30, 1940 by the town clerk of the city of Westminster by virtue of powers delegated to him by the Minister of Health under the General (Defence) Regulations 1939 for the purpose of the said premises being used as a rest centre for persons rendered homeless by enemy action, when hostilities with Germany ceased, it seemed unlikely that the premises would be required any longer for the said purpose, but they were retained by the town clerk, acting under instructions of the Minister, for the temporary accommodation of evacuees. Subsequently on August 13, 1945 the Minister decided to retain possession of the premises for use as a hostel for the reception and housing of wives and children of Canadian soldiers temporarily without accommodation. The plaintiffs under a claim for purchase of the said premises requested the Minister to make arrangements for the release of the premises but the prayer was refused but they secured entry to the premises on August 22, 1945 and purported to take possession of the house. On the same day, Canadian soldiers, under the instructions of the Minister, entered the premises to prepare the house for the purposes envisaged by the Minister's decision. As a result, the plaintiffs commenced proceedings upon contentions among others that the town clerk's right to possession ceased when the premises were no longer used for the purpose for which possession was taken, and that the Ministry while relying on the town clerk's possession had not itself requisitioned the premises for other purposes and had no power to do so. The contention in that case that before the premises could be made available for use for the new purpose, possession should have been given up by the town clerk to the plaintiffs and possession then again taken upon a fresh requisition for that purpose was not accepted by the Court and it was held that where the competent authority had taken possession of land for one purpose, they were empowered by the regulation to use it or direct its use for another purpose, provided that other purpose came within the ambit of the purposes, named in the regulation, and to continue in possession for that oilier purpose.</u>

<u>15. In the instant case, on behalf of the D.I.T. an affidavit was sworn and in paras 12 and 20 thereof it was categorically stated that some area within their scheme viz the project had been kept reserved for the rehabilitation of the affected person and since that lands requestion under L.A. Case No. 142 of 1961-62 were found insufficient for the for the purpose they sough to requisition additional land which was done with the approval of the Government. This assertion could not be controverter on behalf of the appellants in their affidavit-in reply. It may be stated that plot No. 714 was requisition under L.A. Case No. 142 of 1961-62. It is therefore, evident that the idea of rehabilitation of the affected persons, was contemplated in the project which was approved by Government under section 3 of the Requisition of Property Act. The D.I.T. was accordingly competent to use the plot, if it so desired, for the new purpose, which is undoubtedly purpose, as it comes within the ambit of the public purpose for which it was requisitioned. The case of Gordon, Dadds & co. supports the contention of the learned Attorney-General.</u>

There is accordingly no merit in this appeal which is dismissed but without any order as to cost.

End.

full_judgment:
Md Habibul Gani J: On an application under Article 102 of the Constitution this rule was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the malafide action of the respondents initiating process to include the petitioners' property in the 'Ka' schedule gazette of the vested properties should not be declared to be illegal and without lawful authority and/or to pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court seems fit and proper.

2. The short facts for disposal of the rule are that the schedule property measuring an area of 0.52 acres being under CS Khatian No. 52, Plot No. 86, Mouja-Kumarkhali, District-Kumarkhali originally belonged to Yakub Meah and Yasin Meah by equal share. Subsequently Yakub Meah transferred his 8 anas share to one Latif and thereafter Latif and Yasmin transferred their share to one Suboth Chandra Laheri, who died leaving behind 4 sons. The sons of the Suboth Laheri transferred the land to one Abdul Bari in the year 1948 and since then Abdul Bari was possessing the land by paying rent to the then land lord. The SA Khatial of the said land was recorded in the name of the sons of Suboth Laheri and, as such, Abdul Bari filed Title Suit No.811 of 1969 for declaration of title and correction of SA Khatian and obtained ex parte decree on 29-11-1973 which was not challenged by any other party. Subsequently RS record was prepared in the name of Abdul Bari. Then Abdul Bari sold the properly to the petitioners vide registered deed No. 106 on 5-1-1988 and the petitioners were enjoying peaceful possession of the land by paying rent to the Government. Later the office of the land record refused to receive the land revenue showing ground that the properly in question is a vested property and included in the -kha" list. Thereafter in the year 2005 the respondent No. 4. Deputy commissioner Kushtia filed Title Suit No. 22 of 2005 before the Assistant Judge, Kumarkhali against the R.S. recorded owner Abdul Bari seeking declaration that R.S khatian recorded in the name of Abdul Bari is illegal and wrong and sough correction of the khatian but the suit was dismissed on contest on 16.05.2011.The respondent government did not file any appeal against the said dismissal of suit. Subsequently in the year 2012 the property was shown in the "kha" schedule of the gazette of vested properties published by the government under section 9 of the “অর্পিত সম্পত্তি প্রত্যার্পণ আইন-২০০১ (সংশোধিত-২০০১) (shortly Act-2001) and the petitioners filed case before the Tribunal, Kushtia for release of the property from "kha list but subsequently government in the year 2013 again amended the said Act-2001 by inserting section 28 ka in the Act by which the gazette notification in respect of "kha" schedule land of the vested properties was cancelled and government left all sorts of interest, title over the schedule "kha" property and all the suits filed for release of the "kha" schedule property were abated as per term of the second amendment of the Act-2001. The petitioners then filed application to the Assistant Commissioner land for mutating the property in the name of the petitioners and to receive land revenue from the petitioners but the same was not disposed of. Later the petitioners somehow came to know that the property in question is being processed to be included in the "ka" schedule of the gazette as vested property. The petitioners then gave a representation to the Ministry of Land and considering the application of the petitioners the respondent No. 3 Deputy Commissioner, Ministry of Land called for a report on 21-1-2014 over the matter. The petitioners then filed this application challenging the action of the respondents starting process to include the petitioners' property in the "ka" schedule gazette of the vested properties and sought direction upon the respondents not to include the same in the -ka" schedule of the gazette of the vested properties.

3. The respondent No.4 Deputy Commissioner, Kushtia by filing an affidavit-in-opposition controverted the material allegations made in the application and asserted that the property in question was listed in the Census list in the year 1965 as enemy property and subsequently it was vested upon the government as non-residence property and enemy property renamed as vested property. The property being vested property government leased out the property to Kumarkhali Degree College vide VP Lease Case No. 02(X)/1991. It is further stated in the affidavit-in-opposition that the property in question was included in the "kha schedule of the gazette in page 191299 being SI No. 13 dated 12-8-2012 and the property is now being processed to be included in the "ka" schedule of the vested property. The petitioners by procuring fabricated papers claimed the title of the property and obtained ex parte decree.

4. Mr. Jaman Akter the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner disclosing the chain of title of the petitioners submits that the property in question is in possession of the petitioners and the property was included in the "kha" schedule of the gazette as vested property on 12-8-2012 and subsequently government has left all sorts of title and interest over the '`kha" schedule property by inserting section 28ka in the “অর্পিত সম্পত্তি আইন-২০০১ vide second amendment of the Act -2001 in the year 2013 (Act 46 of 2013). Learned Advocate further submits that Ministry of Land vide circular issued under memo No. 31.00.0000.045.53. 065.12 (part)-242 dated 22-5-2014 gave some sorts of instructions in respect of mutation, opening new holdings and receiving land revenues of "kha" schedule properties under section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and the "kha" schedule properties will be treated as khash land if it is not claimed and mutated by the respective claimants within I (one) year from the date of aforementioned circular. Learned Advocate contended that the respondents ought to mutate the name of the petitioners as per circular dated 22-5-2014 and receive the land revenue from the petitioners but the respondent No. 6 and 4 defying the said circular are trying to include the property in question in the "ka" schedule of the gazette violating the provisions of law. Learned Advocate finally submits that the apprehension of the petitioners regard to inclusion of the property in question in the "ka" schedule of the gazette becomes true while the respondent No. 4 Deputy Commissioner, Kushtia in the affidavit-in-opposition clearly admitted that it is under process to include the property in the "ka" schedule of the gazette of the vested properties, as such, a direction is required upon the respondents not to include the property in question in the ka schedule gazette of the vested properties.

5. Mr. Biswojit Roy, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the respondents submits that the land in question is in Census list since 1965 as enemy property (now vested property) Learned DAG further submits that the property in question is under possession and control of the government by leasing the same to Kumarkhali Degree College vide VP Lease Case No.02(X)/91 and the lease is still continuing. The learned DAG contended that the land in question though listed in the "kha" schedule of the government gazette at page 191299 in SL No. 13 published on 12-8-2012 and though government left its title and interest over "kha" schedule land but the official record shows that the property is under control of the government and, as such, it is being processed to be included in the "ka" schedule of the gazette. Learned DAG finally contended that the property has not yet included in the "ka" schedule of the vested properties and mere apprehension of the petitioners cannot be a ground to file writ petition under Article 102 of the constitution, as such, the writ petition is premature one and the rule is liable to be discharged.

6. We have perused the writ petition, supplementary affidavit thereto, affidavit in opposition and considered the submissions of the learned Advocates.

7. It appears that admittedly the property in question was included in the "kha" schedule of the gazette in page No. 19199 as serial No. 13 published under section 9 of the “অর্পিত সম্পত্তি প্রত্যার্পণ আইন-২০০১ (সংশোধিত-২০০১) by the government and subsequently government by promulgating second amendment of the said “অর্পিত সম্পত্তি প্রত্যার্পণ আইন-২০০১) vide Act 46 of 2013 inserted section 28ka in the said Act-2001. It appears that by inserting section 28ka Government has left all sorts of right, title and interest over "kha" schedule property. For better understanding we like to reproduce the newly inserted section 28ka which runs as follows:

২৮ক। (১) অর্পিত সম্পত্তি প্রত্যার্পণ (দ্বিতীয় সংশোধন) আইন, ২০১৩ কার্যক্রম হইবার সঙ্গে সঙ্গে অর্পিত সম্পত্তি সম্পর্কিত ‘খ’ তফসিল বাতিল এবং উহা এমনভাবে বাতিল হইবে যেন, উক্ত তফসিলভুক্ত সম্পত্তি কখনোই অর্পিত সম্পত্তির তালিকাভুক্ত হয় নাই।

(২) এই আইনের অধীন স্থগিত ট্রাইব্যুনাল, আপীল ট্রাইব্যুনাল বা বিশেষ আপীল ট্রাইব্যুনাল কর্তৃক উপ-ধারা (১) এর অধীন বিলুপ্তকৃত ‘খ’ তফসিলভুক্ত সম্পত্তির বিষয়ে ইতোমধ্যে নিষ্পত্তিকৃত যে কোন মামলার রায় বা ডিক্রী বাতিল ও অকার্যকর বলিয়া গণ্য হইবে এবং উক্ত ট্রাইব্যুনাল, আপীল ট্রাইব্যুনাল বা বিশেষ আপীল ট্রাইব্যুনালে বিচারাধীন উক্ত ‘খ’ তপসিলভুক্ত সম্পত্তি সম্পর্কিত সকল মামলা abate হইয়া যাইবে এবং এইরুপ abatement  এর জন্য সংশ্লিষ্ট আদালত কর্তৃক আনুষ্ঠানিক আদেশ প্রদানের প্রয়োজন হইবে না।

(৩) উপ-ধারা (১) এর অধীন বাতিলকৃত খ তফসিল সম্পর্কিত কোন আবেদন বা নালিশ জেলা কমিটি, বিভাগীয় কমিটি বা কেন্দ্রীয় কমিটিতে যে কোন পর্যায়েই থাকুক না কেন উহা স্বয়ংক্রিয়ভাবে বাতিল হইয়া যাইবে।

(৪) উপ-ধারা (১) এর অধীন ‘খ’ তফসিল বাতিল হওয়া সত্ত্বেও উক্ত তফসিলভুক্ত সম্পত্তিতে সরকার বা কোন ব্যক্তির কোন স্বত্ব বা স্বার্থ সম্পর্কে প্রচলিত আইনের অধীন প্রতিকার লাভে কোন আইনগত বাধা থাকিবে না।

(৫) উপ-ধারা ২০ক বিলুপ্ত হওয়া সত্ত্বেও উক্ত ধারার অধীন গঠিত কোন বিশেষ আপীল ট্রাইব্যুনালে ‘ক’ তফসিলভুক্ত সম্পত্তি সম্পর্কিত কোন মামলা বিচারাধীন থাকিলে উহা এমনভাবে চলমান থাকিবে যেন, উক্ত ট্রাইব্যুনাল বিলুপ্ত হয় নাই এবং উক্ত মামলার প্রদত্ত ডিক্রী ধারা ২(ছ) এর উদ্দেশ্য পূরণকল্পে প্রদত্ত ডিক্রী হিসাবে গণ্য হইবে।

8. The Ministry of land for effective implementation of the said section 28ka further circulated Memo No. 31.00.0000.045.53.065.12 (Part) dated 22-5-2014 for mutation of the "kha" schedule land and to receive land revenue from the respective parties after scrutinizing and determining the title of the respective parties. অর্পিত সম্পত্তি প্রত্যর্পণ (দ্বিতীয় সংশোধন) আইন, ২০১৩ এর মাধ্যমে ‘খ’ তফসিল বাতিল হওয়ায় উক্ত বাতিলকৃত ‘খ’ তফসিলভুক্ত সম্পত্তির বিষয়ে জারিকৃত ২১-১১-২০১৩ খ্রিঃ তারিখের ৩১.০০.০০০০.০৪৫.৫৩.০৬৫.১২-৬১৫ নং পরিপত্র বাতিলক্রমে নিম্নরুপ নির্দেশনা প্রদান করা হলোঃ

(ক) অর্পিত সম্পত্তি প্রত্যর্পণ (দ্বিতীয় সংশোধন) আইন-২০১৩ এর ধারা অনুযায়ী অর্পিত সম্পত্তি প্রত্যর্পণ আইন, ২০০১ এ সন্নিবেশিত ২৮ক ধারার বিধান মতে বাতিলকৃত ‘খ’ তফসিলভুক্ত সম্পত্তির হোল্ডিং বৈধভাবে খোলা হয়েছিলো এবং ভূমি উন্নয়ন কর পূর্ববৎ আদায় করতে হবে;

(খ) রেজিষ্ট্রিকৃত বৈধ দলিলাদি থাকার পরেও যাদের নামে হোল্ডিং খোলা হয়নি তাদের নামে হোল্ডিং খুলে ভূমি উন্নয়ন কর আদায় করতে হবে;

(গ) আইনানুগ রেজিষ্ট্রিকৃত বিনিময় দলিলের অন্তর্ভূক্ত ভূমির ক্ষেত্রে যদি পৃথক খতিয়ান খোলা না হয়ে থাকে তবে সে সব ক্ষেত্রে দলিলের সত্যতা যাচাইপূর্বক পৃথক হোল্ডিং খুলে ভূমি উন্নয়ন কর গ্রহণ করতে হবে;

(ঘ) ‘খ’ তালিকা গেজেটে প্রকাশিত হওয়ার পূর্বেও উপযুক্ত আদালতের রায়ের প্রেক্ষিতে যে সকল সম্পত্তি অবমুক্তির আদেশ দেওয়া হয়েছে তা বাস্তবায়ন করতে হবে;

(ঙ) ‘খ’ তফসিলভুক্ত যে সকল সম্পত্তির ১/১ খতিয়ান অথবা অর্পিত সম্পত্তি হিসেবে অন্য কোন খতিয়ানে (যেমন ব্যক্তির নামীয় খতিয়ানে হাল সাং ভারত ইত্যাকারে) রেকর্ড হয়েছে তা অর্পিত সম্পত্তি প্রতর্পণ (দ্বিতীয় সংশোধন) আইন, ২০১৩ কার্যকর হওয়ার সাথে সাথে বাতিল বলে গণ্য হবে এবং উক্ত খতিয়ান বৈধ দাবিদারের নামে সংশোধন করার জন্য রাষ্ট্রীয় অধিগ্রহণ ও প্রজাস্বত্ব আইন ১৯০৫ এর ১৪৩ ধারা অনুযায়ী ব্যবস্থা গ্রহণ করতে হবে;

(চ) ভূমি উন্নয়্ন কর আদায়ের ক্ষেত্রে বকেয়াসহ হাল সন পর্যন্ত আদায় করতে হবে;

(ছ) বাতিলকৃত ‘খ’ তফসিলভুক্ত যে সব সম্পত্তির ভোগদখলকারী তাদের মালিকানায় সমর্থনে এ পরিপত্র জারির ১ (এক) বছরের বৈধ প্রমানপত্র বা দলিলাদি উপস্থাপনে ব্যর্থ হবেন, সেসব সম্পত্তি রাষ্ট্রীয় অধিগ্রহণ ও প্রজাস্বত্ব আইন, ১৯৫০ এর ৯২ ধারা মতে ঘোষণা করতে হবে;

(জ) জেলা প্রশাসক ও বিভাগীয় কমিশনারগণ রাজস্ব সম্মেলনে এ পরিপত্রে বর্ণিত কার্যক্রমের বাস্তবায়ন অগ্রগতি পর্যালোচনা পূর্বক ভূমি মন্ত্রনালয়ে নিয়মিত প্রতিবেদন প্রেরণ করবেন;

২। উপরিউক্ত নির্দেশনা অনুযায়ী জরুরী ব্যবস্থা গ্রহণের জন্য সংশ্লিষ্ট সকলকে অনুরোধ করা হলো।

৩। জনস্বার্থে জারিকৃত এ পরিপত্র অবিলম্বে কার্যকর হবে।

স্বাক্ষরিত/-

তারিখঃ ২২-৫-২০১৪ খ্রিঃ

(মোঃ ইব্রাহিম হোসেন খান)

অতিরিক্ত সচিব (আইন)

<u>9. The grievance of the petitioners is that though Government left the right, title and interest over the "kha" schedule property by inserting section 28ka in the Act-2001 and the property of the petitioners admittedly being -kha" scheduled property, the respondent No. 6 Assistant Commissioner land and respondent No.4 Deputy Commissioner, kushtia are not mutating the name of the petitioners defying the aforementioned circular dated 22-5-2014, rather, in violation of the provisions of law trying to include the property in question in the -ka" schedule gazette of the vested properties. This apprehension of the petitioners seems true while the respondent No. 4. Deputy Commissioner, Kushtia in the affidavit -in- opposition admitted that the land in question is under process to be included in the -ka" schedule of the gazette of the vested properties. This Court got no satisfactory answer from the learned DAG on the query of the court that if the property is leased out to kumarkhali Degree College under VP. Lease Case No. 02 (X)/1991 how it was included in the "kha" schedule of the gazette and further learned DAG failed to show us any provision of law that empowered the respondents to start process to include the property in question in the "ka" schedule of the gazette while government completed publication of final gazette notification of vested properties under section 9 of “অর্পিত সম্পত্তি প্রত্যার্পণ আইন-২০০১ (সংশোধিত-২০১১)” We also found nothing in the Act- 2001 that empowered the authority to publish further gazette of -ka" schedule including more properties in the schedule. However, the government can seek remedy through usual course of law under sub section 4 of section 28ka of the Act-2001 if any government interest is involved with any "kha" schedule properties even after cancellation of kha schedule gazette. There is no scope in the law to include any more property in the "ka" schedule by publishing further gazette. Now-a-days it is a very common allegation that the Assistant Commissioners (land) are very reluctant to receive and dispose of the mutation application of the parties filed under section 143 of the State Acquision and Tenancy Act and further they are keeping pending mutation applications for uncertain period. The Assistant commissions (land) are assigned by the Government in the land revenue offices to render services to the public in accordance with law. They should not create unnecessary hassle or harass the people at large. The respondents should not act arbitrarily but to proceed in accordance with law while dealing with a mutation proceeding. We find that the petitioners have filed an application under section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 to the respondent No. 6, Assistant Commissioner land, Kumarkhali which was received by his office on 14-11-2014 (Annexure 'D' to the writ petition) for mutation but the said application was not disposed of nor any mutation case number was given to start mutation proceeding. It is the statutory duty of the concern officer to dispose of the application under section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 read with rule 23 of the State Acquisition Rule, 1955. We have already discussed above the legal proposition of law in dealing with the "kha" schedule properties. In the premises discussed above we think it will be fit and proper to direct the respondent No.6 to dispose of the application for mutation already received by the office of the respondent 6 on 14-11-2014 (Annexure-D) in accordance with law.</u>

10. In that view of the matter the respondent No. 6 Assistant Commissioner land, Kumarkhali is hereby directed to dispose of the application for mutation received by its office on 14-11-2014 (Annexure `D' to the writ petition) within 45 days from the date of receipt of this Judgment keeping in mind the legal proposition as discussed above.

Accordingly, this rule is disposed of.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated the 8th day of November, 2012 passed by the Appellate Division in Civil Appeal No. 132 of 2006).
full_judgment:
Md. Abdul Wahhab Miah J: The delay in filing the petition is condoned.

2. This civil review petition has been filed by the appellant for reviewing the judgment passed by this Court on 8th November, 2012 in Civil Appeal No. 132 of 2006 dismissing the appeal by majority. The said civil appeal arose from the judgment and order dated 19-4-2005 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1910 of 2003 making the Rule absolute.

3. Facts necessary to dispose this review petition are that respondent Nos. 1-6 as the plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 252 of 1979 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Second Court, Dhaka for declaration that they were the sixteen annas owners of the suit plot on the averment, inter alia, that plot No. 41 of Road No. 15, section 13 (old) New-3 of the Layout Plan of Uttara Residential Model Town measuring 612 square yards and 6 square feet (hereinafter referred to as the suit plot) of the then DIT, at present RAJUK, was allotted to one Mrs Khaleda Rahman, wife of Md Mujibur Rahman and a standard lease agreement was executed on 12-1-1970 and registered on 12-2-1970 on payment of full premium amounting to Taka 19,029.94 and possession was handed over to the allottee along with a sketch map showing the location of the suit plot. The aforesaid allottee, after getting delivery of possession enjoyed the suit plot from 12-12-1970 to 24-10-1998 by exercising all acts of possession through her caretaker and being in urgent need of cash money, obtained income tax clearance certificate vide TP Certificate No. 139/87-88 dated 1-6-1988 from the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes Circle-"P" and transferred the suit plot to the predecessor of the plaintiffs, namely: Amanullah on payment of transfer fee and service charges amounting to Taka 1,72,313 and Taka 886 respectively after obtaining necessary permission from RAJUK vide their letter No. RAJUK U-PA(A).173-Stha dated 24-1-1988. The transaction was complete between the vendor and the vendee in presence of defendant No. 2 and nothing was left to be done from their part as per the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. After purchase of the suit plot from the original allottee, the predecessor of the plaintiffs had to stay in the United States of America and in the European Countries for quite a long time for the purpose of business as well as for treatment and kept the suit plot under the custody of his caretaker. In the meantime, defendant No.1 brought some bricks and sand to make some construction therein and while the plaintiffs predecessor protested, defendant No. 1 fled away and did never come forward. Thereafter, the plaintiffs 'predecessor fell seriously sick and ultimately died leaving behind them to inherit his property. Getting knowledge of the death of the true owner of the suit plot, defendant No. 1 again "stepped in the scene and tried to start making construction " in the suit plot and when the plaintiffs lodged heavy protest, defendant No. 1 stated that he got allotment from defendant No. 2 (in the plaint, it has wrongly been written as defendant No. 1). Getting vibe of allotment, the plaintiffs sent a letter to defendant No. 2 on 29-4-1997 which was received by him by putting original seal and signature, but he did not give any reply. Neither defendant No.1 got any right and title in the suit plot nor did defendant No. 2 get any right to re-transfer the same to anybody including defendant No. 1. No notice was served either upon the plaintiffs or their predecessor or on the original allottee "so far in respect of the suit land stating violation of the terms of lease agreement" and, as such, if anything was done beyond the knowledge of the plaintiffs or their predecessor that will be simply illegal, ultravires and against the principle of equity and good conscience. The cause of action for the suit first arose on 25-7-1997 and again on 15-8-1997 when defendant No. 1 verbally stated about getting allotment of the suit plot from defendant No.2 within Police Station-Gulshan and under the jurisdiction of the Court.

4. After filing the suit, the prayer was amended deleting the word "owner" by replacing the words "Lease hold right holder " and further prayer was added to the effect "and cancellation of lease if any in respect of the suit plot is illegal, malafide and not binding upon the plaintiffs. "

5. The suit was contested by the defendants by filing separate sets of written statement. In the written statement filed by defendant No. 1, it was contended, inter alia, that he was allotted plot No. 79 at Road No. 18 Sector-7, in Uttara Model Town, Dhaka by DIT, in 1984. The said plot was a small one being more or less than 3 (three) kathas land. The defendant having a large family, the said plot was considered to be not suitable for his purpose and, as such, he applied to the Chairman, RAJUK for a bigger plot preferably in its Baridhara Project and in the said application, all relevant facts including the allotment of the aforesaid Uttara plot to him were disclosed vividly. Then RAJUK allotted a five kathas plot to him at Baridhara on 1-1-1986. Subsequently, by a letter dated 26-8-1986, RAJUK cancelled the allotment of Baridhara plot. In the said circumstances, the defendant filed Writ Petition No. 241 of 1991 before the High Court Division "which was accepted" and operation of the order of cancellation of Baridhara plot was stayed. Thereafter, on 12-12-1995, the defendant filed an application to defendant No. 2 for allotment of a bigger plot above 7 (seven) kathas in Uttara Model Town in exchange of the earlier 3 (three) kathas plot. In reply, RAJUK by its letter dated 6-1-1996 informed the defendant that his prayer for allotment of a bigger plot at Uttara Model Town could not be considered till disposal of the said writ petition. The defendant, therefore, filed an application before the High Court Division for withdrawal of the said writ petition and the application for withdrawal was allowed on 24-1-1996. The defendant filed an application to defendant No. 2 on 4-2-1996 with the certified copy of the order dated 24-1-1996 passed by the High Court Division praying for expeditious allotment of a bigger plot in Uttara Model Town. On the prayer of the defendant, defendant No. 2 allotted the suit plot comprising an area of 7 kathas, 10 chhataks and 23 square feet on completion of all legal formalities and a standard lease deed was executed on 23-9-1996. Originally, the suit plot was shown measuring an area of 3 (three) Kathas, but subsequently, by measurement, it was found that actually, the area of land was 7 (seven) kathas, 10 chhataks and 23 square feet equivalent to 5513 square feet and therefore, an excess of 4 kathas, 10 chhataks and 23 square feet was there in the plot. Accordingly, the price of the said excess land of 4 kathas, 10 chhatacks and 23 square feet was fixed at Taka 2,72,556 and the defendant was directed by RAJUK under cover of letter dated 9-6-1996 to deposit the said amount as price of the excess land by 20-7-1996. The defendant, accordingly, deposited the said amount in Sonali Bank, RAJUK, Bhaban Branch, Dhaka by voucher No.6186 dated 23-6-1996. The defendant got his name mutated and paid rents from 139C BS up to 1403 BS. The possession of the suit plot was duly delivered to the defendant by RAJUK and since then he has been in possession thereof by demarcation and specification as a bonafide lessee under RAJUK without any notice of the alleged right of the plaintiffs or their predecessor as claimed by them.

6. After amendment of the plaint, defendant No.1 also filed an additional written statement stating, inter alia, that the plaintiffs are neither owners nor they have any lease hold right in the suit plot. The original allottee, Mrs. Khaleda Rahman, having failed to transfer the suit plot within 4 (four) months in favour of Amanullah Mia, predecessor of the plaintiffs and not having deposited the certified copy of the "Deed purported to be executed by her in the office of RAJUK" as directed in RAJUK's letter dated 26-6-1988, the transfer permission stood cancelled. The lease of the suit plot in the name of the original allottee, Mrs Khaleda Rahman, on the basis of the standard lease agreement dated 12-1-1970 registered on 12-2-1970 having been cancelled by RAJUK long before the filing of the instant suit and the suit plot having been allotted to the defendant and the lease deed having been executed in his favour on 23-9-1996 for valuable consideration then registered by RAJUK before institution of the suit, the amended prayer of the plaintiffs was not entertainable. The lease having been cancelled due to the failure of the original allottee to make construction on the suit plot within the specified time, she ought to have challenged the cancellation of the lease. The plaintiffs had no legal right and authority to challenge the cancellation.

7. Defendant No. 2 in his written statement contended, inter alia, that the plaintiffs did not file any agreement, affidavit and certified copy of the registered document within the stipulated time of 4 (four) months from 26-6-88 and as a result, RAJUK cancelled the allotment of the original lease on 22-5-1995. After cancellation of the original lease, the suit plot was allotted to defendant No. 1 observing all formalities.

8. Eventually, the suit having been transferred to the Court of Sixth Additional Assistant Judge, Dhaka was renumbered as Title Suit No. 129 of 1999. At the hearing of the suit, the plaintiffs examined three witnesses including plaintiff No. 1 and filed documents which were marked as exhibits. On behalf of defendant No. 1, two witnesses including defendant No. 1 himself and on behalf of defendant No. 2, superintendent of RAJUK was examined as DW 3. The learned Assistant Judge by his judgment and decree dated 12-7-1999 dismissed the suit.

9. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree of the learned Assistant Judge, the plaintiff-respondents filed Title Appeal No. 520 of 1999 before the District Judge, Dhaka. The learned Additional District Judge, Second Court, Dhaka by his judgment and decree dated 8-2-2003 dismissed the appeal and affirmed those of the learned Assistant judge. Against the said judgment and decree of affirmance, the plaintiffs filed Civil Revision No. 1910 of 2003 before the High Court Division. A Single Bench hearing the revision by the judgment and order dated 19-4-2005 made the Rule absolute setting aside those of the Courts below and directed RAJUK to mutate the suit plot in the name of the petitioners after perusal of the documents filed by them before it and to cancel the subsequent allotment of the suit plot to opposite party No. 1 (defendant No.1). Against the judgment and order of the High Court Division, defendant No.1 filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 884 of 2005 before this Division and leave was granted on 16-8-2006 giving rise to Civil Appeal No. 132 of 2006.

10. This Division by the judgment sought to be reviewed dismissed the appeal with modification of the ordering portion of the High Court Division in the following terms:

"It appears from the operative part of the judgment of the High Court Division that though it made the Rule absolute and set aside "the judgments of the Courts below", it did not say anything about the fate of the suit and, as such, the operative part of the judgment of the High Court Division needs to be corrected as well by invoking the same power (in the appeal power vested in this Court under article 104 of the Constitution was invoked for doing complete justice). Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed. The suit is decreed. It is declared that the plaintiffs have sixteen annas lease hold interest in the suit plot. The cancellation of lease deed executed on 12-1-1970 in favour of Mrs. Khaleda is declared illegal and void and it is further declared that the lease deed executed and registered by RAJUK in favour of defendant No. 1-appellant in respect of the suit plot is illegal and not binding on the plaintiffs. The other order/direction of the High Court Division except "and cancel the subsequent allotment of the suit plot to opposite party No. 1" is maintained."

11. Now the appellant wants to review this judgment on the following grounds:

"I. For that the impugned judgment and decree are liable to be reviewed for the apparent error of law and fact in as much as the plaintiffs do not and cannot claim more than 3 (three) katha (612 square yards and 6 square feet), and, as such, the impugned Judgment is required to be modified by way of review expressly mentioning therein to the effect that right, title, interest and possession of Defendant No. 1 (present petitioner) upon 4 (katha) 10 chhataks 23 sft of land out of 7 (seven) kathas 10 chhatacks 23 sft of land covered by. Registered Sale Deed dated 23-9-1996 will not be affected and Defendant No. 1's title to and possession in the said quantum of land shall remain intact.

II. For that having regard to the continuous possession of the petitioner (defendant no. 1) in the suit plot which is further evidenced from the utility bills and security company bills for the last 1 (one) year as contained in the additional paper book, the majority decision as to the maintainability of the suit without prayer for recovery of possession is required to be reviewed."

<u>12. Heard Mr. Probir Neogi, learned Counsel for the petitioner, perused the judgment sought to be reviewed and the other materials on record. We do not find any mistake or error apparent on the face of the record in the judgment calling for reviewing the same dismissing the appeal with the modification of the decree of the High Court Division as quoted hereinbefore. Mr. Probir Neogi also failed to show any mistake or error apparent on the face of the record in the judgment sought to be reviewed so far as it relates to the dismissal of the appeal. Of the two grounds taken in the review petition so far as ground No. II is concerned, it is basically a question of fact and this Court on threadbare discussions of the evidence on record clearly found that it is the plaintiffs who are in possession of the suit plot. So there is no scope of re-opening the matter by way of review as there is no scope of re-hearing on a question of fact in a review petition already decided, because hearing a review petition is not re-hearing the appeal. However, Mr. Probir Neogi has stressed very much upon ground No. 1. In this ground, it has been stated that the plaintiffs did not claim more than 3 (three) kathas (612 square yards and 6 square feet) land and, as such, the judgment sought to be reviewed is required to be modified by expressly mentioning to the effect that the right, title, interest and possession of defendant No. 1, i.e. the present petitioner upon 4 kathas, 10 chhataks and 23 square feet land out of 7 kathas, 10 chhataks and 23 sft land covered by registered sale deed dated 23-9-1996 would not be affected and defendant No. 1's title to and possession in the said quantum land shall remain intact. By taking this ground the defendant No.1-petitioner has, in fact, sought declaration of his right, title, interest and possession in respect of 4 kathas, 10 chhataks, 23 sft land in the suit plot. But in a suit brought by the plaintiffs, this Court cannot give a declaration of the defendant's right, title, interest and possession as claimed in the ground. Moreso, when this Court gave clear decision that the lease deed executed and registered by RAJUK in favour of the petitioner (defendant No. 1) in respect of the suit plot was illegal and not binding on the plaintiffs and further, such a case was never made out by defendant No. 1 at any point of time.</u>

13. The schedule to the plaint was as under:

"SCHEDULE

Plot No. 41, Road No. 15, Sector No. 13 (old) New. 3 of the layout plan of the Uttara Residential Model Town within Mouja Faidabad, PS Uttara, District Dhaka measuring 612 square yards and 6 sq. ft."

14. The area of the land as mentioned in the schedule to the plaint comes to 3 kathas land. Therefore, the plaintiffs cannot get a decree more than the land described in the schedule to the plaint. In the judgment sought to be reviewed, we have given clear finding that defendant No. 1 (the present petitioner) did not get possession of the land allotted to him after cancelling the lease of the plaintiffs vendor; Mrs. Khaleda Rahman.

15. However, to secure the ends of justice, the ordering portion of judgment of this Court is modified adding the words "as described in the schedule to the plaint quoted hereinbefore" after the words "in the suit plot" and if there is any excess land in the suit plot, ie more than 612 square yards and 6 sft as claimed by the plaintiffs, they shall have no claim therein. It is the RAJUK to decide whether defendant No. 1 petitioner would get the excess land in the suit plot, if there be any, if so advised, the petitioner may approach the RAJUK to ventilate his grievance. But we make it very clear that RAJUK shall not in any way encroach upon the land of the plaintiffs as described in the schedule to the plaint quoted hereinbefore.

With the above modification of the ordering portion of the judgment sought to be reviewed, this petition is disposed of.

End.
